## BigCommerce Platform Overview and Market Focus

BigCommerce can be best described as an ecommerce platform that is enterprise-ready and is based on the concept of ‘open SaaS,’ which is the combination of infrastructure with flexibility enabled through APIs. At its core, the platform is centered around the idea of having a centralized admin section to control catalogs, orders, customers, and storefronts, with the ability to support both traditional and headless approaches through the likes of Stencil and Catalyst, as well as the support for REST and GraphQL APIs.

BigCommerce’s market narrative is distinct: it emphasizes “open SaaS” and enterprise-grade capabilities for both B2C and B2B, with multi-storefront and headless options as first-class patterns. Its corporate parent rebranded as Commerce.com, Inc., framing growth around AI-powered “agentic commerce” and ecosystem solutions. Commerce/BigCommerce reported [$342.3M](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/CMRC/commerce-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-year-2025-financial-guawgkq5fapj.html) total revenue and $31.7B GMV for fiscal year 2025, plus an ARR of $359.1M and 6,648 enterprise accounts as of December 31, 2025 — signals of its heavier weighting toward enterprise customers and subscription economics.

![The Shopify Platform Overview and Strategic Positioning](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%20824%20348%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Shopify Capabilities in Detail

Shopify’s capabilities shine when you want a cohesive admin experience, fast launch, and a deep catalog of third-party (and increasingly native) functionality — from marketing automations to AI — without running infrastructure yourself.

Core features and commerce infrastructure

Shopify frames itself as an “all-in-one commerce platform” that supports selling online, in-store, and across channels, with product/inventory/payments/shipping and marketing components available from one admin.

Its POS positioning is similarly “unified”: Shopify’s own pricing page explicitly states the online store synchronizes with Shopify POS and that inventory/product/payment updates apply in POS.

For developers and modern architectures, the platform supports both themed storefronts and headless builds. Shopify’s own guidance explicitly references going headless with Hydrogen and using Shopify APIs for custom stacks.

Shopify’s headless stack continues evolving: the Hydrogen update notes storefront support for “Storefront MCP” intended to enable AI assistants using real-time store data via the Storefront API.

![Core features and infrastructure](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Pricing structure and growth tiers

Shopify’s published 2026 plan pricing (as summarized on Shopify’s own site) lists: Starter $5/month, Basic $27/month, Grow $72/month, Advanced $399/month, and Shopify Plus $2,300/month. Shopify also states it offers 25% off yearly subscriptions for Basic/Grow/Advanced, and that Shopify Plus is available on 1- or 3-year terms. A critical pricing rule: Shopify charges third-party transaction fees when you use an external payment provider (not Shopify Payments), and the pricing page lists 2% (Basic), 1% (Grow), 0.6% (Advanced).

![Pricing structure growth tiers](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Strengths that drive adoption

Shopify’s biggest advantage is the ecosystem flywheel: the platform advertises “over 16,000 apps,” and Shopify’s developer changelog states merchants have “more than 16,000 apps to choose from” and that Shopify paid out “more than $1B” to developers in the prior year — evidence of a large, economically meaningful partner ecosystem. Shopify is also pushing deeper into AI-native operations.

Shopify’s help center describes Shopify Magic as a suite of free AI features integrated across workflows, and Sidekick as an AI-enabled commerce assistant powered by Shopify Magic. This matters on busy teams because content generation, analysis, and workflow assistance are increasingly “built-in” rather than purely app-based — all inside the same admin surface. Automation is another strong area: Shopify’s help center explicitly routes custom marketing automations into Shopify Flow and notes eligibility (store must be on Basic or higher, with Flow installed for full functionality).

![Limitations consider at scale](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Limitations to consider at scale

Shopify’s ecosystem strength can result into ecosystem complexity. Shopify itself highlights that apps are how you extend beyond “the basics,” which is powerful — but it also means governance (app bloat, overlapping functionality, vendor management, and incremental subscription fees) becomes part of operations. At the technical-SEO level, Shopify has notable structural constraints.

A Shopify community response (from a Shopify staff/partner forum context) states that Shopify’s URL structure cannot be changed via the admin and that code-based workarounds aren’t something Shopify would support directly. Shopify does allow editing robots.txt via robots.txt.liquid, but that’s still theme-level control rather than full server-side control. Finally, payment economics can be a scaling factor: if a merchant uses third-party processors (by choice or because Shopify Payments isn’t available for their business location), Shopify’s third-party transaction fees can become substantial at high GMV.

![Strengths that drive adoption](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## BigCommerce Capabilities in Detail

BigCommerce’s strengths center on native capability depth, flexible architectures (including headless), and a pricing philosophy that avoids platform-level transaction fees — while still enforcing growth tier thresholds based on annual online sales.

Core features and native functionality

BigCommerce’s native capabilities support advanced merchandising strategies, including customer-specific pricing, segmentation, and faceted search for large and complex catalogs. Its Multi-Storefront solution page describes managing multiple storefronts from one dashboard and lists capabilities such as connecting distinct domains/SSL, setting default currency, customizing emails, and building customer-specific pricing using price lists and customer groups.

A 2022 corporate press release frames Multi-Storefront as enabling enterprise merchants to manage multiple storefronts in a single BigCommerce store and notes storefronts can be Stencil-based or headless (e.g., using Next.js) and even mixed within one account. In headless commerce, the platform is aggressively productizing the front-end. BigCommerce’s Catalyst page describes Catalyst as a headless storefront framework built with Next.js and React, powered by BigCommerce APIs, and claims “Google Lighthouse score of 100” out of the box. Complementing that, BigCommerce promotes its GraphQL Storefront API as enabling core shopper-journey capabilities (customer login, address management, orders, reviews), with examples of this being used in Catalyst.

![Core features and infrastructure](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Pricing model and revenue thresholds

BigCommerce publishes clear monthly list pricing in USD: Standard $39, Plus $105, Pro $399, with Enterprise being custom. Unlike Shopify’s transaction-fee model, BigCommerce states it does not charge transaction fees on top of plans or based on which processor you use. The important structural nuance is revenue thresholds and automatic upgrades. BigCommerce states “online sales per year” thresholds (trailing 12 months) of $50k (Standard), $180k (Plus), $400k (Pro), with Enterprise being custom. It also explains automatic upgrades and incremental pricing above Pro: once you exceed thresholds you are upgraded, and for every additional $200,000 beyond the Pro allowance, there is an added $150/month charge until Enterprise discussions.

![Pricing structure growth tiers](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Competitive advantages

BigCommerce’s “native depth” is represented in their plan matrix, which includes features such as customer groups, segmentation, abandoned cart saver, persistent cart, credit card storage, faceted search, and price lists. BigCommerce is also showing their API capabilities as a key integration enabler with features such as “Unlimited API Calls” and using APIs to sync data from external systems such as ERPs. With SEO, BigCommerce’s product SEO page highlights their features such as microdata support (“rich snippets”), automated redirects and URL rewrites, unique URLs to avoid duplicate content issues, and editing their robots.txt file. This is a compelling combination, especially in scenarios where SEO needs are high and engineering support is lacking.

![Limitations consider at scale](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Potential constraints

BigCommerce’s biggest operational constraint is that scaling can trigger plan threshold mechanics. The platform is transparent about trailing-12-month sales limits and automatic upgrades, but these mechanics can still create budgeting friction for fast-growing stores (especially those with spiky seasonality). Also, while BigCommerce has an app ecosystem, it tends to advertise this in terms of “hundreds of apps” rather than the five-figure sum that Shopify emphasizes, so there is potentially a greater choice available on Shopify.

![Strengths that drive adoption](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%2040%2040%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Shopify vs. BigCommerce: A General Comparison

The following table is a side-by-side comparison of some of the key differences between Shopify and BigCommerce, which will enable you to quickly compare which of these options is best for your business model and needs.

| Dimension | Shopify (2026) | BigCommerce (2026) | What typically wins |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ease of use** | Unified admin + fast launch positioning | Product-tour-driven “build/manage with ease” message; strong admin focus | Shopify often for speed-to-launch; BigCommerce often for complex catalogs/ops |
| **Built in features vs apps** | “Covers the basics…for everything else, there’s apps” (16k+) | Many mid-market features included in plans (segmentation, faceted search, etc.) | Shopify for ecosystem breadth; BigCommerce for native feature depth |
| **Customization & flexibility** | Theme customization with Liquid + headless via Hydrogen/APIs | Stencil themes + Catalyst ([Next.js](/services/technologies/next-js-development-services/)) headless | Headless-first teams often like BigCommerce; Shopify is strong if you want Hydrogen |
| **SEO & technical control** | robots.txt.liquid editing allowed; URL structure largely fixed | SEO tooling: microdata, redirects, URL rewrites, robots control messaging | BigCommerce typically for tighter SEO control without workarounds |
| **Payments & fees** | Third-party transaction fees if not using Shopify Payments | No platform transaction fees; 55+ providers | BigCommerce often wins on fee predictability with 3rd-party gateways |
| **Total cost** | Base plan + apps + possible 3rd-party transaction fees | Base plan + possible forced upgrades at revenue thresholds | Depends on your margins + payment routing + growth curve |
| **Automation** | Marketing automations route into Shopify Flow | Automation more integration-led; strong API orientation | Shopify for “workflow builder” convenience; BigCommerce for API-driven ops |
| **Headless & APIs** | Hydrogen + Storefront API; AI-assistant storefront hooks announced | Catalyst + GraphQL Storefront API; composable focus | Either works; pick based on dev stack preference and governance |
| **Multi-store & multichannel** | Plus supports 9 expansion stores (10 total) | Multi-Storefront management is a flagship capability | BigCommerce often for many storefronts under one roof; Shopify Plus for expansion-store model |
| **B2B features** | Growing native B2B features; payment terms docs exist | B2B Edition and plan-level price lists, segmentation | BigCommerce frequently chosen for built-in B2B depth; Shopify for unified B2B+DTC when on Plus |
| **Enterprise scalability** | Plus adds expansion stores, priority support, unlimited staff | Enterprise adds unlimited API calls, multi-storefront, enterprise services | Both scale; decision usually turns on architecture + ops model |
| **International selling** | Managed Markets sells to 150+ countries; Global-e handles complexities | Multi-storefront and multi-currency selling messaging; enterprise has multi-currency transact/settle | Shopify for “merchant-of-record style” add-on; BigCommerce for multi-store operational segmentation |
| **Promotions & pricing** | Discounts: codes + automatic discounts; gift card handling documented | Coupons/discounts/gift cards are listed in enterprise feature set | Roughly comparable; differences are in edge cases and admin workflows |
| **Integration ecosystem** | 16k+ apps; partner payout economics disclosed | “Hundreds of apps” + strong partner orientation | Shopify usually wins on breadth; BigCommerce is strong for core enterprise tools |
| **Technology partnerships** | Ecosystem-driven composability narrative | Catalyst ecosystem includes modern partners and tooling references | Depends on your existing martech/tech stack |
| **Point of sale** | Native POS integration; sync promise described on pricing page | POS integration product page; “never charges additional transaction fees” | Shopify often wins for a single-vendor POS+ecom; BigCommerce wins if you want POS freedom |
| **Customer segmentation** | Flow supports segments/tags; segmentation strongly app-extendable | Customer groups/segmentation is a plan feature | BigCommerce for built-in segmentation; Shopify for segmentation + ecosystem depth |

## Enterprise Comparison: Shopify Plus vs BigCommerce Enterprise

The following table illustrates the main differences between Shopify Plus and BigCommerce Enterprise in the areas that are most important for a large-scale ecommerce operation.

| Category | Shopify Plus | BigCommerce Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Product management** | Unified admin for products, inventory, and omnichannel sync (including POS); extensible via apps | Strong native catalog management with segmentation, price lists, and multi-storefront product control |
| **Multi-store model** | Up to 10 stores (1 main + 9 expansion) under contract, with eligibility rules | Multi-Storefront marketed as multi-brand/geo/segment capability from one dashboard |
| **Admin experience** | Highly cohesive and user-friendly admin optimized for speed and ease of use across teams | Admin designed for complex operations, with more built-in controls for multi-store, B2B, and segmentation workflows |
| **Performance** | Optimized SaaS infrastructure with fast deployment; performance can depend on apps and theme complexity | Headless-ready architecture (Catalyst, APIs) with strong performance potential and modern frontend frameworks |
| **API / extensibility** | Strong API + headless support; Hydrogen + [AI](https://sam-solutions.com/services/ai-software-development/) storefront roadmap | Enterprise plan references unlimited API calls and headless/composable roadmap via Catalyst |
| **Fees** | Third-party transaction fees depend on payment setup; Shopify documents fee mechanics | No platform transaction fees; BigCommerce states 0% transaction fees |
| **B2B posture** | B2B features expanding; payment terms and B2B workflows documented | B2B Edition positioning + native segmentation/price lists support |
| **Security and compliance** | Shopify is PCI DSS Level 1; compliance reports available | Trust center lists ISO certifications and NIST alignment; SOC reports messaging exists |

## Real World Examples and Use Cases

Real-world fit is easier to understand when you separate platform choice by operating model: high-velocity DTC campaigns, omnichannel retail, multi-brand portfolios, or B2B catalogs with customer-specific pricing and purchasing workflows.

Brands using Shopify

Shopify’s investor materials cite enterprise adoption by naming brands such as Aldo, BarkBox, Carrier, SKIMS, Supreme, and Vuori. The key takeaway is less about the logos and more about the pattern: Shopify is positioning itself as capable of supporting both independent businesses and large brands on a single commerce foundation.

Brands using BigCommerce

BigCommerce’s official communications cite brands such as Ben & Jerry’s, Molton Brown, S.C. Johnson, Skullcandy, Solo Stove, Ted Baker, and Vodafone as examples of companies using the platform. BigCommerce also highlights multi-storefront adoption in its product announcements, including a case example featuring Bullitt Group leveraging Multi-Storefront for localized experiences.

B2C use cases

Shopify is often a strong fit when you want to launch fast, run frequent campaigns, and rely on a large marketplace of specialized extensions (reviews, subscriptions, loyalty, CRO tooling, personalization, etc.). Shopify explicitly frames apps as the path to customization beyond core features. BigCommerce tends to be compelling for B2C retailers with larger catalogs and higher operational complexity that benefit from built-in capabilities like faceted search, stored cards, segmentation, and multi-storefront governance.

B2B and wholesale use cases

For B2B, the differences are clearer:

1. Shopify is building tighter native B2B operations inside the platform, with documented workflows like payment terms and published enterprise updates focused on unifying B2B processes.
2. BigCommerce markets B2B Edition and plan-level tools (price lists, customer groups/segmentation) that directly support customer-specific pricing and catalogs behind logins — classic wholesale requirements.

If your business runs both DTC and B2B, the deciding factor is often whether you want one admin and one operational model (Shopify’s push) or separate storefront experiences and governance under one “open SaaS” roof (BigCommerce’s multi-storefront narrative).

## Conclusion

So, which is better: BigCommerce or Shopify? Shopify is a strong default when your priority is speed, operational cohesion, and ecosystem breadth — especially if your roadmap leans on rapid experimentation, app-based extensibility, and unified POS + online operations.

BigCommerce is often the stronger choice when you need built-in mid-market/enterprise capabilities, no platform transaction fees, and a platform posture that naturally supports multi-storefront, segmentation-driven experiences, and composable/headless architectures.

## FAQ

Is Shopify or BigCommerce better suited for subscription-based ecommerce models?

Shopify supports subscriptions as a purchase option, documents subscription behavior in its help center, and provides APIs (selling plan APIs and subscription contract APIs) for building subscription apps. Shopify also positions subscription selling as possible online and in-store via Shopify Subscriptions or compatible third-party subscription apps. BigCommerce’s model is more clearly “app-led” for subscriptions: BigCommerce’s support content for recurring billing points merchants to subscription apps in its app marketplace (including ReCharge), and the marketplace has a dedicated recurring billing/subscriptions category.

How do Shopify and BigCommerce handle data portability and vendor lock-in risks?

Both platforms support data export (CSV) and API access, enabling portability — but lock-in risks differ. Shopify’s risk stems from Liquid themes and app dependencies, which can increase switching costs. BigCommerce, with its open SaaS and API-first approach, allows easier decoupling via headless setups. To mitigate risk: maintain regular exports, use APIs for sync, document dependencies, and design flexible integration layers.

How do AI-powered personalization tools integrate with Shopify and BigCommerce ecosystems?

Shopify offers built-in AI (Shopify Magic, Sidekick) plus a strong app ecosystem (e.g., Nosto, Algolia) and headless APIs for custom AI experiences. BigCommerce relies more on integrations and partnerships (e.g., Bloomreach, Stripe Agentic Commerce), supporting composable, API-driven setups. Choose Shopify for embedded AI workflows and apps; BigCommerce for flexible, headless, partnership-driven AI commerce.

Businesses with complex or highly customized needs may find certain technical restrictions. Additionally, Shopify Plus may require third-party apps for features that are built-in on other platforms, which can add extra costs and operational complexity.

### What is the disadvantage of BigCommerce?

The main disadvantage of BigCommerce is that it often requires more technical resources to fully maximize its open architecture. While BigCommerce offers great flexibility, businesses may need skilled developers to build custom experiences or maintain integrations. The app marketplace is also smaller compared to Shopify's, which means fewer plug-and-play solutions are available for non-technical users.

### Why should I upgrade to Shopify Plus?

Upgrading to Shopify Plus makes sense for businesses that are growing rapidly and need access to advanced features like automation (through Shopify Flow), custom checkout experiences (using Scripts), and powerful multi-channel selling. Shopify Plus also provides better scalability, dedicated account management, priority support, and access to exclusive tools that are not available on lower Shopify plans. Shopify commands 10.32% of the global ecommerce platform market and approximately 29% of the United States ecommerce software market as of 2025, making it the fourth-largest platform worldwide and the dominant player domestically. The platform currently powers 4.8 million active storefronts globally, with roughly 3 million of those stores based in the United States.

Key statistics include: 10.32% global ecommerce platform market share, 29% U.S. ecommerce software market share, 4th place ranking among global ecommerce platforms, 26.2% share of all ecommerce websites globally, and 28.8% market share among top 1 million websites.

Global market share has grown consistently from 8.6% in 2020 to 10.32% in 2025, with active stores increasing from 1.7 million to 4.8 million over the same period. Shopify ranks 4th globally behind WooCommerce (20.1%), custom/proprietary solutions (~15-18%), and Wix ecommerce (~8-10%), while ahead of Squarespace Commerce (~4-6%).

Regionally, Shopify dominates the U.S. market with 29% share (vs. WooCommerce at 18-20%), holds 25-27% in EMEA with 42% YoY GMV growth, 14% in Asia-Pacific with 18.5% CAGR projected, and 5% in Latin America.

Shopify's performance varies by website tier: 28.8% of top 1 million sites, 19% of top 100k sites, 15% of top 10k sites, and 26.2% of all ecommerce sites. Shopify Plus represents 0.22% of all stores but generates disproportionate revenue with merchants processing 10-50x more volume than standard accounts.

The platform's App Store contains over 16,000 applications, and pricing ranges from $29-$399+ monthly. Competition remains healthy, with WooCommerce serving different needs (flexibility vs. managed service). Key growth drivers include international expansion, enterprise adoption through Shopify Plus, omnichannel retail, and B2B commerce. Risks include economic sensitivity due to SMB merchant concentration, increased competition from Amazon and Square, regulatory changes, and platform fee sensitivity.

# Best Ecommerce CMS Platforms 2026: Top 9 Solutions

Compare the 9 best ecommerce CMS platforms—Shopify, BigCommerce, WordPress, and more. Discover pricing, features, and which CMS fits your store.

![](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/Alexa-Collins.png?v=1781548216)

[by Alexa Collins](/blog/authors/alexa-collins)Jul 22, 2026 • 23 min read

![A cloud with multicolored squares floating around it on a blue background.](https://cdn.shopify.com/b/shopify-brochure2-assets/84caec17c4975cadaa061b9b6085cf08.png?originalWidth=1848&originalHeight=782)

An ecommerce content management system (CMS) allows you to present a well-designed, trustworthy website, integrating a user-friendly front-end interface with secure back-end management.

The importance of ecommerce CMS platforms is growing, as eMarketer data projects global ecommerce sales to reach [almost $8 trillion by 2028](https://www.emarketer.com/content/worldwide-retail-ecommerce-forecast-2025).

This guide covers the top CMS platforms powering successful online stores and the key features that set the best ecommerce CMS platforms apart.

## What is an ecommerce CMS?

An ecommerce CMS, also known as an ecommerce [content management system](/blog/content-management-system) or [ecommerce management](/blog/ecommerce-management) system, is software that enables businesses to create and manage digital content on their online stores. That content can include multimedia web pages, product listings, blog posts, and more.

According to Grandview Research, the content management software market size reached almost [$35 billion in 2025](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/content-management-software-market) and is expected to grow to [$77.77 billion in 2033, at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.6%](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/content-management-software-market).

### CMS vs. ecommerce platform

A CMS supports the digital management of content, and an ecommerce platform specifically enables checkout and sales. You don’t always need a separate CMS for ecommerce; platforms like Shopify combine the two.

Here are the key differences between the two:

| Standalone CMS | Full ecommerce platform |
| --- | --- |
| Responsibilities | Collection, management, and organization of digital content like blog posts, landing pages, media assets, and more. | Enables digital commerce through cart and checkout functionality, payment processing, product organization, and inventory and order management. |
| Flexibility | Very high flexibility on both the front end and back end. | Open-source or headless ecommerce platforms can be very flexible. SaaS ecommerce platforms can be less flexible but have lower setup times. |
| Typical use cases | Blogs, portfolios, media sites, and content-first brands. Also works well for creators who initially build a content site and later add commerce. | Brands selling physical or digital goods, marketplaces, crafts, and subscription models. Cases where full commerce features are required from the start. |

## Types of ecommerce CMS solutions

There are two primary types of CMS platforms—[software-as-a-service (SaaS)](/blog/saas-business-model) and [open source](/blog/open-source-ecommerce). [Headless ecommerce platforms](/enterprise/blog/headless-ecommerce-platform) and/or API-first solutions are also options, though they are distinct trade-off models.

### SaaS

[SaaS ecommerce](/blog/saas-ecommerce) CMS services charge a subscription fee to use a CMS hosted in the cloud, ensuring ease of use, security, and continuous updates. Shopify and Squarespace are examples of SaaS platforms.

#### Pros of using a SaaS ecommerce CMS

* Lower upfront costs
* Ease of use
* Scalability
* Automatic updates
* Access from anywhere
* Integrated payment options
* Built-in security features

#### Cons of using a SaaS ecommerce CMS

* Less customizable than open source platforms

### Open source

Open source ecommerce CMS platforms are free to download and adapt, giving users more options for customization. However, they typically require technical coding expertise to operate.

Open-source CMSs provide more control but require managing [ecommerce security](/blog/ecommerce-security), hosting, and platform updates on your own. [WordPress](/compare/shopify-vs-wordpress) is an example of open-source software.

#### Pros of using open source software for ecommerce CMS

* Free to download and use
* Fully customizable

#### Cons of open source software

* Web hosting and development services, which are not included, can get expensive
* Must have development expertise
* Users must manage their own website security

Along with the above cons, [Julian Klenda, founder and CEO at Maine Lobster Now, says](/case-studies/maine-lobster-now), “There’s a weird maintenance aspect to plug-ins on other platforms, where you feel really married to this plug-in, but then there’s a required update that they aren’t maintaining for the long run.”

## Headless CMS vs. traditional CMS for ecommerce

[Headless commerce](/enterprise/blog/headless-commerce) is a model of ecommerce architecture where the front end is separated from the back end of the website. Because businesses can make changes to the front end without having to touch the back end, it provides more flexibility and freedom.

Brands might choose a [headless architecture](/enterprise/blog/headless-architecture) to provide a more omnichannel brand experience or build a customized website.

When a headless CMS is API-first, the back end is entirely decoupled from the front end. APIs deliver content from the back end to any front end you choose, across channels like web and mobile. [Shopify Hydrogen](https://hydrogen.shopify.dev) supports this model alongside platforms like Contentful and Sanity.

In contrast to [headless commerce, traditional commerce](/enterprise/headless-commerce-vs-traditional-commerce) (monolithic systems) couples front-end and back-end systems. While less customizable, they are also less complex to set up.

Choosing a headless versus monolithic model is a key part of your [ecommerce strategy](/blog/ecommerce-strategy). Below, review the benefits of headless architecture.

### Benefits of headless architecture

Applying this concept to commerce provides:

* **Omnichannel experience.** Craft more enriching customer experiences by unifying online and in-store shopping. Provide a multitouchpoint delivery experience: Statista reports that mobile devices accounted for [52.27% of global website traffic in Q1 of 2026](https://www.statista.com/statistics/277125/share-of-website-traffic-coming-from-mobile-devices/).
* **Rich personalization.** Because headless CMS solutions centralize all customer information, it’s easier to show personalized content based on prior purchases and keep online and in-store purchases reconciled.
* **Flexibility.** Take a more modular development process and choose your ideal tech stack with no limitations.
* **Agility and speed to market.** You can benefit from faster web development, as developers can work on the front end and back end of your website at the same time.
* **Scalability and performance.** Grow your website on the front end without disrupting your store’s core ecommerce functionality on the back end.

Brands like Taschen, Denim Tears, Ruggable, and BYLT chose the [benefits of headless commerce](/enterprise/blog/benefits-of-headless-commerce). They’ve achieved strong results going headless or building custom storefronts with Shopify’s [Hydrogen framework](https://hydrogen.shopify.dev).

![Row of TASCHEN’s Library of Esoterica books on astrology, tarot, witchcraft, and more.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/1taschen.png?v=1784763707)

Source: [Taschen](https://www.taschen.com/en/)

Taschen [publishing house](/enterprise/blog/publishers-direct-to-consumer-ecommerce) saw a [20% increase in sales](/case-studies/taschen) after switching to a headless CMS on the [Shopify Plus](/enterprise/upgrade-to-shopify-plus) plan. “Shopify Plus improved the customer experience, our sense of control, and enabled new products to come into play,” says Gaëlle Mehanna, ecommerce director at Taschen.

![Denim Tears homepage featuring model in patterned hoodie with arms crossed.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/2denimtears.png?v=1784763706)

Source: [Denim Tears](https://denimtears.com/)

[Denim Tears’ agency, Kamp Grizzly](/case-studies/denim-tears), leveraged Shopify’s Hydrogen framework and saved time to deliver on Tremaine Emory’s storytelling, museum-like vision.

![Ruggable holiday homepage showing family in festive pajamas by Christmas tree on plaid rug.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/3ruggable.png?v=1784763707)

Source: [Ruggable](https://ruggable.com/)

After switching to a headless CMS, Ruggable gained more than faster [site speed](/blog/shopify-site-speed) and greater reliability. “The site is so much faster for our customers, leading to conversion and SEO boosts. Google sees our website as being much faster now and is sending a lot more traffic to us, which is fantastic,” [says Daniel Graupensperger](/case-studies/ruggable), director of product management at Ruggable.

![BYLT fall collection ad showing man in layered hoodie and jacket.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/4bylt.png?v=1784763707)

Source: [BYLT](https://byltbasics.com/)

“Since moving to Hydrogen, we’ve seen immediate improvements in site performance and server-side rendering,” says [Ryan Groh, head of ecommerce at BYLT](/case-studies/bylt-basics).

The brand was able to unify [brick-and-mortar](/blog/brick-and-mortar) and ecommerce segments of the business, resulting in expansion from one to seven profitable retail stores. It also drove more than 50% of [DTC](/blog/what-is-direct-to-consumer) conversions through [Shopify Payments](/blog/shopify-payments-trust).

**Read:**[DTC to Brick-and-Mortar: 11 Brands That Opened Stores](/blog/dtc-to-brick-and-mortar)

### When to choose traditional vs. headless

Both [traditional and headless](/enterprise/blog/headless-commerce-vs-traditional-commerce) CMS options for ecommerce come with pros and cons. When contemplating which style is best for your business, consider the following:

* **Technical resources.** While headless systems allow for a great amount of flexibility, they also take a lot of time to build and maintain.
* **Overall budget.** Headless platforms are significantly more expensive to develop and maintain than traditional platforms.
* **Go-To-Market urgency.** A traditional ecommerce engine is fast to deploy, whereas headless solutions can take months to build.
* **Current or projected revenue.** Businesses that choose the headless route often generate more than [$100 million in online revenue](/enterprise/blog/headless-commerce-vs-traditional-commerce), versus between $20 million and $50 million with the traditional route.
* **Unique criteria.** You may have specialized requirements a traditional ecommerce CMS cannot provide.

### Shopify

[Shopify](/blog/what-is-shopify) is an all-in-one ecommerce CMS solution designed to help store owners easily build and manage their online businesses. With affordable plans, beautiful designs, and powerful selling features, Shopify is the easiest, most reliable way to [start an online store](/blog/start-online-store).

Shopify captures the largest share of websites in the US that use ecommerce technology, at [28.21%](https://trends.builtwith.com/shop/country/United-States).

Use the AI store builder to [create a free store design](https://accounts.shopify.com/store-create) in minutes or get started with one of many [ready-built themes](http://themes.shopify.com/). [Adam Wolfe, founder and CEO at Boost Auto says](/case-studies/boost-auto), “Within a couple hours I was live and selling.”

Once designed, content management is easy with Shopify’s intuitive user interface (UI) and asset library.

From there, Shopify’s ecommerce functionality handles all of the essential functions of an online store, from inventory management to [payment processing](/blog/ecommerce-payment-processing).

#### Who it’s for

Shopify is built for ecommerce businesses of all sizes, from [solopreneurs](/blog/solopreneur) to large enterprises to everywhere in between.

#### Features

* **AI tools.** Use [Shopify Magic](/magic) to streamline your store design process and create landing pages and product listings, then tap Sidekick as your always-on business consultant.
* **Integrated payment processing.**[Shopify Payments](/payments) is an integrated [payment gateway](/blog/ecommerce-payment-gateway) that accepts all major payment methods. Plus, more than 100 third-party payment providers are compatible.
* **Extensive** [**app store**](/blog/ecommerce-app)**.** Access the [Shopify App Store](https://apps.shopify.com) for more than 8,000 integrations.
* **Customizable checkout.** Offer customers a variety of [payment options](/blog/payment-options), including express checkout, in-store pickup, discount codes, and Shop Pay—the internet’s highest-converting checkout option.
* **Shopify POS.** Integrate with physical retail through [Shopify POS](/pos), blending online and offline sales channels.
* **Shipping and fulfillment.** Built-in order, inventory, and shipping tools generate labels, collect [import taxes](/blog/duties-taxes), provide tracking information, manage returns, and more.
* **Abandoned cart recovery.** Boost sales with automated tools for recovering [abandoned shopping carts](/enterprise/blog/44272899-how-to-reduce-shopping-cart-abandonment-by-optimizing-the-checkout).
* **SEO tools.** Shopify’s built in SEO features handle the minutiae of SEO work—such as generating robots.txt and appending your brand name to meta titles—for you.
* **Advanced** [**analytics**](/blog/ecommerce-analytics-tools)**.** Track sales, customer behavior, and other essential ecommerce metrics with robust analytics and [reporting features](/blog/ecommerce-reporting-tools).
* **Advanced customization and** [**API access**](/enterprise/ecommerce-api)**.** While coding isn’t required, you can tailor your storefront and back-end systems to meet your unique needs with extensive customization options and API support.
* **Omnichannel and** [**multichannel**](/enterprise/blog/multi-channel-software-listing-selling-management) **commerce capabilities.** Ensure a consistent [customer experience](/blog/13251973-creative-ways-to-improve-ecommerce-customer-experience-that-also-boost-loyalty-and-sales) and manage inventory seamlessly across desktop, mobile, social media, marketplace, and in-person retail.
* **24/7 customer support.** Enjoy round-the-clock support via email, live chat, and phone.

#### Plans and pricing

Shopify offers a [wide range of plans](/pricing) to support businesses of all sizes:

* Starter: $5 per month
* Basic: $29 per month billed annually
* Grow: $95 per month billed annually
* Advanced: $360 per month billed annually
* Plus: From $2,300 per month

[Start](/start) your Shopify free trial, no credit card required. Get three days free, then the first three months for $1 per month.

### BigCommerce

[BigCommerce](/compare/shopify-vs-bigcommerce) is an “open SaaS” ecommerce platform, meaning it has SaaS functionality with an open API. BigCommerce has an [enterprise-grade product](/enterprise) along with an Essentials product for small businesses.

#### Who it’s for

BigCommerce’s primary product is for large enterprises.

#### Features

* **Basic website builder functionality.** BigCommerce’s ecommerce CMS for small businesses comes with basic website builder tools such as drag-and-drop page design and built-in mobile responsiveness.
* **SEO capabilities.** BigCommerce comes with SEO features like clean URLs and automatic redirects.
* **Multichannel selling.** Business owners can integrate their stores with social media and marketplace platforms, allowing them to sell products through these channels.
* **Scalable** [**infrastructure**](/blog/ecommerce-infrastructure)**.** BigCommerce’s enterprise product can handle high volumes of traffic and transactions.

#### Plans and pricing

BigCommerce pricing ranges from a Core plan at $29 per month to a Scale plan at $299 per month, billed annually, with a 15-day free trial. Contact sales for Enterprise pricing.

### WordPress + WooCommerce

[WordPress](/compare/shopify-vs-wordpress) is an open-source content management system made for bloggers. You can use a WordPress site as an ecommerce CMS with the addition of the [WooCommerce](/compare/shopify-vs-woocommerce) plug-in, which provides ecommerce functionality like payment gateways. Or, add on [Shopify for WordPress](/blog/113145925-introducing-shopify-for-wordpress) instead.

#### Who it’s for

[WordPress](/blog/what-is-wordpress) can be used by anyone, but it was originally built for bloggers.

#### Features

* **Familiar UI for some.** If you’re familiar with WordPress’s user interface, this allows you to use a platform you already know for managing ecommerce content.
* **Customizable and extendable.** WordPress has thousands of plug-ins and modifiable themes to extend the functionality of a WordPress website and help customize it. This can be a drawback for those unfamiliar with [website development](/blog/ecommerce-website-development), as customization may require knowledge of HTML and CSS.

#### Plans and pricing

WordPress and WooCommerce are free. However, there are [hosting costs](/blog/hosting-costs), as well as expenses associated with domain registration, themes, payment gateways, plug-ins, and more.

### Drupal

Drupal is an open-source CMS that offers deep customization but requires technical expertise. Drupal commerce is an open-source Drupal module that [adds ecommerce tools like](/blog/ecommerce-tools) products, carts, checkout, and orders. Payment gateways, shipping, and fulfillment are available through contributed extensions.

Drupal is flexible and customizable, but as an open-source software, it requires more technical expertise than [ecommerce website builders](/blog/best-ecommerce-website-builder). Drupal recently released a more user friendly CMS version called [Drupal CMS 2.0](https://www.drupal.org/blog/drupal-cms-20-is-here-visual-building-ai-and-site-templates-transform-drupal), which features a tool called Drupal Canvas for editing. The update also includes optional AI tools.

#### Who it’s for

Drupal is for users with some coding skills.

#### Features

* **Customization.** With many modules and themes and the ability to write custom modules, businesses can tailor their online presence.
* **Scalability.** The platform is designed to [scale](/enterprise/blog/scalable-ecommerce-platform) with the growth of a business while maintaining security standards.

#### Plans and pricing

Drupal is a free open-source software. However, there are costs for hosting, [registering a domain name](/blog/register-a-domain-name), themes, payment gateways, and more.

### Adobe Commerce

[Adobe Commerce](/compare/shopify-vs-adobe), formerly known as Magento, is an ecommerce platform that includes a CMS component, designed to enable both business-to-consumer ([B2C](/blog/what-is-business-to-consumer-b2c-definition-and-guide)) and business-to-business ([B2B](/blog/what-is-b2b)) transactions. Adobe Commerce is designed for large, enterprise-level companies looking

for a highly customizable platform.

Anis Tayebali, senior vice president of engineering at Lulu and Georgia found that the “Adobe Commerce app ecosystem wasn’t mature, and their integrations were not seamless.”

“There weren’t enough integrations and apps to help us scale and improve the site,” [Anis says](/case-studies/lulu-and-georgia). “There wasn’t even a solid offering for basic reporting—and with Shopify, even the bare-bone offerings are solid.”

#### Who it’s for

Adobe Commerce is geared toward enterprise businesses.

#### Features

* **B2B buying portals.** Adobe Commerce allows B2B businesses to create self-serve B2B buying experiences.
* **Inventory management.** The platform offers [inventory management](/blog/inventory-management) to support B2C and B2B [catalogs](/blog/ecommerce-catalog-management). It facilitates omnichannel sales by letting customers buy online and pick up orders in the store, or [BOPIS](/blog/bopis).
* **Enriched content.** Modular capabilities allow product information and product links to be embedded in blog articles.

#### Plans and pricing

Adobe Commerce offers Adobe Commerce Pro and Managed Services plans. Contact Adobe for pricing information.

### OpenCart

OpenCart is an open-source ecommerce platform. Its free version requires businesses to secure their own [ecommerce website hosting](/blog/ecommerce-hosts). It integrates with common payment processors and other third-party apps.

After replatforming from OpenCart to Shopify, [Christy Ng saw a 400% revenue growth](/case-studies/christy-ng), 50% reduction in checkout time, and a 97% decrease in order processing time.

#### Who it’s for

OpenCart is for owners of small, simple stores.

#### Features

* **SEO functionality.** OpenCart offers built-in SEO tools to help your site show up in search results.
* **Multilingual and multicurrency support.** The platform supports multiple languages and currencies.
* **Marketplace of designs.** You can find templated page designs and themes in OpenCart’s marketplace. Some are free, and some are available for a fee.

#### Plans and pricing

OpenCart is free. However, hosting, [domain registration](/blog/best-domain-registrars), themes, payment gateways, and more will cost you.

### Wix

[Wix](/compare/shopify-vs-wix) is a website builder and CMS offering design templates and a drag-and-drop interface for [simple website design](/blog/simple-website-design). Wix offers some ecommerce features, but it isn’t purpose-built for ecommerce.

#### Who it’s for

Wix can be used by anyone with basic website needs.

#### Features

* **Simple website builder.** Wix’s drag-and-drop functionality lets users design their ecommerce store without coding.
* **Templates.** Design templates give users a head start in creating an online storefront.
* **Integrated ecommerce features.** Wix includes tools for inventory management, payment processing, and shipping.

#### Plans and pricing

Wix offers plans starting with Light at $17 per month and ranging to its Business Elite plan at $159 per month. Its Enterprise plan is available for businesses with custom pricing. It extends a 14-day money-back guarantee.

### HubSpot

[HubSpot](https://apps.shopify.com/hubspot-2) is a software company best known for its [customer relationship management (CRM)](/blog/crm) and [marketing tools](/blog/ecommerce-marketing-tools), but it also offers a CMS. HubSpot’s CMS isn’t purpose-built for ecommerce, but you can add ecommerce capabilities using HubSpot payment links or by integrating an existing Shopify store.

#### Who it’s for

HubSpot is for businesses that rely on inbound marketing and customer relationship management.

#### Features

* **CRM-powered CMS.** HubSpot’s CMS is integrated with its CRM system, which can help you enable personalized customer experiences.
* **Drag-and-drop page builder.** HubSpot’s drag-and-drop page builder can help you build a website without extensive technical knowledge.
* **Blog maker.** The platform offers a blog maker, allowing users to publish SEO-friendly content with the goal of driving traffic to their website.

#### Plans and pricing

HubSpot CMS offers a free forever plan. Paid plans for Content Hub start at $15 per month, per seat when billed annually.

### Squarespace

[Squarespace](/compare/shopify-vs-squarespace) is a website builder letting business owners create sites with predesigned templates. Its templated styles are both a benefit and a constraint—Squarespace is known for being minimalist and professional-looking, but allows fewer customization options.

Squarespace has integrated ecommerce capabilities as well as [web hosting services](/blog/best-web-hosting-services). It also offers additional features for content creators, such as a course builder.

#### Who it’s for

Anyone with simple website needs can use Squarespace, and the platform has additional features for [content creators](/blog/what-is-a-content-creator).

#### Features

* **Design templates.** Professionally designed templates cater to specific industries and professions, like restaurants, content creators, and photographers.
* **Membership content tools.** Squarespace allows you to gate specific content, like blog articles, behind a paywall, so it’s available only to members.
* **SEO tools.** Squarespace integrates with [Google Search Console](/blog/google-search-console) and has basic SEO tools like clean URLs and an auto-generated sitemap.

#### Plans and pricing

Squarespace offers a 14-day free trial. Paid plans that include commerce features start with Basic at $16 per month, billed annually, and range to the Advanced plan at $99 per month when billed annually.

When choosing an ecommerce CMS, the core ecommerce CMS features to look for include customizable templates, SEO features, a user-friendly interface, support for integrations, omnichannel content delivery, and more.

### Catalog management

Essential ecommerce features to look for in a CMS include catalog management tools. Look for solutions that make listing products fast and simple, offer variant creation, and inventory tracking. Ensure the platform also has [ecommerce product management](/blog/ecommerce-product-management) features.

### Ease of use

You probably didn’t [become an ecommerce entrepreneur](/blog/become-an-entrepreneur) to spend your days tinkering with your online store. An intuitive, easy-to-use ecommerce CMS platform will cut down on time spent managing the technical aspects of running your ecommerce site, so you can focus on growing your business.

For example, home fragrance brand [Pura](https://pura.com/) reduced development time related to checkout functionality [by 50% with Shopify](/case-studies/pura-scents).

Look for an easy-to-navigate dashboard, clear settings, and a high-quality help center (to minimize the need for technical support).

Adam Wolfe, founder and CEO at Boost Auto, [says](/case-studies/boost-auto), “It was pretty clear I needed to go with Shopify. It was what felt right for long-term success, and it was just so intuitive.”

### AI tools

According to Precedence Research, the market size of [AI tools for ecommerce](/blog/ai-tools-for-ecommerce) was [$11.21 billion in 2026](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/artificial-intelligence-in-e-commerce-market) and is expected to grow to almost [$75 billion in 2035](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/artificial-intelligence-in-e-commerce-market) at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 23.59%.

This data shows that [AI tools for business](/blog/ai-tools-for-business) are becoming essential features for ecommerce owners, as a way to boost efficiency and accelerate growth.

For example, Shopify’s AI tools, [Magic and Sidekick](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/shopify-admin/productivity-tools/shopify-magic), make the platform’s user friendly interface even more accessible.

“That’s where Shopify Magic comes in, because it is so much better than myself and most of my staff,” [says Mikey Moran](/blog/shopify-magic-spotlight), founder and CEO at Private Label Extensions.

### Drag-and-drop website builder

Drag-and-drop website builders enable non-technical users to create professional websites with little design or coding experience.

When evaluating the best fit for your business needs, look for SEO tools, customizable templates, [AI tools](/blog/ai-tools), design options that match your brand style, and robust ecommerce tools.

### Media management

A great ecommerce CMS will make it simple to [manage your digital assets](/blog/digital-asset-management) by creating a library of the photos, blogs, videos, and PDFs you’ve used on your website. This organized system can help you save time creating and updating content.

### Support for integrations

A robust ecommerce CMS will offer a wide range of [integrations](/blog/ecommerce-integration) with other [ecommerce software](/blog/ecommerce-software) to make for seamless ecommerce functionality and boost efficiency. For example, an ecommerce CMS might [integrate with your customer relationship management (CRM) system,](/blog/crm-integration) email platform, and [inventory management software](/blog/inventory-management-software).

A large app ecosystem can be powerful. For example, [Adam Wolfe, founder and CEO at Boost Auto, says](/case-studies/boost-auto), “When we started out, it was just me and the app ecosystem.”

### SEO features

A content management system with built-in search engine optimization ([SEO](/blog/seo-checklist-online-store)) tools helps you optimize product descriptions, images, and other content for search engines like Google. Look for a CMS that automatically generates robots.txt and sitemap.xml files—which help search engines crawl your website—and adds canonical tags to pages to prevent duplicate content from harming your search performance.

For businesses using Shopify, implementing [Shopify SEO](/blog/shopify-seo) techniques can help increase search engine rankings. [Ecommerce SEO](/blog/ecommerce-seo-beginners-guide) features can also help you improve the success of your [content marketing](/blog/what-is-content-marketing) strategy with optimized metadata. Effective content marketing can help you build search engine visibility and develop audience trust.

Beyond traditional search, AI shopping assistants like Google AI Mode, Gemini, and Perplexity also rely on structured data and robots.txt access to discover and evaluate products. Use Shopify’s [free audit tool](/agentic-readiness) to check whether your product pages have the schema markup and crawler access these AI assistants need.

[In 2025, 33% of holiday shoppers](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/retail-distribution/holiday-retail-sales-consumer-survey.html) said they planned to use [generative AI](/blog/generative-ai) while they shop, double the percentage from 2024. Whether shoppers use traditional organic search or [GenAI tools](/blog/generative-ai-tools), use the SEO tools in your CMS to increase your site’s visibility.

### Omnichannel content delivery

[Omnichannel commerce](/plus/solutions/omnichannel-commerce) means enabling customers to browse, interact, and purchase across interconnected channels, whether that’s online, via mobile, [IoT/connected devices](/blog/iot-devices), in-store, or on social media, with a seamless, consistent experience.

Ecommerce CMS platforms (especially headless or omnichannel CMSs) support this by delivering unified content across multiple touchpoints.

**Read:**[Omnichannel vs. Multichannel: Key Differences](/enterprise/blog/omni-channel-vs-multi-channel)

### Localization and multicurrency support

Look for CMS solutions that offer [localization and multicurrency support](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/international/localization-and-translation). That means translating your store into different languages based on the regions in which you sell, and offering payment gateways that support local currencies globally.

With help from Shopify, [Snuggle Hunny](https://snugglehunnykids.com/) grew their international sales from [5% to 15% of total sales](/case-studies/snuggle-hunny).

### Site speed and performance

The ecommerce CMS you choose should prioritize site load time and fast performance across channels. These are considered [core web vitals](/blog/how-to-improve-core-web-vitals) by Google and integral to how it ranks your site. They’re also user experience (UX) factors, and affect website usage and sales.

For example, [Ruggable](/case-studies/ruggable) improved [site speed](/enterprise/blog/store-speed-conversion), stability, SEO, and conversions by moving to a headless site architecture with Shopify.

## How to choose the right ecommerce CMS for your business

Whether you’re choosing an ecommerce CMS for the first time or making a crucial [replatforming](/enterprise/blog/ecommerce-replatforming-guide) decision, it’s important to make the right call.

On the technical side, you’ll want to look at scalability, integration capabilities, development flexibility, and security. From a business perspective, consider factors like an intuitive interface, ease of use for non-technical teams, total cost of ownership, time to market, and support for growth strategies like omnichannel selling.

### A 5-step framework for choosing an ecommerce CMS

“Our greatest frustration was seeing our budgets tied up in maintaining the platform, rather than channeling those resources into creating exceptional experiences for our customers,” [says Richard Voyce](/case-studies/the-conran-shop), digital director at The Conran Shop, of the team’s experience with Magento (now known as Adobe Commerce).

Below is a five-step framework for choosing the best ecommerce CMS for your team from the start:

1. **Start with your business stage.** Assess your current order volume, catalog size, team size, and growth trajectory.
2. **Narrow down the platform type.** Decide between a hosted all-in-one platform like Shopify that handles hosting, security, and updates for you, a self-hosted open-source platform you maintain yourself, or a general-purpose CMS with ecommerce added through plug-ins.
3. **List your must-have features.** Write down your non-negotiables, then check each shortlisted platform against that list rather than its marketing.
4. **Weigh the actual cost.** Look past the monthly subscription to total cost of ownership, including transaction fees, apps, hosting, and developer time. After replatforming from Magento to Shopify, The Conran Shop saw a [50% reduction in total cost of ownership](/case-studies/the-conran-shop).
5. **Validate before committing.** Start a free trial, build a test store, and run through workflows (like adding products, configuring checkout, testing a payment, and previewing on mobile) to confirm whether the platform feels right for your team.

### Evaluation criteria checklist

When evaluating CMS ecommerce solutions, these are the minimum capabilities you should expect:

* **Table-stakes ecommerce features.** Product and inventory management, shipping and fulfillment, order tracking, customer data management, and robust security measures.
* **AI-powered tools.** Features like auto-generated product descriptions, personalized recommendations, and image editing.
* **Integrated payment processing.** Acceptance of all major methods, from credit cards to [digital wallets](/blog/digital-wallets).
* **Ecosystem support.** An extensive app store or integrations that plug into your existing tech stack.
* **Flexible checkout.** Customizable flows with express options, discount codes, and in-store pickup.
* **Analytics and reporting.** Visibility into performance across all sales channels.
* **Omnichannel capabilities.** Seamless selling across web, mobile, social, marketplaces, and in-store.
* **Customer support.** Responsive, helpful service when you need it.
* **Marketing automation.** Tools like abandoned cart recovery, email campaigns, and [retargeting](/blog/retargeting-previous-customers).
* **Scalability.** Advanced features for [international selling](/enterprise/international-ecommerce-strategy), B2B, wholesale, and enterprise growth.
* **Site speed and performance.** Fast loading times across platforms and devices: desktop and mobile.

### B2B ecommerce CMS considerations

Grandview Research projects the global B2B ecommerce market to reach [$28 trillion in 2026](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/business-to-business-b2b-e-commerce-market) and [$105.9 trillion by 2033](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/business-to-business-b2b-e-commerce-market). Look for account-specific pricing, the ability to place large or repeat orders quickly, and a self-service experience that mirrors that of a DTC store.

When evaluating a CMS for B2B, look for these capabilities:

* Customized purchasing experiences for each of your customers, including company profiles and customer-specific catalogs.
* Self-service purchasing and account management that supports quick bulk and repeat orders.
* Workflow automations that automate account requests and invoices.
* Design customization to make your wholesale storefront feel on-brand.

A few ecommerce CMS platforms that offer B2B functionality include Adobe Commerce, BigCommerce B2B Edition, Salesforce Commerce, and [Shopify Plus B2B](/plus/solutions/b2b-ecommerce).

Shopify Plus B2B stands out for SMB and mid-market store owners:

After launching wholesale on Shopify, [&Collar increased wholesale revenue by 418%](/case-studies/andcollar). Now their wholesale business accounts for 20% of their total revenue.

For Boost Auto, “When a customer orders our product on somebody else’s website, that order just pops right into our system. It can go through all our standard workflows,” [says founder and CEO Adam Wolfe](/case-studies/boost-auto).

Swimwear brand Kulani Kinis finds the platform’s branding and design capabilities impactful. “We’re all about branding, appeal and aesthetic, and with Shopify Plus, we’ve been able to make the wholesale store feel like us.”

“Shopify’s B2B capabilities have given us the cohesive brand experience we wanted and customization options that meet the needs of our wholesale partners. We’re not bound by others’ constraints," [says co-founder and managing director Alex Babich](/case-studies/kulani-kinis).

### Business size and technical requirements

Here’s a breakdown of which CMS platforms suit small startups, mid-market, and enterprise brands:

Small to medium businesses likely benefit most from a traditional all-in-one ecommerce CMS because of their low upfront cost, ease of getting up and running, and lower maintenance.

Mid-market shops should evaluate all-in-one ecommerce CMS platforms as well as a blended approach between headless and monolithic in order to gain systems like [product information management (PIM)](/enterprise/pim-ecommerce).

Enterprise brands might prefer headless architecture for its flexibility, customization, and strength as an omnichannel platform. However, a blended approach or scalable commerce platform like [Shopify Plus](/plus) could be the right fit.

## Choosing your ecommerce CMS

The right ecommerce CMS depends on your business stage, the types of tools you’re looking for, and how much customization you need. Small businesses and mid-market brands get the most from Shopify, which is an all-in-one, powerful ecommerce CMS solution.

The guide reviews the top 9 ecommerce CMS platforms: Shopify (from $5/month, for all sizes, 28.21% US market share), BigCommerce (from $29/month, for enterprises), WordPress+WooCommerce (free, for bloggers), Drupal (free, for users with coding skills), Adobe Commerce/Magento (custom pricing, for enterprise), OpenCart (free, for small stores), Wix (from $17/month, for simple sites), HubSpot (free/$15/seat, for inbound marketing), and Squarespace (from $16/month, for simple sites).

Must-have CMS features include catalog management, ease of use, AI tools, drag-and-drop builders, media management, integrations, SEO features, omnichannel delivery, localization/multicurrency support, and site speed/performance. A 5-step framework for choosing a CMS is provided: start with business stage, narrow platform type, list must-have features, weigh total cost of ownership, and validate with a free trial. B2B considerations are also covered, with Shopify Plus noted for enabling wholesale operations.

# Carbon Neutral Shipping: The Guide for E-Commerce in 2026

Summarize with AI:

Carbon neutral shipping is the practice of balancing transport emissions through reduction strategies, renewable energy investment, or certified carbon credit programmes. **For e-commerce brands in 2026, it has moved from a nice-to-have to a regulatory and competitive requirement: the EU Emissions Trading System now covers CO₂, methane, and nitrous oxide from large vessels calling at EU ports, and 68% of European consumers say they will pay more for sustainable delivery (Deloitte).**

‍

E-commerce shipping and returns accounted for an estimated 37% of total e-commerce greenhouse gas emissions in 2020 (Coolset, based on MIT Lab data). With global e-commerce revenue reaching an estimated $3.87 trillion in 2026 (Statista), parcel volumes keep climbing, and so does the pressure on brands to reduce logistics emissions.

‍

‍

## **Why is carbon neutral shipping critical for e-commerce in 2026?**

‍

International shipping produces roughly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions (UN, 2025). In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization approved a historic plan to make the sector net-zero by around 2050, with a 20-30% emissions reduction target by 2030. The EU ETS began covering CO₂ from large ships at EU ports in January 2024, phasing in from 40% of reported emissions that year to 70% in 2025 and full coverage from 2026. From January 2026, methane and nitrous oxide are also included.

‍

For online brands, greener logistics is both a regulatory requirement and a customer expectation. UK consumer research shows:

‍

* 79% of UK shoppers favour sustainable delivery methods and are willing to pay more for them.
* 49% are concerned about home delivery sustainability.
* About half of fashion consumers call for initiatives that reduce carbon footprints at checkout.
* 45% of UK shoppers expect fashion brands to commit to plastic-free products.
* 70% of surveyed customers are willing to wait 5 extra days for delivery in exchange for an environmental benefit.

‍

## **What is carbon neutral shipping?**

‍

**Carbon neutral shipping balances the carbon emissions produced during transport through green measures, including renewable energy investments, tree planting, or certified offset projects. The goal is to make the net climate impact of each shipment zero.** For e-commerce brands shipping thousands of parcels per month, it is now a core part of responsible logistics.

‍

Carbon neutral shipping does not eliminate the initial emissions from moving packages. It provides financial support for sustainable projects and research that are vital in reducing long-term climate impact. For e-commerce brands, pairing emission offsets with operational improvements (like route optimisation and right-sized packaging) delivers the strongest results.

‍

## **10 actionable tips to reduce carbon emissions from shipping**

‍

![Chart of average e-commerce shipping emissions by source, based on Coolset and MIT Lab data](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/620f96baa098d24eaecfab18/657c5460cc0a767e24968e0e_2Y0Mef9fHqYU2Q61efHIjr6u1cZ4GY_UF6kNIWtozD6mQcNHEkpT9mVOmPmPRuDzlhG1QxHBYxyM_6K63L28ctAzGuU02tOER4dsfipa8Hj58r0jRe9MF-t4e_4Obm64p2ggcVmduuXyh-GJqQlyNrM.png)

Source: E-commerce average emissions by sources - Coolset based on the MIT Lab report

‍

Once the total carbon emissions have been calculated, the next step is to reduce those emissions as much as possible.

Improving shipping efficiency is the most impactful way for e-commerce businesses to cut emissions and manage the growing demands of delivery.

‍

Here are several actionable recommendations for sustainable shipping practices:

‍

1. **Optimise route efficiency**: Implementing advanced routing software can minimise travel distances and reduce fuel consumption. This includes selecting the most efficient routes and consolidating shipments to maximise load efficiency.‍
2. **Use energy-efficient vehicles**: Transitioning to vehicles that use alternative fuels or electric vehicles can significantly lower emissions.‍
3. **Invest in carbon-offset projects**: Investing in projects like reforestation or renewable energy can offset unavoidable emissions.‍
4. [**Eco-friendly packaging**](/blog/7-eco-friendly-packaging-options-for-e-commerce-brands): Use minimal, recyclable, or biodegradable packaging to reduce waste and carbon footprint associated with shipping.‍
5. **Local warehousing and fulfilment**: Positioning products closer to the customer base reduces the distance for delivery.‍
6. **Use technology in inventory management**: Adopt advanced systems to better predict product demand, helping to avoid excess stock and reduce unnecessary shipping.‍
7. **Encourage bulk purchases**: Incentivising customers to buy multiple items at once can reduce the number of individual shipments.‍
8. [**Offer flexible shipping options**](/blog/frais-de-transport-enjeu-rentabilite-e-commercants): Provide customers with a choice of eco-friendly shipping options, even if it means slower delivery times.‍
9. **Educate customers**: Increase awareness among customers about the environmental impact of shipping and promote eco-friendly practices.‍
10. **Implement carbon accounting**: Regularly measure and report on the carbon emissions from shipping activities to identify areas for improvement.

‍

By applying these strategies, e-commerce brands can improve efficiency, reduce their carbon footprint, and build a more resilient supply chain.

‍

## **Carbon neutral shipping options for e-commerce**

‍

**France:‍**

* Colissimo: Offers green delivery solutions, including carbon-neutral options.
* DHL France: Features the GoGreen service for eco-conscious shipping.
* FedEx France: Focuses on sustainable logistics with EarthSmart.

**Spain:‍**

* Correos: Delivers an array of eco-friendly and carbon-neutral shipping services.
* SEUR: As part of DPDgroup, it provides green shipping solutions with Total Zero.
* UPS Spain: Supports businesses with environmentally responsible shipping options.

**United Kingdom:‍**

* DPD UK: Integrates carbon-neutral shipping in its Green Delivery initiative.
* Royal Mail: Offers sustainable, carbon-conscious parcel delivery.
* UPS UK: Offers green shipping solutions, including carbon-neutral options.

‍

## **How can a green logistics partner reduce your emissions?**

‍

Working with a green logistics provider gives e-commerce brands access to supply chain expertise, emission reduction strategies, and cost savings through better route planning and packaging optimisation. These partners handle the operational complexity of sustainable shipping so brands can focus on growth.

‍

Green 3PLs typically offer advanced technology for route planning and inventory management, reducing both environmental impact and operational costs. Their large-scale operations also mean better shipping rates.

‍

For growing e-commerce businesses, such partnerships offer the scalability and flexibility to adjust to changing demand without the burden of managing logistics in-house. European fulfilment providers like Bigblue, ShipBob, and Huboo now include sustainability features as part of their standard offering.

‍

## **Bigblue’s approach to greener logistics**

‍

Bigblue, a European fulfilment platform serving 600+ D2C brands, launched the “Collectif pour une Logistique Responsable” with partners including Hipli and Lizee to promote [greener logistics](/blog/bigblue-commitment-to-greener-logistics) across the industry.

‍

The company uses plastic-free, recyclable packaging materials and powers its data servers with 100% renewable energy. Bigblue’s packaging algorithm selects the best box size for each order, reducing packaging volume by an average of 22% and cutting both [shipping costs](/blog/frais-de-transport-enjeu-rentabilite-e-commercants) and carbon emissions. The system also flags address errors before dispatch, preventing failed deliveries and unnecessary return trips.

‍

Its carrier-agnostic transport management system evaluates multiple carriers per route, finding the best balance of speed, cost, and environmental impact.

‍

‍

## **What comes next for carbon neutral shipping?**

‍

Carbon-neutral shipping has moved from a differentiator to a baseline expectation for e-commerce brands in Europe. With the EU’s expanding emissions regulations and rising customer demand for transparency, brands without a clear logistics sustainability plan risk falling behind on both compliance and customer trust.

‍

The tools are available at every scale. Carrier carbon-offset programmes, packaging optimisation algorithms, and 3PL partners with built-in sustainability features give e-commerce businesses a clear path to lower their shipping footprint.

‍

‍

Frequently asked questions

Everything you need to know.

What is carbon neutral shipping?

Carbon neutral shipping means offsetting the carbon emissions produced during transportation. You can achieve this through investing in renewable energy or supporting environmental projects.

Why is carbon neutral shipping important?

It's vital for reducing the environmental impact of transporting goods. By achieving carbon neutrality, companies can help combat climate change and promote sustainability.

What are the benefits of carbon neutral shipping?

Besides reducing environmental impact, it enhances brand reputation, meets consumer expectations for sustainability, and can differentiate a brand in a competitive market.

Can carbon neutral shipping reduce operating costs? ‍

Initially, it may require investment, but in the long run, it can lead to savings through efficient logistics and potentially lower fuel costs.

What role do consumers play in carbon neutral shipping?

Consumers are becoming increasingly aware and demanding of sustainable practices. It encourages more companies to adopt greener alternatives.

How can an e-commerce company achieve carbon neutral shipping?

Companies can use energy-efficient transport modes, optimise logistics, invest in carbon offset projects, and use eco-friendly packaging.
