# What is Carbon-Neutral Shipping & How to Achieve It

Verified & Reviewed

Last updated on October 28, 2025 Written By [Kristina Lopienski](https://www.shipbob.com/author/klopienski/)

![Photo up to the tree top shot from below_2289909985](https://www.shipbob.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/f54a7353c4291d3eebf4c0275e823ed0.jpg?w=580)

Last updated on October 28, 2025 Written By [Kristina Lopienski](https://www.shipbob.com/author/klopienski/)

![](/wp-content/themes/shipbob-2022/resources/svg/blog-subscribe.svg)

## Subscribe for More

Table of Contents

\*\* Minutes

[What is carbon-neutral shipping?](#h-what-is-carbon-neutral-shipping)

[Top solutions for carbon-neutral shipping](#h-top-solutions-for-carbon-neutral-shipping)

[Consumers care about their carbon footprint](#h-consumers-care-about-their-carbon-footprint)

[How to reduce carbon emissions from shipping](#h-how-to-reduce-carbon-emissions-from-shipping)

[Sometimes offsets aren’t enough](#h-sometimes-offsets-aren-t-enough)

[Carbon-neutral shipping FAQs](#h-carbon-neutral-shipping-faqs)

Carbon emissions are a leading cause of the climate crisis and the repercussions we face today. Many industries are looking for ways to reduce emissions in attempt to slow down the damage made to the environment. 

When it comes to logistics, shipping emits a high volume of black carbon affecting the carbon dioxide in the air.

In an effort to reduce carbon emission in the ecommerce industry, a growing number of online brands are participating in sustainable practices, including the option of carbon-neutral shipping. 

In this article, you will learn what carbon-neutral shipping, why it’s important, and how you can reduce carbon emissions from shipping.

## What is carbon-neutral shipping?

“Carbon-neutral” refers to practices that, when executed properly, produce a net zero amount of carbon dioxide. Carbon-neutral shipping aims to reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping packages.

Since carbon-dioxide is one of the leading reasons for climate change, switching to carbon-neutral shipping brings us one step closer to helping protect the environment and is a major effort in helping to monitor our carbon dioxide emissions. 

## Top solutions for carbon-neutral shipping

There are different ways to accomplish carbon-neutral shipping. One way is to work with a fulfillment provider that has solutions in packing and shipping products more efficiently and sustainably.

For instance, ShipBob is a third-party logistics [3PL](https://www.shipbob.com/3pl/) company that provides carbon-neutral shipping solutions for online brands, including an integration and partnership with Ecocart.

ShipBob partners with Ecocart so you can purchase carbon credits by allowing your customers to choose (and optionally, pay for) carbon offsets on a per-order basis, and allowing you to offset the carbon impact of product manufacturing and even last-mile delivery.

By integrating with Shopify, brands that use Ecocart and. ShipBob (or build a custom integration) can automatically calculate and offset their carbon footprint.

> *“Our goal was simple: offset carbon emissions. In our search for the right partner, ShipBob was proactive. We can now share accurate data with our customers regarding the success of our reforestation initiatives.”*
>
> Michael Klein, Co-Founder at Herbaly

## Consumers care about their carbon footprint

Did you know…

* The cardboard used for the approximately [165 billion packages](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonbird1/2018/07/29/what-a-waste-online-retails-big-packaging-problem/?sh=2fa48ab1371d) shipped in the United States each year equates to 1 billion trees.
* Fast delivery such as [2-day shipping](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/guide-offering-affordable-2-day-shipping/) is a significant contributor to climate change.

As climate change continues to worsen and more consumers turn to online shopping, consumers are choosing brands based on their efforts to protect the environment, including the ability to reduce their carbon footprint.

If fully aware of the carbon footprint that is left from packages and deliveries, some consumers are more likely to opt in to sustainable shipping solutions.

With information like this out there, consumers are becoming more aware of the impact carbon has on the environment.

> *“Our business is built on sustainability and we aim to provide our customers with carbon-neutral products from our natural sources to their front door. That is why we work with ShipBob to offset carbon emissions from our ecommerce supply chain.*
>
> *Minimize upfront investment and maximize positive impact on the planet by utilizing the simplest way to incorporate sustainability into your brand’s operations, carbon offsetting.”*
>
> Fannar Jonsson, Quality and Environment Manager at Blue Lagoon Skincare

## How to reduce carbon emissions from shipping

In addition to going carbon-neutral, it is important to also focus on reducing emissions throughout the supply chain. Here are different ways your business can reduce carbon emissions during the fulfillment and shipping process. 

### Use recycled & recyclable packing materials

With more people shopping online than ever before, more packing materials are being used to pack and ship orders, leaving the customer responsible for disposing waste. Eco-friendly packaging can help minimize waste and add a sustainable practice to your business. 

For some ecommerce businesses, your packaging is almost as important as your products. Packing materials should not only ensure that items are delivered safely, but there should also be a focus on sustainably.  

There are a range of materials that could be used to satisfy eco-friendly packaging for your business. 

[Eco-friendly packaging](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/eco-friendly-packaging/) options for ecommerce include: 

* Papers and cardboard
  + Easily reusable and recyclable
  + Easy to source in quantities that suit the business
* Bioplastics
  + Usually derived from plant-based materials
  + Well-suited for composting
* Biodegradable plastic packaging
  + Traditional plastics that have been modified to break down faster through the presence of heat or light
* Plant fibers
  + Eco-friendly packaging materials in the form of reusable tote bags to wrap your product
  + Made from jute and cotton
* Inflatable air pillows
  + Inflatable plastic film bags that can be used to protect products
  + Made from post-consumer recycled materials
* Corrugated bubble wrap
  + An alternative to dunnage which is the packaging to protect the goods during the shipping process (packing peanuts, bubble wrap)
  + Typically made out of 100% recycled cardboard

Some options help enable carbon-neutral shipping more than others, and the prices foe each vary. ShipBob partners with eco-friendly packaging companies like [noissue](https://www.shipbob.com/partners/noissue/) and [Packlane](https://www.shipbob.com/partners/packlane/) for brands that want [custom branded packaging](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/custom-packaging/) that’s also environmentally-conscious.

### Minimize the amount of overall packaging

Can you think of the last time you received a package in a large box when only the item took up one-third of the space?

Packing a small item in a big box is a [common packing mistake](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/packing-shipping-mistakes-businesses-makes/) and one that customers notice right away — but also one that costs businesses.

[Dimensional weight](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/dimensional-weight-explained/) is a pricing technique used by carriers that calculates the amount of space a package takes up. Sometimes, a lighter package can take up more room than a heavier one based on the DIM weight, which is computed by multiplying length x width x height. The more you minimize the amount of packaging used, the more money you might be able to save for a smaller DIM weight. 

### Avoid as much single-use plastic as possible

When it comes to keeping items safe while in transit, a lot of the time bubble wrap isn’t needed and there are plenty alternatives such as recycled kraft paper. Another option is the use of corrugated bubble wrap, which can be used in replace of packing peanuts and regular plastic bubble wrap.

### Distribute your inventory to multiple fulfillment centers

Distributing your inventory across multiple fulfillment centers can help not only [reduce shipping costs](https://www.shipbob.com/ecommerce-shipping/reduce-shipping-costs/) while speeding up transit times, but it can also reduce carbon emissions. When you [split inventory](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/split-inventory-across-multiple-fulfillment-centers/) across locations, the [distribution center](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/distribution-center/) closest to where the customer lives will pick, pack, and ship the order.

ShipBob offers a robust fulfillment network with locations across the US and globe, where you can ship customer orders through the most efficient route, saving on fuel (carbon) and getting your orders delivered sooner. 

Since ShipBob makes it easy to [track inventory](https://www.shipbob.com/inventory-management/inventory-tracking/) in real time across our fulfillment network, you can prevent different items in an order from being shipped from different locations (known as a [split shipment](https://www.shipbob.com/blog/split-shipments/)) to make sure orders are fulfilled together. This can help reduce the amount of packaging used while providing a positive customer experience.

> *“Utilizing ShipBob’s network of fulfillment centers allows us to lessen our carbon footprint as well. We’re currently storing inventory in some of ShipBob’s Southern California and Chicago facilities, which means that when we receive an order destined for someplace like New York, we don’t have to ship it from all the way across the country. By shortening the transit distance, we get to shorten transit time and reduce the amount of pollution produced in the shipping process. Even in the final stages of fulfillment and last-mile delivery, ShipBob enables us to stay true to our mission!”*
>
> — Juliana Brasil, Director of Operations at Food Huggers

# Delivery Decarbonization Pathway

![Home](/etc.clientlibs/oliverwymanv2/clientlibs/clientlib-site/resources/images/house_icon.svg)

The breadth of products offered through e-commerce has expanded, and more categories are now available online, from a greater number of vendors around the globe. Online and offline shopping are more closely integrated, and second-hand goods are increasingly popular. More delivery options are available, and related services — such as tracking and rerouting — are becoming standard.

This growing diversity offers customers more opportunity and choice to find what they want. But it also makes it increasingly difficult for both shoppers and retailers to understand the environmental impact of online purchases — and, more specifically, of delivery.

[Our previous study of e-commerce, published in 2021](/our-expertise/insights/2021/apr/is-e-commerce-good-for-europe.html), highlighted that in Europe, the environmental impact of e-commerce is positive: Online shopping in Europe generates an average of between 1.5 and 2.9 times less greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions than offline shopping. The study also demonstrated that emissions from both types of shopping vary significantly by product type, country, and — more importantly — customers’ locations and purchasing behavior.

The objective of this study is to go to a further level of granularity and focus on delivery emissions — to compare the emissions from various delivery models, to identify the main drivers, and to determine how delivery-related emissions of CO2 equivalent (CO2e) can be further reduced. Does home delivery generate higher emissions than pickup-point delivery (PUDO: pick up, drop off)? Does faster delivery result in higher emissions? How can the best technologies available today help reduce delivery emissions? What would it take to reach a 30% reduction in emissions per parcel by 2030 compared to the 2019 level?

Several major parcel operators have committed to at least matching the EU Green Deal target of being climate-neutral by 2050. Among them, the sustainability leaders are aiming to reach net zero by 2040, 10 years earlier. Most initiatives address the entire value chain, encompassing renewable energy sourcing and production, carbon-neutral buildings, carbon-neutral packaging, and zero-emissions transport — and complementing these measures with carbon offsetting.

To substantially reduce delivery-related emissions, resources and efforts will need to be focused on the levers with the greatest impact, and multiple complex solutions will have to be navigated. This calls for a comprehensive assessment of the emissions generated by today’s delivery modes and an understanding of possible trajectories to decarbonize these modes.  
This new study focuses on six countries, which together account for over 60% of European online sales: France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. It is based on an analysis of official statistics, our proprietary CO2e impact model, data made public by delivery operators and confirmed through interviews, and consumer surveys conducted in 2022.

## Customer standpoint: Faster delivery, more delivery options, more attention to the environment

Beyond prices, consumers are often faced with three major questions when choosing a delivery option: Do they want a parcel delivered to their home – or to a nearby location where they can pick it up? How fast do they want to get their purchase? And what is the environmental impact of the available options?

Home delivery remains the preferred option for receiving an article purchased online in the six countries studied. On average, more than 60% of e-shoppers say they favor it:  
Fast delivery (in less than two days) is an important decision factor for 45% of e-shoppers and for up to 72% of frequent buyers. Next-day delivery is offered by 70% of the largest  
European e-stores.

87% of all e-shoppers are keen to change their habits if it can reduce their environmental impact. Their preferred actions are, in order: grouping orders (26%), favoring national shipment (16%), walking to a PUDO location (16%), and choosing an environmentally friendly merchant (16%). The least-popular action, preferred by just 13%, is a delayed delivery if it could reduce delivery emissions.

## Emissions from delivery models: Scale and country energy mix matter more than speed

Our analysis shows that delivering at home a single, 1 kg parcel through a country’s most common postal system in two days or more generates an average of 1,075 gCO2e, a measure of the global-warming effect of greenhouse gases in terms of the equivalent quantity of carbon dioxide. Different delivery models were compared to understand the key emissions drivers. The results show that the best way to minimize emissions per parcel is not to reduce delivery speed but to optimize last mile delivery and use the largest possible vehicles in the linehaul and maximize their loads.

The second most important factor influencing emissions is the size and location of buildings — hubs, delivery stations, and pickup points. Buildings’ impact can be even greater than that of transportation, especially in countries that depend heavily on fossil fuels to produce electric power, such as Germany and Italy (500 to 600 gCO2e per parcel compared to the average of 300 gCO2e per parcel).

Delivery speed by itself does not drive emissions. When ranking delivery options by lead time for the consumer (the gap between ordering and delivery), emissions form a U-curve: the fastest and slowest options have the highest emissions (see Exhibit 1). The slowest option (international delivery in 10 days or more) has the highest emissions (six times the level of national delivery). National deliveries in one to four days generate emissions ranging between 10% lower and 15% higher than national standard delivery. Same day options can generate emissions up to three or four times higher than national standard.

![](/content/dam/oliver-wyman/v2/publications/2023/may/Exhibit%201-web%20exhibit_780%20px.png)

## Decarbonization pathway: 30% reduction by 2030, then 60% reduction at full potential with known technologies

Reaching a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 would require action on all sources of emissions, through the generalization of today’s best practices, the deployment of emerging clean motorization technologies, and the improvement of countries’ energy mixes. This 30% goal has been derived from the various targets set by the EU Commission for trucks, vans, packaging, national energy mixes, and other factors.

In the long term, pushing decarbonation drivers to the maximum level technically possible could lead to a reduction in overall emissions of between 55% and 60% to 448 gCO2e. That would leave 40% to 45% remaining before full carbon neutrality is achieved, through new technologies or infrastructure that is even more energy efficient.

The study does not use any private information from Amazon or other retailers or transport operators. Consumer behavior data is based on proprietary surveys conducted by Oliver Wyman in 2022 across Europe (France, Germany, United Kingdom, Sweden, Italy, Spain).*

# Carbon Neutral Shipping: What It Is, How It Works, and Benefits

**Posted By:**  [Amy Roach](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/author/amy-roach/)

**Tags:** [Green Logistics](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/tags/green)

Growing demand for greener logistics has made carbon-neutral shipping a key strategy for reducing carbon emissions and shrinking the carbon footprint of global trade. By adopting neutral shipping, companies help lower global greenhouse gas emissions, meet environmental goals, and stay relevant in a fast-changing market.

[Shipping goods across countries](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/9-best-practices-for-global-logistics-management/) and oceans has become the backbone of modern trade. Yet, this fast-paced shipping industry leaves a heavy environmental footprint. With rising concern over [climate change](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/weathering-climate-change-and-supply-chain-risk/), businesses are under pressure to adopt sustainable methods that make a real difference.

Carbon-neutral shipping is one powerful way to take action. It tackles high carbon emissions and fuel consumption in supply chains, showing why is carbon-neutral shipping important for building a cleaner, more responsible logistics future.

Since the supply chain is a significant contributor to [greenhouse gas emissions](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/solving-the-emissions-challenge/), switching to eco-friendly transportation helps reduce carbon emissions and promotes a sustainable future for logistics.

## What Is Carbon Neutral Shipping?

Carbon-neutral shipping means balancing out the carbon emissions created during the shipping process by reducing what you can and offsetting the carbon you can’t.

Companies first track emissions, then lower them through eco-friendly steps, and finally use carbon offsets like reforestation initiatives or carbon credits to handle the remaining emissions. Every stage of the delivery journey, right from the warehouse to [last-mile delivery](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/last-mile-delivery/), can support [carbon neutrality](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/carbon-neutrality-is-shaping-fleets-of-the-future/).

With rising pressure from the climate crisis and stricter laws, carbon-neutral shipping options give businesses a chance to show commitment to [sustainable practices](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/g75-inbound-logistics-75-green-supply-chain-partners/) and a positive environmental impact.

## How Carbon Neutral Shipping Works?

Many shipping companies use this structured process to lower their carbon footprint and move toward [net-zero emissions logistics](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/biomass-gasification-waste-logistics/). Here’s how it works:

* **Measuring shipping emissions:** Companies use freight data or carbon footprint assessment tools to track emissions generated across each leg of the supply chain. Calculating the total amount of carbon comes first.
* **Reducing emissions:** Route planning, alternative fuel vehicles, and optimized logistics help reduce carbon and fuel consumption. Smart changes can also drive waste reduction and save shipping costs.
* **Offsetting emissions:** Firms purchase carbon offsets through verified environmental projects such as carbon removal, green energy, or reforestation initiatives to balance out the carbon dioxide emissions that remain.
* **Verifying emissions reductions:** Independent audits confirm claimed emissions reductions. Certification ensures transparency, avoids greenwashing, and builds trust in carbon-neutral operations.

Every step pushes companies closer to achieving carbon neutrality and delivering eco-friendly transportation solutions.

## Environmental and Business Benefits

Many companies now focus on [sustainable practices](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/green-logistics/) because cutting carbon emissions improves long-term performance, meets sustainability goals, and supports a more sustainable future for logistics. The following are the key environmental and business benefits:

### Emissions Reduction and Climate Impact

Using carbon-neutral shipping helps cut down carbon dioxide emissions across the entire shipping process. Lowering greenhouse gas emissions through carbon offset shipping programs supports efforts to combat climate change.

Firms that switch from fossil fuels to cleaner energy sources help drive emissions reductions. Pairing carbon offsets with smarter operations reduces the amount of carbon released and makes a measurable positive impact on the environment.

### Enhanced Brand Image

Consumers prefer brands that offer carbon-neutral shipping and support eco-friendly values. Buyers expect companies to act responsibly when it comes to climate change and the environmental impact of their services.

Using eco-friendly packaging, biodegradable packing peanuts, and carbon-neutral shipping options can improve reputation and loyalty. Clear action, backed by real data, proves commitment to a carbon-neutral future and strengthens market position.

### Regulatory Preparedness

New rules around greenhouse gas tracking and [carbon footprint](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/whitepapers/the-easiest-way-to-reduce-your-companys-carbon-footprint/) reporting will change how shipping works. Businesses that adopt neutral shipping now stay ahead of future legislation. By investing early in carbon capture, carbon credits, and emissions tracking, they avoid sudden costs and delays later.

Adopting carbon-neutral shipping signals readiness for policy shifts, aligns operations with future regulations, improves long-term strategy, and helps companies stay competitive as global climate standards and market expectations continue to evolve.

### Operational Efficiency

Improving fuel usage and packaging choices helps reduce carbon emissions while saving shipping costs. Tactics like fuel-efficient routing, load consolidation, and switching to biodegradable packaging materials lower fuel consumption.

Businesses also cut waste by selecting smarter packing materials and planning smarter delivery routes. In the long run, carbon-neutral shipping not only helps the planet but also creates leaner, more cost-effective operations.

## Challenges of Implementing Carbon Neutral Shipping

Companies aiming for carbon-neutral shipping face several obstacles. Tracking data, managing costs, and avoiding misleading claims require focus, tools, and clear action to stay credible and efficient. The following are the potential implementation challenges:

### Data Accuracy and Emissions Tracking

Collecting accurate data across a full supply chain is difficult. Different regions, carriers, and shipment types create gaps in tracking emissions generated during the shipping process. Without clear numbers, it’s hard to reduce carbon emissions effectively or prove carbon offset shipping success.

Investing in systems for [real-time tracking](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/real-time-load-tracking-improving-productivity-and-customer-service-and-reducing/) and emissions monitoring helps improve transparency, ensures accurate reporting of carbon data, builds trust with stakeholders, and supports consistent progress toward reliable and measurable carbon-neutral operations.

### Cost of Offsetting

Buying carbon offsets and joining verified programs often raises expenses. Smaller logistics providers and [ecommerce](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/ecommerce-fulfillment-how-to-keep-it-rolling/) businesses may struggle with upfront investments while balancing customer expectations. Offset pricing depends on location, project type, and scale.

Without smart planning, efforts to reduce emissions may cut into margins. Choosing flexible options and aligning offsets with carbon-neutral shipping goals can ease the impact while building a more eco-friendly brand image.

### Greenwashing Concerns

Brands that offer carbon-neutral shipping without proof risk being called out for greenwashing. Unsupported claims damage trust and invite criticism. Customers expect honesty and results, not marketing buzzwords.

Transparent reporting, third-party audits, and clear use of carbon offsets validate progress. Making real changes, like switching to eco-friendly packaging or reducing power consumption, backs up words with action and helps maintain a strong reputation in a competitive space.

## Best Practices for Businesses Adopting Carbon Neutral Shipping

Companies that act with intention and clarity gain long-term benefits from carbon-neutral shipping. Success starts with a clear roadmap, the right tools, and steady improvements over time. Here are the best practices:

* **Start with a Carbon Footprint Assessment:** Analyze your carbon emissions across operations to identify high-impact areas and map out a plan to reduce carbon emissions effectively using real shipment data.
* **Choose Carriers That Offer Offset Options:** Partner with carriers that support offsetting carbon through trusted carbon offset shipping programs aligned with recognized climate standards and third-party verification.
* **Invest in Emissions Tracking Software:** Use tools that track emissions generated in real time and support decisions across packaging, routing, and power consumption for smarter performance.
* **Integrate Route Optimization and Smart Packaging:** Plan routes that reduce travel time and use compact packing materials to lower fuel use, cut waste, and reduce carbon emissions.
* **Purchase Verified Carbon Credits:** Buy carbon offsets from credible providers linked to real carbon dioxide reductions, ensuring that your efforts lead to measurable environmental progress.
* **Communicate Your Strategy Transparently:** Share your carbon-neutral shipping goals, progress, and numbers clearly across customer channels, earning trust and support through honest engagement.
* **Continuously Review and Adjust Your Sustainability Goals:** Track changes, monitor outcomes, and align with evolving standards to improve your impact and avoid setbacks across the shipping process.

## Conclusion

Growing demand for greener logistics has made carbon-neutral shipping a key strategy for reducing carbon emissions and shrinking the carbon footprint of global trade. By adopting neutral shipping, companies help lower global greenhouse gas emissions, meet environmental goals, and stay relevant in a fast-changing market.

Smart changes like consolidating shipments, optimizing fuel use, and offsetting carbon emissions support both cost savings and sustainability. Evaluate your current methods, set clear goals, and invest in solutions that reduce emissions and fuel consumption.

Choosing carbon-neutral shipping today helps save resources, earn trust, and build long-term value with more money saved over time.

Join them by signing up for our free, weekly newsletter for supply chain and logistics news you can use.

Climate Action

# Reducing emissions from the shipping sector

> On 17 July 2026, the European Commission proposed a targeted **revision of the** [**EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS)**](/areas-action/carbon-markets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets_en) to strengthen Europe's industrial competitiveness and support the delivery of the EU's [2040 climate target](/areas-action/climate-strategies-targets/2040-climate-target_en).
>
> The proposal reinforces the EU ETS as a driver of investment, with significant additional support for industrial decarbonisation through a new Industrial Decarbonisation Bank, an Investment Booster and continued funding under the [Innovation Fund](/areas-action/eu-funding-climate-action/innovation-fund_en) and the [Modernisation Fund](/areas-action/eu-funding-climate-action/modernisation-fund_en).
>
> It also modernises the carbon market, strengthens incentives for companies to invest in decarbonisation in Europe, updates the rules on free allocation and the [Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)](https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism_en), strengthens the existing ETS for aviation and maritime transport, and gradually extends emissions trading to municipal waste incineration.
>
> **This page will be updated shortly with detailed information on the proposed reforms.**
>
> Relevant links:
>
> * [Press release](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1596)
> * [Regulation proposal - Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) of maritime emissions (including Annex)](/document/download/2a0f3e9c-5562-4253-8327-dc7bea886ed8_en)
> * [Impact assessment on the ETS Directive (including ETS maritime)](/document/download/6e4dc8de-dd98-46c4-89d1-efa66085532d_en) + [Executive summary](/document/download/df131f37-7733-486f-9361-08ea88436ee0_en?filename=swd_2026_617_en.pdf)

While maritime transport plays an essential role in the EU economy and is one of the most energy-efficient modes of transport, it is also a large and growing source of greenhouse gas emissions. In 2018, global shipping emissions represented 1 076 million tonnes of CO2, and were responsible for around 2.9% of global emissions caused by human activities.

Projections show that these emissions could increase by up to 130% [of 2008 emissions](https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Environment/Pages/Fourth-IMO-Greenhouse-Gas-Study-2020.aspx) by 2050. If the climate change impact of shipping activities grows as projected, it will undermine the objectives of the [Paris Agreement](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement): a global framework to avoid dangerous climate change by limiting global warming to well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

At EU level, maritime transport represents 3 to 4% of the EU’s total CO2 emissions, or over [124 million tonnes of CO2 in 2021](/document/download/e3ddba7a-c068-4f87-a7c2-e98d63e56cf0_en?filename=swd_2023_54_en.pdf).

In order to significantly reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping, effective global measures are desirable. In July 2023 the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) made a step on this path committing to new targets for GHG emissions reductions and to develop and adopt in 2025 a basket of measure(s), delivering on these reduction targets. The next years to come will show which measures will be adopted and become applicable and whether they will commensurate with achieving these targets and the objectives of the Paris Agreement. The EU action to make sure maritime transport plays its part in achieving climate neutrality in Europe by 2050 is an essential step in incentivising the necessary reductions.

## EU action

### Inclusion of maritime emissions in the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)

Since January 2024, the [EU's Emissions Trading System](/areas-action/carbon-markets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets_en) (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.

The system covers:

* 50% of emissions from voyages starting or ending outside of the EU (allowing the third country to decide on appropriate action for the remaining share of emissions);
* 100% of emissions that occur between two EU ports and when ships are within EU ports.

The EU ETS covers CO2 (carbon dioxide), CH4 (methane) and N2O (nitrous oxide) emissions, but the two latter only as from 2026.

Emissions from maritime transport are included in the overall ETS cap, which defines the maximum amount of greenhouse gases that can be emitted under the system. The cap is reduced over time to ensure that all ETS sectors contribute to the EU’s climate objectives. This will incentivise energy efficiency, low-carbon solutions, and reductions of the price difference between alternative fuels and traditional maritime fuels.

The system builds on the provisions in place for other EU ETS sectors, as well as the recently revised [EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification Regulation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02015R0757-20240101) for maritime transport (‘MRV Maritime Regulation’).

In practice, shipping companies have to purchase and surrender (use) EU ETS emission allowances for each tonne of reported CO2 (or CO2 equivalent) emissions in the scope of the EU ETS system. It is the role of administering authorities of EU Member States to ensure compliance using similar rules as for the other ETS sectors.

To ensure a smooth transition, shipping companies only have to surrender allowances for a portion of their emissions during an initial phase-in period:

* 2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024;
* 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025;
* 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions.

The [first surrendering deadline](/news-other-reads/news/changes-existing-ets-and-mrv-applying-1-january-2024-2024-04-26_en) falls due in September 2025 in all Member States, in respect of emissions reported as taking place from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024.

A reporting and review clause is included to monitor the implementation of the rules applicable to the maritime sector and to take into account relevant developments in the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

These rules were adopted on 16 May 2023 and entered into force on 5 June 2023. You will find the legal texts below:

* [Amendments to the Regulation on the Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) for maritime transport (Regulation (EU) 2015/757)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/957)
  + [Consolidated version](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02015R0757-20240101)
* [Amendments to the ETS Directive (Directive EC/2003/87/EC)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/959)

### Legislative process

The legislation on the inclusion of maritime emissions in the EU ETS has been complemented by several implementing and delegated acts. These spell out detailed rules and allow for a timely inclusion of the emissions from maritime transport within the EU ETS.

Those acts notably cover the following topics:

* the administration of shipping companies by Member States;
* the submission of aggregated emissions data at shipping company level;
* rules for the monitoring of greenhouse gas emissions;
* updates of the relevant templates;
* verification and accreditation procedures;
* identification of neighbouring container transhipment ports;
* small islands and transnational routes under public service obligation or contract subject to specific provisions under the ETS Directive.

To prepare these acts, the Commission is assisted by a maritime formation within the existing [Expert Group on Climate Change Policy (CCEG)](https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/expert-groups-register/screen/expert-groups/consult?lang=en&do=groupDetail.groupDetail&groupID=3590&Lang=FR), where experts from Member States are represented. In addition, the Commission has consulted the [European Sustainable Shipping Forum (ESSF) where industry and civil society are also represented](https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/sustainable-transport/european-sustainable-shipping-forum_en). The acts are also prepared with the support of the [European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA)](https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/institutions-and-bodies/search-all-eu-institutions-and-bodies/european-maritime-safety-agency-emsa_en).

In October 2023, the [EU Climate Change Committee](https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/comitology-register/screen/committees/C13600/consult?lang=en) gave a favourable opinion on three implementing acts. These acts have been adopted by the Commission and published in the Official Journal of the European Union:

* [Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2297 of 26 October 2023 identifying neighbouring container transhipment ports pursuant to Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2297)
* [Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2449 of 6 November 2023 laying down rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards templates for monitoring plans, emissions reports, partial emissions reports, documents of compliance, and reports at company level, and repealing Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1927](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2449)
* [Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2599 of 22 November 2023 laying down rules for the application of Directive 2003/87/EC as regards the administration of shipping companies by administering authorities in respect of a shipping company](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202302599)

Three delegated acts have also been published in the Official Journal of the European Union in December 2023:

* [Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2849 of 12 October 2023 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2015/757 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the rules for reporting and submission of the aggregated emissions data at company level](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R2849&qid=1702630146956)
* [Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2776 of 12 October 2023 amending Regulation (EU) 2015/757 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the rules for monitoring greenhouse gas emissions and other relevant information from maritime transport](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R2776&qid=1702640649198)
* [Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 of 20 October 2023 on the verification activities, accreditation of verifiers and approval of monitoring plans by administering authorities pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2015/757 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the monitoring, reporting and verification of greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport, and repealing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2917)

Also in December 2023, the Commission has adopted an implementing act laying down the list of islands and ports and the list of transnational public service contracts concerned by the specific derogations pursuant to Article 12(3-d) and (3-c) of the ETS Directive:

* [Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2895 of 19 December 2023 laying down the list of islands and ports referred to in Article 12(3-d) of Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and the list of transnational public service contracts or transnational public service obligations referred to in Article 12(3-c) of that Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202302895)

The Commission adopted an implementing act on the list of shipping companies on 30 January 2024, specifying their responsible administering authority:

* [Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/411 of 30 January 2024 on the list of shipping companies specifying the administering authority in respect of a shipping company in accordance with Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202400411)

### Monitoring, reporting and verifying GHG emissions

Since 1 January 2018, large ships over 5 000 gross tonnage loading or unloading cargo or passengers at ports in the European Economic Area (EEA) must monitor and report related GHG emissions (currently only CO2 emissions, but also nitrous oxide and methane emissions as of 1 January 2024) and other relevant information. Monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) of information must be done in conformity with the ‘MRV Maritime Regulation.

The MRV Maritime Regulation was conceived as a first step before the inclusion of these emissions within the scope of the EU Emissions Trading System. The MRV Maritime Regulation was [revised in 2023](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/957) in the light of the inclusion of maritime transport emissions within the scope of the EU ETS.

The MRV Maritime Regulation is complemented by four other legal acts:

* [Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/2072 on the verification activities and accreditation of verifiers](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32016R2072)
* [Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/2071 as regards the methods for monitoring carbon dioxide emissions and the rules for monitoring other relevant information](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2016.320.01.0001.01.ENG)
* [Implementing Regulation 2016/1927 on templates](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32016R1927)
* [Implementing Regulation 2016/1928 further defining cargo carried for some ship categories](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32016R1928)

**Main obligations** for companies eligible under the MRV Maritime Regulation:

* **Monitoring:** companies must – in line with their respective monitoring plans – monitor, for each of their ships, greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption and other parameters, such as distance travelled, time at sea and cargo carried on a per voyage basis, so as to gather annual data into an emissions report verified by an accredited MRV shipping verifier.
* **Emissions report:** by 30 April of each year (31 March as of 2025), companies must, through [THETIS MRV](https://mrv.emsa.europa.eu/), submit to the Commission and to the States in which those ships are registered (‘flag States’) a satisfactorily verified emissions report for each ship that has performed maritime transport activities in the European Economic Area in the previous reporting period (calendar year). As from 31 March 2025, emissions reports should also be submitted to the responsible administering authority trough THETIS-MRV.
* **Document of compliance:** by 30 June of each year, companies must ensure that all their ships that have performed activities in the previous reporting period and are visiting ports in the European Economic Area carry on board a document of compliance. This might be subject to inspections by Member States' authorities.

Every year, the Commission publishes a report to inform the public about the greenhouse gas emissions and energy efficiency information of the monitored fleet. You can find the annual reports in our [Documentation](#documentation) section below.

### Delivering the European Green Deal with maritime transport

As part of the European Commission’s legislative proposals to [deliver the European Green Deal](https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal_en) - the ‘Fit for 55’ package - published on 14 July 2021, several proposals addressed maritime transport’s climate impact, in addition to the extension of the EU ETS.

This includes:

* A new FuelEU maritime Regulation to boost the demand for marine [renewable and low-carbon fuels](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021PC0562), by setting a maximum limit on the greenhouse gas content of energy used by ships calling at European ports and by encouraging zero-emission technology at berth (where ships stay in ports), with a technology-neutral approach;
* Revising the [Directive on Deployment of Alternative Fuels Infrastructure](https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/clean-transport/alternative-fuels-sustainable-mobility-europe/alternative-fuels-infrastructure_en), which would set, among other benefits, mandatory targets for shore-side electricity supply at maritime and inland waterway ports;
* Accelerating the supply of renewables in the EU, through a [revision of the Renewable Energy Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021PC0557) (RED), which increases the current EU target of at least 32% of renewable energy sources in the overall energy mix to at least 40% by 2030, with a focus on sectors where progress has been slower to date – including transport;
* [Revising the existing Energy Taxation Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021PC0563) (ETD), which aims to align the taxation of energy products with the EU’s climate objectives and remove outdated exemptions, such as those for the intra-EU maritime transport sector.

This basket of measures reflects the EU’s goal to cut greenhouse gas emissions by addressing the various barriers to the decarbonisation of the shipping sector (technological barriers, economic barriers, etc.). The Commission aims to do that through two complementary angles: first, the improvement of energy efficiency (i.e. using less fuel) and, second, the greater use of renewable and low-carbon fuels (i.e. using cleaner fuels). These measures will allow the creation of a virtuous ecosystem for such cleaner fuels, as they will boost at the same time fuel demand, distribution, and supply.

Besides continuing to push for global action at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), the Commission will continue supporting research and innovation towards the decarbonisation of maritime transport, in particular through [Horizon Europe](https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en) and the [Innovation Fund](/areas-action/eu-funding-climate-action/innovation-fund_en).

## Global action

### IMO Data Collection System

Following the adoption of the MRV Maritime Regulation in 2015, the IMO established an IMO Data Collection System.

The system requires owners of large ships (above 5 000 gross tonnage) engaged in international shipping to report information on fuel consumption of their ships to the flag States of those ships. The flag States then report aggregated data to the IMO, which must produce an annual summary report to the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee.

The collection of fuel consumption data under the IMO Data Collection System started on 1 January 2019.

In February 2019, the European Commission made a [proposal](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CONSIL:ST_6117_2019_INIT) to amend the MRV maritime Regulation to take appropriate account of the global data collection system, with the objective to streamline and reduce administrative effort for companies and administrations as possible.

### 2023 IMO greenhouse gas strategy

In July 2023, the IMO agreed to revise its initial greenhouse gas emissions reduction strategy.

The revised 2023 strategy sets a goal of net zero emissions from ships “by or around, i.e. close to, 2050”. This is a major increase in the level of ambition compared to the existing 2018 strategy, which aimed at reducing emissions from ships by just 50% in the same time horizon.

A trajectory has also been agreed with indicative checkpoints set at reducing GHG emissions from ships by at least 20% - striving for 30% - in 2030 and at least 70% - striving for 80% - in 2040, both in comparison to 2008 levels.

The strategy also sets an important target of at least 5% - striving for 10% - uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources by 2030.

These levels of ambition and indicative checkpoints take into account the lifecycle GHG emissions from marine fuels with the objective of reducing emissions within the boundaries of the energy system of international shipping.

The IMO reached consensus on the need to adopt additional GHG reduction measures by 2025 to reach the agreed targets. These measures should comprise a standard regulating the gradual reduction of the marine fuels' GHG intensity, and a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. They will be developed on the basis of a comprehensive impact assessment ensuring that they effectively reduce emissions from the sector, while contributing to a level playing field and a fair and equitable transition leaving no one behind.

## EU support to IMO energy efficiency project

The European Commission contributes €10 million in funding to an [EC-IMO energy efficiency project](http://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/PressBriefings/Pages/01-2016-MTCC-.aspx).

As part of a 4-year project, Maritime Technology Cooperation Centres have been set up in 5 regions: Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America and the Pacific.

Through technical assistance and capacity-building, the centres promote the uptake of low carbon technologies and operations in maritime transport in less developed countries.

This will also support the implementation of the internationally agreed **energy efficiency rules and standards** – Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) and Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP).

args.summary:
This European Commission webpage details EU policies and actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the shipping sector, a key part of the European Green Deal and "Fit for 55" package.

**Key Context:** Global shipping emissions were ~1,076 million tonnes of CO2 in 2018 (~2.9% of global emissions). At EU level, maritime transport represents 3-4% of total CO2 emissions (over 124 million tonnes in 2021). Projections show emissions could increase by up to 130% of 2008 levels by 2050.

**EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) for Maritime:**
- Since January 2024, the EU ETS covers CO2 emissions from all large ships (≥5,000 gross tonnage) entering EU ports, regardless of flag.
- Coverage: 50% of emissions from voyages starting/ending outside the EU; 100% of emissions between two EU ports and within EU ports.
- Covers CO2, and from 2026 also CH4 (methane) and N2O (nitrous oxide).
- Phase-in period for surrendering allowances: 2025 (40% of 2024 emissions), 2026 (70% of 2025 emissions), 2027 onwards (100%).
- First surrendering deadline: September 2025.
- Rules adopted 16 May 2023, entered into force 5 June 2023.

**Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV):**
- Since 1 January 2018, large ships must monitor and report GHG emissions via THETIS-MRV.
- Annual emissions reports due by 30 April (31 March as of 2025). Documents of compliance must be carried on board by 30 June annually.

**Broader "Fit for 55" Package for Maritime:**
- FuelEU Maritime Regulation: Sets limits on GHG content of energy used by ships calling at European ports; encourages zero-emission technology at berth.
- Revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Directive: Mandatory targets for shore-side electricity supply at ports.
- Revised Renewable Energy Directive: Targets at least 40% renewable energy by 2030.
- Revised Energy Taxation Directive: Aligns taxation with climate objectives, removes exemptions for intra-EU maritime.

**Global Action:**
- IMO 2023 revised strategy: Net-zero emissions from ships "by or around 2050." Indicative checkpoints: at least 20% (striving for 30%) reduction by 2030; at least 70% (striving for 80%) by 2040 (vs 2008). At least 5% (striving for 10%) uptake of zero/near-zero emission technologies by 2030.
- IMO to adopt additional GHG reduction measures by 2025, including a fuel GHG intensity standard and a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism.

**On 17 July 2026**, the European Commission proposed a targeted revision of the EU ETS to strengthen industrial competitiveness and support the EU's 2040 climate target, including a new Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and updates to rules for maritime transport.

--- SOURCE 6: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)? ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/learn/what-is-artificial-intelligence

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive guide from Google Cloud explaining artificial intelligence (AI) in simple terms. AI is defined as a field of computer science focused on creating smart machines that can perform tasks requiring human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. AI systems learn from vast amounts of data by identifying patterns to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed for every scenario.

**How AI works:** AI relies on data, algorithms, and computational power. Key areas include Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Computer Vision.

**Types of AI by capability:**
- **Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI):** The only existing form of AI, designed for specific tasks like image recognition or chatbots. Examples include voice assistants and generative AI models like Gemini.
- **Artificial General Intelligence (AGI):** A proposed future AI that would perform a broad range of tasks with human-like reasoning. Does not yet exist.
- **Artificial Superintelligence (ASI):** A theoretical self-aware entity surpassing human intelligence, potentially posing existential risks.

**Types by functionality:** Reactive machines (no memory, e.g., IBM's Deep Blue), Limited memory (most modern AI, e.g., self-driving cars, chatbots), and Theory of mind (does not yet exist, would emulate human emotions and social interaction).

**Benefits of AI:** Automation, reducing human error, eliminating repetitive tasks, fast and accurate data processing, infinite availability, and accelerated research and development.

**Real-world applications:** Daily life (smartphone assistants, recommendations, spam filters, navigation), healthcare (diagnosing diseases, drug discovery), transportation (autonomous vehicles), business operations (customer service, fraud detection, supply chain optimization), and entertainment (video games, content creation).

**History of AI:** The concept dates back to the 1940s-1950s with Alan Turing's Turing Test (1950). The field was officially born at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project in 1956. Early successes (ELIZA chatbot, Shakey the Robot) were followed by "AI Winters." The 1980s-2000s saw revival through expert systems and machine learning, with IBM's Deep Blue defeating a chess grandmaster in 1997. The modern boom (2010s-present) is driven by advances in computing power, massive datasets, and deep learning.

**Cutting-edge developments:** Generative AI (creates new content), Large Language Models (LLMs) powering sophisticated text-based applications, AI agents (systems that perceive, plan, reason, and act autonomously), and Agentic AI (autonomous operation capability).

The guide also addresses common myths: AI is not conscious or emotional, AI can be biased based on training data, and AI is more likely to augment human jobs rather than replace them entirely.
</summary>

4. **Inventory accuracy rate** – Measures the difference between physical stock and system-recorded stock. A 3PL can improve this through cycle counts, scanner tracking, software integrations, and advanced forecasting models.

5. **Average cost per order** – Total fulfillment costs (inbounding, storage, picking, packing, shipping) divided by total orders. A 3PL can identify cost drivers and optimize operations to reduce costs.

6. **Listing Quality and Ranking Metrics** – Best Seller Rank (BSR, updated hourly), Sessions (unique visitors within 24 hours), and Conversion Rate (Unit Session Percentage, recommended at least 15%).

URL: https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/transport-decarbonisation/reducing-emissions-shipping-sector_en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This European Commission webpage details EU policies and actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the shipping sector, a key part of the European Green Deal and "Fit for 55" package.

**Key Context:** Global shipping emissions were ~1,076 million tonnes of CO2 in 2018 (~2.9% of global emissions). At EU level, maritime transport represents 3-4% of total CO2 emissions (over 124 million tonnes in 2021). Projections show emissions could increase by up to 130% of 2008 levels by 2050.

**EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) for Maritime:**
- Since January 2024, the EU ETS covers CO2 emissions from all large ships (≥5,000 gross tonnage) entering EU ports, regardless of flag.
- Coverage: 50% of emissions from voyages starting/ending outside the EU; 100% of emissions between two EU ports and within EU ports.
- Covers CO2, and from 2026 also CH4 (methane) and N2O (nitrous oxide).
- Phase-in period for surrendering allowances: 2025 (40% of 2024 emissions), 2026 (70% of 2025 emissions), 2027 onwards (100%).
- First surrendering deadline: September 2025.
- Rules adopted 16 May 2023, entered into force 5 June 2023.

**Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV):**
- Since 1 January 2018, large ships must monitor and report GHG emissions via THETIS-MRV.
- Annual emissions reports due by 30 April (31 March as of 2025). Documents of compliance must be carried on board by 30 June annually.

**Broader "Fit for 55" Package for Maritime:**
- FuelEU Maritime Regulation: Sets limits on GHG content of energy used by ships calling at European ports; encourages zero-emission technology at berth.
- Revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Directive: Mandatory targets for shore-side electricity supply at ports.
- Revised Renewable Energy Directive: Targets at least 40% renewable energy by 2030.
- Revised Energy Taxation Directive: Aligns taxation with climate objectives, removes exemptions for intra-EU maritime.

**Global Action:**
- IMO 2023 revised strategy: Net-zero emissions from ships "by or around 2050." Indicative checkpoints: at least 20% (striving for 30%) reduction by 2030; at least 70% (striving for 80%) by 2040 (vs 2008). At least 5% (striving for 10%) uptake of zero/near-zero emission technologies by 2030.
- IMO to adopt additional GHG reduction measures by 2025, including a fuel GHG intensity standard and a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism.

**On 17 July 2026**, the European Commission proposed a targeted revision of the EU ETS to strengthen industrial competitiveness and support the EU's 2040 climate target, including a new Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and updates to rules for maritime transport.
</summary>

**Straits Research (E-Commerce Platform Software Market):**
- The global e-commerce platform software market was valued at **USD 8.09 billion in 2025** and is projected to grow from **USD 9.06 billion in 2026 to USD 22.51 billion by 2034**, registering a **CAGR of 12.04%** during the forecast period (2026-2034). [Source 11]

The most commonly cited figures place the 2025 market size around **$7-9 billion** and the 2026 market size around **$8-10 billion**.

### 1B. Total Global E-Commerce Market (GMV / Revenue)

This is the total value of goods and services sold through e-commerce channels.

**IMARC Group:**
- The global e-commerce market was valued at **USD 33.80 Trillion in 2025** (including B2B and B2C) and is projected to reach **USD 243.40 Trillion by 2034**, growing at a **CAGR of 24.54%** (2026-2034). The market is forecast to reach **USD 101.17 Trillion by 2030**. [Source 1]

**The Business Research Company (TBRC):**

**Research Nester:**
- The global E-commerce market was valued at **USD 37.2 trillion in 2025** and is projected to reach **USD 215.2 trillion by 2035**, growing at a **CAGR of 19.2%** from 2026 to 2035. The 2026 estimated market size is **USD 44.3 trillion**. [Source 4]

**Grand View Research:**

**MarketScale / Market Research Future (July 2026 report):**

**Speed Commerce:**
- Global retail ecommerce sales totaled approximately **$6.42 trillion in 2025**. For 2026, multiple forecasters converge on a figure near **$6.88 trillion**, suggesting year-over-year growth of roughly **7.2%**. [Source 24]

- **Cloud-Based platforms** led (~49% of deployments) in headless commerce. [Source 4]
- **Omnichannel Commerce** leads (~54% of enterprise integrations) in headless commerce applications. [Source 4]
- **Retail Companies** dominate (~57% of deployments) in headless commerce. [Source 4]
- **India** recorded 31% annual growth in composable storefront integrations. [Source 4]
- **May 2026:** Shopify processed over **USD 100 billion in quarterly gross merchandise volume**. [Source 4]

**Coherent Market Insights (Headless Commerce Market):**
- The Global Headless Commerce Market is estimated to be valued at **US$ 2.13 Bn in 2026** and expected to reach **US$ 7.24 Bn by 2033**, growing at a **CAGR of 22.6%** from 2026 to 2033. [Source 5]
- **Web-based commerce** leads with **53.4% share in 2026**. [Source 5]
- **Back-end technologies** lead with **60.4% share in 2026**. [Source 5]
- **North America** leads with **38.6% share in 2026**, driven by tech giants (Amazon, Google, Facebook). [Source 5]
- **Asia Pacific** (23.7% share) is the fastest-growing region. [Source 5]

### 4E. Adoption Rates Summary for Platform Types

| Platform Type | Market Share / Adoption | Growth Rate |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud-based (SaaS) | Dominant; >65% of deployments | High; on-premise is fastest-growing sub-segment |
| On-premise | Smaller share but growing | Fastest-growing among large enterprises |
| Open-source (WooCommerce, Magento, etc.) | WooCommerce: 39% of all e-commerce sites; Shopify: 6.7% of CMS market | Steady |
| Headless/Composable | 73% of businesses have implemented; $2.1-2.2B market in 2026 | 22.6-23.5% CAGR |

---

## 5. KEY METRICS

### 5A. Total Global E-Commerce Sales (GMV) for 2025 and 2026 Projections

**Retail / B2C E-Commerce GMV:**
- **2025:** ~$6.42 trillion (multiple sources converge here) [Source 16][Source 20][Source 22][Source 24]
- **2026:** ~$6.88 to $7.4 trillion (multiple sources converge) [Source 17][Source 18][Source 21][Source 24]
- **YoY Growth:** ~7-8% from 2025 to 2026 [Source 18][Source 24]

**B2B E-Commerce GMV:**
- **2026:** $36 trillion (ITA estimate) [Source 5][Source 25]
- **CAGR:** 14.5% through 2026 [Source 5][Source 25]
- **APAC will comprise 80% of B2B market share by 2026** [Source 5][Source 25]

**Total E-Commerce (B2B + B2C):**
- **2025:** $33.8 trillion (IMARC) to $37.2 trillion (Research Nester) [Source 1][Source 4]
- **2026:** $44.3 trillion (Research Nester estimate) [Source 4]

### 5B. E-Commerce Penetration Rates by Region

**Global:**
- E-commerce accounts for ~20.5% of global retail sales in 2025, rising to **21.1% in 2026** and **22.5% by 2028**. [Source 17][Source 24]
- 21.8% of retail purchases will take place online in 2026, which is the highest to date. [Source 17]
- E-commerce projected to account for 24% of all global retail by end of 2026. [Source 22]

**United States:**
- 16.4% of total retail sales in 2025. [Source 1][Source 24]
- Q2 2026: 17.1% of total sales (seasonally adjusted). [Source 23]
- 18% projected for 2026. [Source 18]
- The U.S. retail e-commerce market accounts for around 20% of global sales. [Source 11]

**Asia Pacific:**
- China: 47% e-commerce penetration. [Source 21]
- India: ~5% e-commerce penetration. [Source 21][Source 24]
- Indonesia: 31.9% penetration. [Source 21]
- South Korea: 30% penetration. [Source 21]

**Europe:**
- United Kingdom: 30.6% penetration. [Source 21]
- Germany: ~18% penetration. [Source 21]
- France: ~17% penetration. [Source 21]
- 94% of EU individuals aged 16-74 used the internet in 2024; 77% made online purchases. [Source 4]

**Other:**
- Canada: ~12% penetration. [Source 21]
- Japan: ~15% penetration. [Source 21]

### 5C. Number of Online Stores Globally

- There are over **28 million e-commerce websites/sites globally**. [Source 16][Source 17][Source 19]
- **26.5 million** e-commerce sites globally (Ecommercetrix). [Source 22]
- **2.64 billion** online shoppers by end of 2023, representing 33% of the global population. [Source 11]
- **Over 3 billion** people now buy something online entering 2026. [Source 16]
- **2.86 billion** people around the globe are making online purchases from dedicated eCommerce platforms or social media stores. [Source 17]
- **2.9+ billion** online shoppers worldwide in 2026. [Source 21]
- User penetration will reach 53.9% in 2024 and is estimated to hit **63.2% by 2028**, turning 4.5 billion people into e-commerce market consumers over the next four years. [Source 11]

### 5D. Additional Key Metrics

**Mobile Commerce:**
- Mobile commerce accounts for **~59-60% of total online retail sales** in 2026. [Source 16][Source 18][Source 21]
- Mobile commerce market is projected to grow from **$2.42 trillion in 2026 to over $5 trillion by 2034**. [Source 18]
- Approximately **1.65 billion people** will shop via smartphone in 2026. [Source 16][Source 18]
- Mobile accounts for **71% of e-commerce traffic**; conversion rates: 2% mobile vs. 3% desktop. [Source 22]
- Mobile commerce sales expected to reach **$2.74 trillion in 2026**. [Source 17]
- Smartphones in the device segment are anticipated to hold a **75.4% share** during 2026-2035 in the e-commerce market. [Source 4]

**Social Commerce:**
- Social commerce sales have exceeded **$1.17 trillion globally**. [Source 16]
- U.S. social commerce sales will exceed **$80 billion in 2026**. [Source 16]
- TikTok Shop's global GMV reached **$64.3 billion in 2025** (nearly double from $33.2B in 2024), projected to hit **$112.2 billion in 2026**. [Source 18]
- Global social commerce sales forecasted to hit **$2.9 trillion**. [Source 17][Source 22]
- **Facebook** will reach 80 million social shoppers in the U.S. by 2026. [Source 16]

**Digital Wallets:**
- Digital wallets now account for **~50% of global online transactions** (53% in 2025). [Source 12][Source 19]
- Over **5.6 billion mobile wallet users** globally in 2024 (13% increase from 2023). [Source 6]
- India's **UPI** processed 14 billion monthly transactions. [Source 12]
- Nearly **40% of online shoppers** prefer digital wallets. [Source 3]

**Average Order Value / Conversion:**
- Global average e-commerce conversion rate: **1.9%–3.3%**, depending on vertical and traffic source. [Source 18]
- Average cart abandonment rate: **70.22%** (70.2% per Baymard Institute). [Source 16][Source 17][Source 18][Source 22]
- Primary cart abandonment drivers: unexpected shipping costs (55%), complicated checkout (21%), trust concerns (17%). [Source 18]
- Average e-commerce return rate: **16.9%**; returned products cost U.S. retailers $890 billion in 2024. [Source 16]
- Average e-commerce repeat purchase rate: **28.2%**. [Source 18]

**E-commerce Fraud:**
- Global fraud losses projected to exceed **$48 billion in 2026**. [Source 22]
- For every $100 in fraudulent orders, merchants lose $207 after chargebacks and overhead. [Source 22]
- Global e-commerce platforms experienced a **29% increase in cyberattacks in 2024** compared to 2023. [Source 6]

**AI in E-commerce:**
- AI-powered e-commerce tools market: **~$17 billion by 2030**. [Source 22]
- AI-powered recommendation engines exceeded **$22 billion in spending in 2024**. [Source 12]
- Amazon attributes **35% of its total revenue** to algorithmic recommendations. [Source 12]
- Effective personalization lifts revenue **10-15%** and cuts marketing waste by up to 30%. [Source 12]
- AI expected to handle **80% of customer interactions** by 2030. [Source 22]
- 34% of U.S. customers comfortable with agentic commerce (AI shopping for them). [Source 22]

**Dropshipping:**
- Global dropshipping market: **$372.47 billion (2025)**, expected to reach **$476.10 billion in 2026**. [Source 22]
- Average dropshipping profit margins: **15%–20%**. [Source 22]

**Live Commerce:**
- Live commerce market size was valued at **$172.9B in 2025** and is projected to grow from **$230.3B in 2026 to $2,546.5B by 2033**, at a **CAGR of 41.0%** from 2026. [Source 9]

**Last-Mile Delivery:**
- Last-mile delivery now accounts for **41% of total supply chain costs**, with labor tightness and fuel volatility continuing to push that figure upward. [Source 12]

**BNPL (Buy Now Pay Later):**
- The BNPL market is projected at **$28.44 billion in 2026**. [Source 16]
- Klarna reported a **24% increase in BNPL usage** in Q1 2025 amid inflation. [Source 8]

**Number of Online Shoppers by Country:**
- **China:** 904 million digital shoppers (44% of global total), expected to rise to 1.33 billion by 2027. [Source 22]
- **India:** 660 million people use smartphones in India (46.5% penetration rate). [Source 4]

---
