## [Frequently Asked Questions](#faqs)

Who uses BigCommerce?

BigCommerce is used by 11,665 companies worldwide, including Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Cox Enterprises Inc, National Grid, based on our analysis of 29.6M crawled domains at TechnologyChecker.io. It's particularly popular in the Retail industry (19.59% of customers).

How many customers does BigCommerce have?

BigCommerce has 11,665 active customers detected through our full-sweep crawl of 29.9M live business domains. We enriched 7,073 of these with LinkedIn company data on TechnologyChecker.io to generate detailed insights. An additional 29,920 sites that previously used BigCommerce are also tracked.

What is BigCommerce's market share?

BigCommerce holds 0.36% of the Ecommerce Platforms market, ranking #12 in the category — based on our analysis of 29.6M domains and 40K+ technologies at TechnologyChecker.io.

What are the best alternatives to BigCommerce?

The top alternatives to BigCommerce include Shopify (34.72% market share), WooCommerce (22.23% market share), Wix eCommerce (16.52% market share), Squarespace Commerce (15.56% market share) — based on our market share data across 29.6M crawled domains.

Which countries use BigCommerce the most?

United States leads with 5,035 BigCommerce customers, followed by United Kingdom (608), Australia (533), Canada (286), Brazil (132), based on our enriched company data at TechnologyChecker.io.

What size companies use BigCommerce?

The most common company size is 1-10 employees, representing 73.2% of BigCommerce customers, based on our analysis of 7,073 enriched companies. This is followed by 11-50 employees (18.6%) and 51-200 employees (5.7%).

How old are companies that use BigCommerce?

The majority of BigCommerce customers were founded in the 2010s (31.78%), followed by the 2000s (24.65%), based on our analysis of 7,073 enriched companies. This suggests BigCommerce is most popular among relatively young companies.

What is the ideal customer profile for BigCommerce?

The ideal BigCommerce customer is: Company Size: 1-10 employees, Location: US, UK, or Australia, City: London, Los Angeles, Irvine, Chicago, Founded: 2010-2019, Company Age: ~5-15 years old — based on our analysis of 7,073 enriched companies at TechnologyChecker.io.

What big companies use BigCommerce?

The biggest companies using BigCommerce include AMD, Pearson, National Grid, Gildan Activewear, Cox Enterprises, and First American. These are primarily 10,000+ employee public companies that use BigCommerce for branded merchandise stores and marketplace subdomains rather than their primary commerce operations.

Is BigCommerce better than Shopify?

It depends on your needs. Shopify dominates with 46.9% market share vs. BigCommerce's 0.22%, per TechnologyChecker.io data. BigCommerce offers built-in B2B features and no transaction fees on any plan. Shopify has a larger app ecosystem. Our migration data shows 2,976 companies moved from BigCommerce to Shopify, while only 393 went the other direction.

Is BigCommerce an ecommerce platform?

Yes, bigCommerce is a cloud-hosted ecommerce platform founded in Sydney, Australia in 2009. It powers 11,665 active online stores detected in our crawl data. The platform provides hosted storefronts, payment processing, and order management. Pricing starts at $39/month for Standard, with Enterprise plans for high-volume merchants.

Which is better, WooCommerce or BigCommerce?

WooCommerce is self-hosted and free (plus hosting costs), while BigCommerce is fully hosted starting at $39/month. WooCommerce has 81x more market share at 18.15%. Our migration data shows relatively balanced movement: 683 companies switched from WooCommerce to BigCommerce, while 898 went the other direction. A 0.76:1 ratio.

Does BigCommerce do dropshipping?

Yes, bigCommerce supports dropshipping through integrations with suppliers like Spocket, Printful, and Wholesale2B via its app marketplace. The platform doesn't include native dropshipping but its API-first architecture and lack of transaction fees make it practical for dropshipping businesses that need flexible fulfillment setups.

Is BigCommerce going out of business?

No, our detection data shows BigCommerce grew from 30 domains in 2011 to 11,675 active domains by March 2025, consistent growth over 14 years. The company went public on Nasdaq in August 2020 and continues to operate as an independent ecommerce platform serving retail, manufacturing, and wholesale merchants.

How much does BigCommerce cost compared to Shopify?

BigCommerce starts at $39/month (Standard), $105/month (Plus), and $399/month (Pro). Shopify starts at $39/month (Basic), $105/month (Shopify), and $399/month (Advanced). The key pricing difference: BigCommerce charges no transaction fees on any plan, while Shopify charges 0.5-2% unless you use Shopify Payments.

Is Shopify Plus better than BigCommerce Enterprise?

Shopify Plus has far larger market adoption, Shopify's overall 46.9% share dwarfs BigCommerce's 0.22%. BigCommerce Enterprise offers built-in B2B, multi-storefront, and headless commerce without add-on costs. Our data shows enterprise companies like AMD and Pearson choose BigCommerce, while Shopify Plus dominates DTC fashion and beauty.

Does BigCommerce work for B2B businesses?

Yes, our data shows 4.39% of BigCommerce customers operate in Manufacturing and 4.35% in Wholesale, two core B2B verticals. BigCommerce Enterprise includes built-in B2B features like custom pricing, purchase orders, and company accounts. Companies like Brandt Group and Advanced Technology Services use BigCommerce for B2B operations.

What types of businesses use BigCommerce?

Retail dominates at 19.59% of BigCommerce customers, followed by Manufacturing (4.39%), Wholesale (4.35%), and Retail Apparel (3.55%). The platform attracts a commerce-heavy mix with concentrations in sporting goods, wellness, food and beverage, and automotive parts. Physical product sellers are BigCommerce's sweet spot.

Can BigCommerce handle high-volume sales?

Yes, bigCommerce Enterprise serves companies like AMD and American Apparel with 10,000+ employees. The platform has no hard limits on products, bandwidth, or file storage on any plan. Pro and Enterprise plans support annual sales up to $400K and unlimited respectively, with built-in CDN and 99.99% uptime guarantee.

Does BigCommerce offer a free trial?

Yes, bigCommerce offers a 15-day free trial on all standard plans (Standard, Plus, Pro) without requiring a credit card. Enterprise plans require contacting sales for a custom demo. This trial period lets merchants test the full platform including checkout, payment integrations, and theme customization before committing.

# News Release

July 31, 2023

# BigCommerce To Launch New Google Cloud AI-Powered Ecommerce Features

[PDF Version](/node/10086/pdf)

*Google Cloud AI tools will extend the platform’s capabilities to allow enterprise merchants worldwide to work smarter, faster and more efficiently to improve sales, boost conversions and heighten customer experiences*

AUSTIN, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 31, 2023-- [BigCommerce](http://www.bigcommerce.com) (Nasdaq: BIGC), a leading Open SaaS ecommerce platform for fast-growing and established B2C and B2B brands, today announced it will add new AI-powered features to its platform, leveraging Google Cloud’s AI technologies. With these new features, enterprise merchants will have the potential to improve operational efficiencies, elevate customer experiences, enhance product discovery and help drive more sales. BigCommerce AI-powered solutions will start to be globally available by the end of 2H 2023.

“BigCommerce is deeply invested in AI that will allow enterprise merchants to optimize their ecommerce operations using the most advanced and innovative technologies to drive operational efficiencies, deliver more targeted and personalized shopping experiences, and ultimately sell more worldwide,” said Troy Cox, senior vice president of product at BigCommerce. “Creating AI-powered solutions with Google Cloud cements the significance of our collaborative partnership as we move to strengthen AI in the ecommerce industry together.”

With the BigCommerce and Google Cloud partnership expansion, BigCommerce will accelerate its use of AI technologies to help merchants innovate and succeed with a simplified and modernized approach to enterprise ecommerce. Among the upcoming AI-powered solutions scheduled to release, the following key AI features will give merchants the ability to work smarter, faster and more efficiently to:

* **Create compelling product descriptions with AI-powered writing features.** Leveraging [Google Cloud’s Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai) on the backend, merchants can save time and simplify the writing and creative process that enable product catalogs to get to market more quickly and efficiently – helping to improve SEO rankings, product discovery, increasing traffic and conversion rates that aid in more sales.
* **Deliver highly personalized storefronts.** Powered by [Google Cloud’s Recommendations AI](https://cloud.google.com/recommendations), merchants will have a seamless way to create personalized product recommendations that are tailored to each customer’s taste and preference – elevating product discovery to potentially increase average order value (AOV), conversions and lifetime value (LTV).
* **Gain deeper insight into business performance with AI-driven data analytics.** Looking ahead, the BigCommerce [Ecommerce Insights](https://www.bigcommerce.com/insights/) tool will evolve to feature new AI capabilities enabling merchants to derive deeper data insight and analytics into store performance, customer trends and respond to business changes as soon as they happen.

By automating processes with AI across their ecommerce operations, merchants can organically save time and improve operational efficiency and productivity by using AI algorithms to streamline workflows, accelerate product development cycles, reduce costs and accelerate time-to-market.

The new AI integration is coming at a time where adoption of AI among retailers is expected to surpass [US $127 billion by 2033](https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/artificial-intelligence-in-retail-market), according to Future Market Insights. The demand for AI in retail is expected to grow by 28% CAGR between 2023 and 2033.

“Successful companies will be those that can leverage AI to solve time-intensive business problems in a seamless, efficient way,” said Carrie Tharp, vice president, strategic industries at Google Cloud. “Through Google Cloud Vertex AI, BigCommerce will be able to transform ecommerce functions for more merchants, enabling them to access, build and deploy machine learning models and AI applications at scale all in one single platform.”

To register for the BigCommerce X Google BigAI Hackathon happening from August 7-18, 2023, [click here](https://bigaihackathon.splashthat.com/). [Visit BigCommerce](https://www.bigcommerce.com/articles/ecommerce/ecommerce-ai/?utm_medium=pr&utm_source=businesswire&utm_campaign=com_global_all_mme_cus_ent-core_brand_ct_2023_q3_ai-features&utm_content=google-cloud-ai) to learn more about how AI is influencing and advancing ecommerce. To sign up for a free trial or demo, [contact BigCommerce Sales](https://www.bigcommerce.com/contact-sales/?utm_medium=pr&utm_source=businesswire&utm_campaign=com_global_all_mme_cus_ent-core_brand_ct_2023_q3_ai-features&utm_content=google-cloud-ai).

**About BigCommerce**

BigCommerce (Nasdaq: BIGC) is a leading open software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecommerce platform that empowers merchants of all sizes to build, innovate and grow their businesses online. BigCommerce provides merchants sophisticated enterprise-grade functionality, customization and performance with simplicity and ease-of-use. Tens of thousands of B2C and B2B companies across 150 countries and numerous industries use BigCommerce to create beautiful, engaging online stores, including Ben & Jerry’s, Molton Brown, S.C. Johnson, Skullcandy, Solo Stove, Ted Baker and Vodafone. Headquartered in Austin, BigCommerce has offices in London, Kyiv, San Francisco, and Sydney. For more information, please visit [www.bigcommerce.com](http://www.bigcommerce.com/) or follow us on [Twitter](http://twitter.com/BigCommerce), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/bigcommerce/), [Instagram](http://instagram.com/bigcommerce) and [Facebook](http://facebook.com/bigcommerce).

# 5 Killer BigCommerce Features for Enterprises

![5 Killer BigCommerce Features for Enterprises](/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/E-commerce-copy-scaled.jpg)

[BigCommerce](/category/bigcommerce/)[Website](/category/website/)

Published on July 1, 2026

![John Kuefler](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/93dae049abc46bb28e887f87dede8843835462e204ca98f17b9fdf740f135cd2?s=96&d=mm&r=g) John Kuefler

BigCommerce offers enterprise features like headless commerce, multi-storefront management, and advanced APIs that enable speed and scalability. These capabilities help brands deliver high-performance shopping experiences at scale

## Introduction

When it comes to enterprise ecommerce, choosing the right platform can make or break your online success. [BigCommerce](https://www.bigcommerce.com/) is an ecommerce platform known for its robust capabilities, extensibility, and enterprise-friendly features that help large online stores thrive. Many businesses often compare [BigCommerce vs Shopify](/blogs/shopify-vs-bigcommerce-ecommerce-platform-comparison/) when evaluating scalable solutions for growth. Both platforms offer a broad set of tools to build and run digital storefronts, but BigCommerce's key advantages (extensibility, B2B capabilities, advanced checkout features, ease of use, and excellent support) set it apart for enterprise needs. In this post, we’ll delve into five killer BigCommerce features you need to know about and briefly compare BigCommerce vs [Shopify](https://www.shopify.com/) on these points, providing valuable insights for enterprise-level businesses planning their ecommerce strategy.

## 1. Unmatched Extensibility and Customization

One of BigCommerce’s biggest strengths is its extensibility. The platform is highly flexible and user friendly, allowing enterprises to customize and integrate almost every aspect of their store. BigCommerce provides an open API and supports headless commerce, enabling seamless integration with ERP systems, CRMs, and other enterprise software. In fact, BigCommerce offers a more robust API and more built-in functionality than Shopify, giving merchants greater flexibility to tailor their stores and avoid heavy reliance on apps. For example, BigCommerce supports up to 600 product variants (SKUs) per product, with up to 250 values per option. Shopify raised its own ceiling to 2,048 variants per product in October 2025, but it still caps each product at three options, whereas BigCommerce lets you combine more option types (plus unlimited modifiers) for the deep, complex catalogs enterprises actually run. That flexibility ensures your platform can grow with your business.

BigCommerce also packs many features natively within the platform that other platforms offer only via apps or higher-tier plans. It includes capabilities like unlimited staff accounts, built-in product reviews, and real-time shipping rate quotes right out-of-the-box. These built in features reduce the need to hunt for third-party solutions and minimize additional cost.

By contrast, Shopify’s app store is more extensive, offering thousands of integrations for customization. Shopify’s approach, however, means not all essential features are native, so many capabilities (such as advanced product filtering or customer segmentation) require installing third-party apps. Not only does searching and managing numerous add-ons take time, but each plugin may come with a monthly fee, an additional cost to consider when scaling up. BigCommerce’s comprehensive native feature set means you’ll rely less on external modules, simplifying your tech stack and reducing long-term costs.

Extensibility extends to SEO customization as well. BigCommerce gives you full control over critical SEO settings like URLs, page titles, and meta descriptions. Both BigCommerce and Shopify let you edit title tags and meta descriptions for your pages (important for search engine optimization), but BigCommerce goes further by allowing fully customizable URL structures and even direct edits to your robots.txt file. This level of control helps optimize your site for search engines and tailor it to your SEO strategy in ways Shopify cannot without apps or workarounds.

Lastly, BigCommerce offers even more extensibility via its flexible metafield setup. While other platforms do offer similar options, including Shopify, metafields are built into the core of BigCommerce. This allows you to easily extend essentially any aspect of your storefront to include customizable fields in a variety of types. Let's face it: every store has some unique pieces of data they need to keep track of. BigCommerce handles this extremely well.

![](/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ink-1024x699.png)

*BigCommerce allows you to extend almost any object in the storefront with metafields, and apps like the Hypa Metafields Manager make this a breeze*

## 2. Powerful B2B Capabilities

Enterprise businesses that sell wholesale or to other businesses need specialized B2B features, and this is an area where BigCommerce shines. BigCommerce has built-in B2B capabilities (especially with its B2B Edition for enterprise plans) that allow you to serve B2B customers alongside retail operations on one platform. It offers features like customer groups with custom pricing, bulk discounts, wholesale catalogs, and even quote management and purchase order support. For instance, you can set up exclusive price lists for different client segments and enable quick reordering, all natively within BigCommerce. You don’t need external modules or heavy custom development to support common B2B scenarios; much is ready out-of-the-box.

Compared to Shopify, which historically focused on B2C and requires apps or an expensive Shopify Plus plan to handle B2B needs, BigCommerce provides robust wholesale tools by default. BigCommerce even offers a dedicated B2B Edition package with features specifically designed for business-to-business selling, such as advanced account management, volume pricing, and purchase order workflows. These capabilities empower your sales team to manage large orders and negotiate pricing easily. By contrast, Shopify lacks many specialized B2B tools natively, so merchants often have to rely on apps or custom work to fill the gaps. In practical terms, BigCommerce’s B2B strength means an enterprise can run a combined B2B/B2C storefront seamlessly, without bolting on multiple plugins.

Scalability is also a factor for B2B merchants handling high-volume orders and large catalogs. As noted earlier, BigCommerce can handle complex product catalogs (with hundreds of variants) and supports bulk operations well, which is ideal for wholesale ordering. Its platform performance is tuned for heavy load, so whether you’re dealing with large corporate purchases or frequent bulk orders, BigCommerce won’t be the bottleneck. Ultimately, if your enterprise has a significant B2B component, BigCommerce’s native wholesale and account management features offer a substantial advantage.

![](/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ink-1-1024x580.png)

*The B2B module of BigCommerce offers a wide variety of customization options to best serve the needs of even the most complex B2B setups*

## 3. Advanced Checkout Features and Payment Options

A smooth and flexible checkout experience is vital for any large ecommerce operation. BigCommerce delivers with an optimized one-page checkout and a plethora of payment options. You can offer customers a frictionless checkout flow that’s mobile-friendly and highly customizable. BigCommerce supports digital wallets like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and PayPal One-Touch out-of-the-box, as well as multi-currency payments and localization to [improve conversion rates globally](/blogs/is-your-ecommerce-website-leaving-money-on-the-table/). Additionally, BigCommerce’s checkout is open for customization, and developers can use the Checkout SDK to tailor the experience or integrate with external systems (for example, to apply custom tax logic or third-party fulfillment services) without compromising security.

Payment flexibility remains an enterprise strength, though the economics changed in 2026. BigCommerce supports over 65 payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal, Authorize.net, and many more), so you are never locked into a single processor and can shop for the best rates. For years BigCommerce charged no added platform fee on those transactions, and that was a real edge over Shopify. That changed on June 1, 2026, when BigCommerce introduced an Open Payment Provider Fee on orders processed through gateways that are not on its embedded list: 2% of eligible GMV on the Core plan, 1% on Growth, and 0.6% on Scale, while enterprise Performance contracts are custom and carry no such fee under their terms. Importantly, the most common processors, including Stripe and PayPal, are embedded providers and stay fee-exempt, so many merchants avoid the charge entirely just by using them. Shopify applies similar logic from the other direction: it strongly encourages its proprietary Shopify Payments system, and using a third-party payment provider adds a transaction fee (up to 2% on the Basic plan, dropping to 0.15% on Shopify Plus) on top of regular credit card fees. The practical takeaway for a high-volume enterprise store is that both platforms now reward staying on a natively supported processor, and on BigCommerce an enterprise Performance agreement paired with an embedded gateway keeps per-order fees at zero.

BigCommerce also excels in abandoned cart recovery features. Recovering lost sales from abandoned carts can significantly boost revenue, so BigCommerce includes an Abandoned Cart Saver system (starting on its mid-tier plans) that automatically sends a series of customizable emails to re-engage customers who left items in their cart. This built-in abandoned cart recovery tool is a powerful asset for increasing conversions without extra effort. While Shopify also provides an abandoned checkout email feature, on its Basic plan this capability is quite limited (typically only a single automated email) and more advanced recovery tools require an upgrade or app. By contrast, BigCommerce gives you a robust multi-email cart recovery system as a standard feature.

For enterprises operating both online and offline, BigCommerce integrates with leading point-of-sale solutions to unify in-store and online transactions. Shopify offers its own POS system (Shopify POS) as part of its ecosystem, which is a plus for merchants invested in Shopify’s retail hardware. BigCommerce doesn’t have a proprietary POS hardware system, but it makes up for it by seamlessly connecting with top POS providers (such as Square, Clover, and Lightspeed) via apps and integrations. This means you can still run omnichannel retail across physical and online stores on BigCommerce without missing a beat. The checkout flexibility extends to these integrations, giving you choice in how you manage orders across channels.

Overall, BigCommerce’s checkout and payment features provide an enterprise-ready solution: a highly optimized checkout to reduce friction, extensive payment method support without penalties, and built-in tools like couponing, gift cards, and cart recovery to maximize sales. Customers get a convenient experience, and you retain control and user friendly flexibility in how you operate.

![](/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ink-2-1024x560.png)

*BigCommerce natively supports the ability to ship to multiple addresses, which is critically for ecommerce storefronts that do gifting.*

## 4. Ease of Use and Streamlined Management

Despite its power, BigCommerce remains user friendly and relatively easy to use, an important consideration for enterprise teams that need to manage the system daily. The admin interface is modern, intuitive, and designed to make managing a large product catalog and processing orders as straightforward as possible. Even if your company is migrating from another platform or if your staff is used to Shopify, they’ll find BigCommerce’s learning curve quite manageable. The dashboard provides a clear overview of your store’s performance, and tasks like adding products, updating title tags and meta descriptions, or creating discount campaigns can be done with a few clicks.

BigCommerce strikes a balance between advanced functionality and simplicity. The platform offers all the tools you need to run a large online store while still being accessible: you don't need to be a developer or tech expert to take advantage of its powerful features. This is especially beneficial for enterprise environments where your ecommerce team might include marketing managers, content editors, or sales personnel in addition to developers. Each team member can use BigCommerce’s interface with ease: for example, the marketing team can create promotions and view analytics, while the merchandising team can organize products into categories or set up bulk pricing rules without IT involvement.

![](/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ink-3-1024x545.png)

*BigCommerce features an intuitive page building experience, that allows for both built-in and custom widgets to be used to build pages in a visual fashion*

Another aspect that enhances ease-of-use is BigCommerce’s emphasis on built-in functionality. With many features baked into the platform, your staff spends less time installing/updating apps or juggling multiple dashboards. Everything from SEO settings to gift card management is available in one unified admin. This not only saves time but also reduces potential bugs or conflicts that can occur when relying on numerous third-party plugins. The result is a more streamlined store management experience, a big win for productivity, especially in a fast-paced enterprise setting.

It’s also worth noting that BigCommerce provides extensive documentation, a community forum, and a knowledge base to help users master the platform. If a new team member joins, they can quickly find resources to learn how to perform any task. Moreover, because BigCommerce is a fully hosted SaaS solution, your team doesn’t have to worry about server maintenance or applying security patches: it's all handled in the background. In short, BigCommerce is designed to be user-friendly for businesses of all sizes, from small business merchants up to large enterprises, combining rich functionality with an accessible interface.

## 5. Support

Enterprise-level retailers need more than just software features. They need reliable support and a secure, stable environment. BigCommerce delivers on both counts.

All BigCommerce merchants receive 24/7 technical support included with their plan, meaning if something goes wrong, you can reach out via phone, live chat, or email at any time and get help from a real person. Importantly, this round-the-clock support is provided at no extra charge, even for enterprise clients. BigCommerce’s support team is well-versed in both technical and business aspects of ecommerce, so they can assist with everything from configuration questions to best practices.

Beyond human support, BigCommerce offers a strong infrastructure that gives enterprises peace of mind. The platform boasts a 99.99% uptime rate and is built on a secure, scalable architecture. Security features like SSL certificates, PCI compliance, and DDoS protection are included, ensuring your online stores and customer data are safeguarded without you having to invest in third-party security apps. BigCommerce also performs automatic updates and maintenance, so your store is always running on the latest version with the newest features and security patches. This eliminates a lot of the IT burden on your team and reduces risk.

Another support-related advantage is how BigCommerce’s business model avoids conflicts of interest in assistance. Because BigCommerce has so many native capabilities, when you do need help, you often get a solution from one source. On Shopify, if you encounter an issue caused by a third-party app, their support might refer you to that app’s developers, potentially slowing down resolution. With BigCommerce, fewer moving parts mean the support team can usually address your issue directly. This “one throat to choke” scenario is beneficial for enterprises that require quick, accountable support to keep operations running smoothly.

In summary, BigCommerce backs up its feature set with enterprise-grade service and security. You get the confidence that comes with 24/7 support, robust built-in security, and a platform that can handle peak traffic without faltering. For a mission-critical ecommerce platform powering significant revenue, that level of reliability and support is a killer feature in its own right.

# WooCommerce in 2026: Market Share, Stats, Trends and What's Next

28 min read ·Jun 08, 2026

The eCommerce landscape shifts fast, and the platforms powering online stores are no exception. Yet one name continues to dominate the conversation year after year. WooCommerce remains one of the most widely adopted eCommerce solutions in the world, but understanding exactly where it stands in 2026 requires more than a surface-level glance at market share numbers.

This analysis cuts through the noise. Whether you are evaluating WooCommerce for a new project, benchmarking it against competitors, or simply trying to understand where the platform is headed, the data and trends covered here will give you a clear, grounded picture of its current position and future trajectory.

Inside, you will find up-to-date market share statistics, adoption trends across industries, performance benchmarks, and an honest assessment of what the platform's evolution means for developers, store owners, and digital strategists alike. The goal is not to hype or dismiss WooCommerce, but to present a clear-eyed view of what the numbers actually tell us and what smart operators should be paying attention to heading into the next phase of eCommerce growth.

## What Is WooCommerce and Why Does It Dominate?

Launched on September 27, 2011, by WooThemes developers Mike Jolley and James Koster, WooCommerce set out to solve a straightforward problem: giving WordPress site owners a flexible, cost-free way to sell online. The plugin gained rapid adoption, and by May 2015, Automattic recognized its strategic value and [acquired WooThemes and WooCommerce](https://techcrunch.com/2015/05/19/automattic-buys-woocommerce-the-popular-plugin-for-turning-wordpress-into-a-store/) in what was described as the company's largest acquisition at the time. That move cemented WooCommerce's place at the center of the WordPress ecosystem while preserving its [open-source identity](https://scarletmedia.net/ecommerce-business-consultant/), a decision that continues to pay dividends over a decade later.

The business model is deliberately asymmetric. The core plugin remains completely free, lowering the barrier to entry for millions of merchants. Automattic then monetizes through premium extensions, WooPayments, themes, and managed hosting solutions. Industry estimates attribute roughly $250 to $300 million in annual revenue to these Woo-related products, demonstrating how powerfully a free-to-start model can generate commercial scale when the surrounding ecosystem is rich enough.

What genuinely separates WooCommerce from hosted SaaS alternatives is full merchant ownership. Store owners control their data, their codebase, and their hosting environment without being subject to vendor pricing changes, forced migrations, or platform restrictions. This data sovereignty is a compelling proposition for businesses prioritizing long-term flexibility and cost predictability.

Distribution is another structural advantage. [According to Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WooCommerce), WooCommerce operates within the WordPress ecosystem, which currently powers more than 40% of all websites globally. That installed base functions as a built-in acquisition channel; any WordPress site owner can add full e-commerce functionality simply by installing a free plugin.

The ecosystem depth compounds these advantages further. With 59,000+ compatible WordPress plugins and support for 65+ payment gateways, including [Square](https://squaresyncforwoo.com/blog/square-integration-with-woocommerce), Stripe, PayPal, and regional processors, merchants can construct highly customized storefronts without bespoke development for the vast majority of use cases. Among self-hosted e-commerce solutions, no competing platform approaches this level of extensibility.

## The 6 Biggest WooCommerce Trends Shaping Stores in 2026

The WooCommerce ecosystem is not standing still. Six structural shifts are reshaping how merchants build, operate, and scale their stores in 2026, and understanding each one is essential for anyone serious about long-term platform competitiveness.

### High-Performance Order Storage Is Now the Foundation

HPOS represents the most significant architectural change WooCommerce has made in years. By replacing the legacy WordPress post-based order storage system, which relied on the wp\_posts and wp\_postmeta tables, with dedicated, optimized database tables, HPOS eliminates the scalability ceiling that plagued high-volume merchants for a decade. Stores processing thousands of orders daily previously experienced sluggish dashboards, slow order queries, and checkout friction that compounded at scale. Enabled by default for new installations since WooCommerce 8.2, HPOS is now mainstream across the ecosystem, with existing stores migrating steadily using compatibility mode that allows safe testing and rollback. The result is measurably faster order processing, reduced database load, and infrastructure that can actually support enterprise-level growth without custom engineering workarounds.

### AI Integration Is Moving from Experiment to Infrastructure

The WooCommerce MCP (Model Context Protocol) beta, introduced in WooCommerce 10.3, marks a decisive turning point for AI inside the platform. AI assistants can now directly query and manage store data, including products, orders, and customer records, through a standardized protocol that removes the need for brittle custom integrations. Beyond the MCP beta, agentic commerce tools are emerging that handle automated product recommendations, dynamic pricing adjustments, and marketing workflow execution with minimal human input. A May 2026 WooCommerce survey of 225 commerce leaders highlighted agentic commerce as a primary strategic bet for the near term. For intermediate merchants, the practical near-term value lies in AI-assisted merchandising, automated email triggers, and personalization engines that previously required expensive developer time to implement.

### Headless Architectures Are Becoming a Serious Performance Play

Performance-focused developers are increasingly decoupling WooCommerce from its traditional front-end and pairing the commerce backend with React or Next.js interfaces. The appeal is straightforward: sub-second load times, complete design flexibility, and better Core Web Vitals scores, all while retaining WooCommerce's mature product catalog, order management, and payment infrastructure. The global headless commerce market is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of approximately 22.6%, signaling that this is not a niche developer preference but a broader industry direction. WooCommerce's Store API provides the foundation for these decoupled builds, and [2026 analysis from leading WooCommerce observers](https://www.elsner.com/news/woocommerce-news-updates/) consistently places headless architecture among the top technical priorities for stores competing on experience and speed.

### Omnichannel and POS Integration Has Become a Baseline Expectation

The gap between online and physical retail operations is closing, and merchants who manage both channels separately are paying for it in operational overhead and customer experience inconsistency. Real-time synchronization of inventory, orders, customers, and loyalty programs across WooCommerce and Square POS is no longer a premium capability; it is table stakes for any merchant operating in multiple selling environments. WooCommerce formally named Square its preferred POS partner in May 2025, reflecting the depth of demand in this area. For merchants who need granular control over that synchronization, tools like SquareSync for Woo provide bidirectional real-time sync across products, inventory, orders, customers, loyalty programs, and discounts, while features like "Find Square Matches" prevent the duplicate listings that manual or partial sync solutions routinely create. Merchants using this level of automation report saving approximately eight hours per week in reconciliation and manual data entry.

### Mobile-First Checkout Is a Conversion Imperative

With roughly 70% of WooCommerce store visits originating from mobile devices and cart abandonment rates hovering near 70%, the checkout experience on smaller screens directly determines revenue outcomes. WooCommerce's block-based checkout, improved guest checkout flows, and the Interactivity API are converging to deliver faster, smoother mobile experiences that reduce the friction responsible for abandoned carts. Merchants who have not yet audited their mobile checkout journey are leaving measurable revenue on the table, particularly given that mobile conversion rates continue to trail desktop despite dominating traffic share.

### Subscriptions Are Reshaping Revenue Planning

WooCommerce Subscriptions and Pre-Orders are seeing increased adoption as merchants recognize the compounding value of predictable recurring revenue over relying solely on one-time transactions. The global subscription e-commerce market is projected to grow from roughly $3.09 trillion in 2026 at a 14.4% compound annual rate, and WooCommerce's extension ecosystem is well-positioned to capture that shift. Merchants across categories from consumables to digital products are building hybrid models that combine subscription offerings with standard purchases, creating more stable revenue bases that reduce dependence on acquisition-heavy promotional cycles.

## Honest Assessment: WooCommerce's Challenges and Criticisms in 2026

The platform's scale and customizability come with genuine trade-offs that merchants deserve to evaluate honestly before committing to WooCommerce as their long-term infrastructure.

### The Operational Burden Is Real

WooCommerce's self-hosted architecture places a meaningful maintenance workload on whoever runs the store. Core WordPress updates, WooCommerce version releases, theme patches, and plugin compatibility checks do not happen automatically. Each update cycle carries risk: a plugin that worked flawlessly at WooCommerce 8.x may introduce fatal conflicts at 9.x, requiring either a developer fix or a rollback. Merchants without dedicated technical support frequently absorb these disruptions as unplanned downtime, lost sales, or emergency agency fees. Add hosting management, SSL renewal, malware scanning, and database backups to the list, and the true operational cost becomes substantial. TCO analyses published in 2026 consistently show that WooCommerce's free core plugin can exceed the predictable subscription cost of SaaS alternatives once hosting, premium extensions, and developer hours are factored in, often within 18 months of launch.

### Declining Store Count Signals Competitive Pressure

StoreLeads recorded an 11% year-over-year decline in WooCommerce store count in Q1 2026, a figure that reflects more than market maturation. Smaller merchants in particular are migrating toward platforms that offer faster onboarding (often two to eight hours versus WooCommerce's 20 to 80-plus hours), built-in payment processing, and predictable monthly fees. For a solo operator or a small retail business without a developer on staff, the appeal of a managed environment where infrastructure concerns are handled automatically is difficult to argue against. WooCommerce retains clear advantages for merchants who need deep customization and data ownership, but the platform's net store count trajectory is a candid signal that not every merchant profile is well served by the open-source model.

### Security Risk Is Compounding

WordPress ecosystem vulnerabilities rose 42% year-over-year according to Patchstack's 2026 security whitepaper, with plugins accounting for approximately 91% of reported issues. The emergence of AI-assisted development, often described as "vibe-coding," is accelerating the problem. Less experienced developers using large language models to generate custom plugins or store modifications can introduce untested code directly to production environments. Research tracking AI-generated code quality found that roughly 45% of sample outputs contained OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities. For WooCommerce stores with heavy third-party customization, this expands the exploit surface considerably compared to the more controlled update environments of managed SaaS platforms.

### Performance Scales, But Not Automatically

High-Performance Order Storage (HPOS) represents a genuine engineering improvement, delivering up to 40x faster customer order queries and meaningfully faster checkout benchmarks compared to legacy post-based storage. However, HPOS addresses one layer of a multi-layer challenge. High-traffic WooCommerce stores still require deliberate configuration: optimized VPS or cloud hosting, Redis object caching, CDN integration, image optimization, and database query tuning. These are not trivial tasks, and they sit entirely with the merchant or their agency. SaaS platforms absorb this complexity at the infrastructure level, which explains why performance benchmarks frequently favor well-resourced WooCommerce builds in customization and SEO flexibility while noting TTFB and Core Web Vitals gaps on under-optimized self-hosted setups.

### Plugin Dependency Introduces Systemic Fragility

Relying on dozens of third-party plugins creates a dependency chain where a single weak link can destabilize an entire store. A plugin abandoned by its developer stops receiving security patches and eventually breaks after core updates. A compromised plugin can expose customer data or enable unauthorized access before any public advisory is issued. Plugin bloat also degrades performance in ways that are difficult to diagnose without profiling tools. This fragility is not a hypothetical edge case; it is a recurring operational reality for WooCommerce stores built on complex stacks, and it underscores why honest platform selection must weigh the ecosystem's extensibility against the management overhead that extensibility demands.

This article provides a comprehensive analysis of WooCommerce's position in the eCommerce landscape in 2026, covering market share statistics, adoption trends, performance benchmarks, and future projections. Published on SquareSync for Woo's blog on June 8, 2026.

**Key Statistics for 2026:**
- Approximately 4.29 to 4.53 million live WooCommerce stores globally, representing ~33.4% of all tracked eCommerce stores (out of an indexed universe of 13.5-13.6 million sites), making WooCommerce the single largest eCommerce platform by raw store count.
- WooCommerce stores generate an estimated $30-35 billion in annual gross merchandise volume, with an average order value of ~$122.
- About 23% of all global online orders are processed through WooCommerce checkout.
- The plugin has surpassed 344 million cumulative downloads with ~7 million active installations on WordPress.org, averaging ~30,000 downloads per day.
- Q1 2026 saw an -11% year-over-year store count decline, attributed to post-pandemic market consolidation (though quarter-over-quarter showed a +5.3% increase). Industry analysts project stable 30-35% market share through 2027.

**History and Business Model:**
- Launched September 27, 2011 by WooThemes developers Mike Jolley and James Koster; acquired by Automattic in May 2015.
- Core plugin is free; Automattic monetizes via premium extensions, WooPayments, themes, and managed hosting (estimated $250-300 million in annual revenue).
- Key advantages: full merchant data/code ownership, WordPress ecosystem (powers 40%+ of all websites), 59,000+ compatible plugins, 65+ payment gateways.

**Market Share Details:**
- Among top 1 million traffic-ranked sites, WooCommerce holds only ~18-20% share (vs. 33% overall), revealing dominance is concentrated among small/micro-merchants.
- Geographic distribution: US 12.2% (~523,000 stores), UK 4.3%, India 3.2%, Germany 2.8%.
- Top categories: Home and Garden (11.1%, ~477,000 stores), Apparel (8.7%), Business/Industrial (7.7%).
- Growth potential in Southeast Asia and Latin America (LatAm projected 9.43% CAGR through 2029).

**Operational Metrics:**
- Mobile devices account for ~70% of store traffic.
- Cart abandonment sits at ~69-70%, with over 70% of stores deploying cart recovery plugins.
- ~33,000 WooCommerce stores use Square as integrated payment and POS solution.

**Six Key 2026 Trends:**
1. High-Performance Order Storage (HPOS) — replaces legacy post-based storage, eliminates scalability ceiling, enabled by default since WooCommerce 8.2.
2. AI Integration — WooCommerce MCP (Model Context Protocol) beta in version 10.3 enables AI assistants to query/manage store data.
3. Headless Architectures — pairing commerce backend with React/Next.js (headless market growing at ~22.6% CAGR).
4. Omnichannel and POS Integration — WooCommerce named Square its preferred POS partner in May 2025; real-time sync is now table stakes.
5. Mobile-First Checkout — conversion imperative given 70% mobile traffic.
6. Subscriptions — global subscription eCommerce market projected to grow from ~$3.09 trillion in 2026 at 14.4% CAGR.

**WooCommerce vs. Shopify:**
- WooCommerce: 4.29-4.53 million stores vs. Shopify's ~2.86-4 million, but Shopify generates dramatically higher GMV per merchant and processes over $100 billion per quarter.
- Shopify grew +11% YoY in Q1 2026 while WooCommerce declined -11%. Shopify's native AI, one-click integrations, and predictable pricing draw merchants away.
- WooCommerce's moat: open-source ownership, no revenue-based transaction fees, deep customization, superior data control.

**Ecosystem:**
- 59,000+ WordPress plugins compatible; official Marketplace lists 1,200+ extensions; 65+ payment gateways.
- Official WooCommerce Square extension has gaps: selective variation syncing, multi-location inventory, real-time order sync reliability.
- SquareSync for Woo offers real-time bidirectional sync (products, inventory, orders, customers, loyalty, discounts) and "Find Square Matches" feature; users report saving ~8 hours/week.

**Challenges and Criticisms:**
- Significant operational burden (updates, hosting, security, backups); TCO can exceed SaaS subscription costs within 18 months.
- Smaller merchants migrating to platforms with faster onboarding (2-8 hours vs. 20-80+ hours for WooCommerce).
- Security: WordPress ecosystem vulnerabilities rose 42% YoY per Patchstack's 2026 report; plugins account for ~91% of issues; ~45% of AI-generated code samples contained OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities.
- Performance scaling requires deliberate investment (optimized hosting, caching, CDN, image optimization).
- Plugin dependency creates systemic fragility and security risk.

**2027 Outlook:**
- Projected 30-35% global eCommerce market share through 2027, sustained by WordPress's ~43% web share and SMB adoption.
- AI tooling (MCP integration maturing to production by 2027) expected to reduce operational complexity.
- Omnichannel synchronization expected to become competitive necessity.
- Headless architecture and block-based themes expected to close performance gaps.

If you're choosing between WooCommerce and Shopify, you're looking at the two biggest ecommerce platforms in the world. Between them, they power the majority of online stores.

But how do they actually stack up in terms of market share, store count, and growth? Here's a comprehensive breakdown of the latest data - updated for 2026.

> Want weekly insights into how 7, 8 and 9-figure brands are driving sustainable growth? That's what you get with our value-packed newsletter, *The Retention Edge*. [Subscribe for free today](https://retentionedge.co/).

## Key Takeaways

* **Shopify holds 26.2% ecommerce platform market share**, powering approximately 4.8–6.5 million active stores worldwide.
* **WooCommerce holds between 20-33% market share** (depending on methodology), with over 4.5 million active stores tracked by StoreLeads.
* **Among high-traffic sites, Shopify leads** with 28.8% of the top 1 million ecommerce websites, compared to WooCommerce's 18.2%.
* **Shopify's GMV reached $292 billion in 2024** and is on pace to exceed $350 billion in 2025.
* **WooCommerce's estimated GMV is $30–35 billion** annually - much smaller in transaction volume, but spread across more stores.
* **Together, they power over half of all ecommerce websites** on the internet.

## A Note on Market Share Numbers

Before diving in, it's worth understanding why you'll see different numbers depending on where you look.

We’ve used publicly available data from a few different places - [BuiltWith](https://builtwith.com/), [StoreLeads](https://storeleads.app/) and [W3Techs](https://w3techs.com/).

Market share figures for ecommerce platforms vary significantly based on how they're measured:

* **BuiltWith** scans websites for specific technologies. It tracks checkout implementations and platform fingerprints.
* **StoreLeads** tracks active online stores across platforms using a broader detection methodology.
* **W3Techs** measures CMS usage across the entire web, not just ecommerce sites.

These different approaches produce different results. For example, WooCommerce can show up at 20% in one dataset and 33% in another - both can be accurate within their own methodology. We'll cite the source for each figure so you can evaluate them in context.

## WooCommerce Market Share

WooCommerce commands a significant share of the ecommerce market, though the exact figure depends on how you measure it:

* **20.1%** of all ecommerce websites (BuiltWith, 2025)
* **33.4%** of ecommerce stores tracked globally (StoreLeads, August 2025 - 4.53 million out of 13.6 million stores)
* **18.2%** among the top 1 million ecommerce sites (BuiltWith, 2025)

The gap between these numbers comes down to what counts as a "WooCommerce site." Over 6.5 million websites have WooCommerce elements installed, but not all of them are active stores running WooCommerce checkout. The 4.53 million figure from StoreLeads represents active stores more specifically.

### About WooCommerce

WooCommerce isn't a standalone platform. It's a plugin for WordPress, which powers roughly 43% of all websites on the internet (about 518 million sites, according to W3Techs). Over 10% of WordPress installations include WooCommerce.

That relationship with WordPress is a big deal. It means WooCommerce benefits from the largest CMS ecosystem in the world: tens of thousands of themes, plugins, and developer resources.

It also means WooCommerce stores can be anything from a small side project to a large-scale operation, which partly explains why it shows such high total store counts but lower representation among top-traffic sites.

### Key WooCommerce Statistics (2025–2026)

| Metric | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Ecommerce platform market share (BuiltWith) | 20.1% |
| Ecommerce store share (StoreLeads) | 33.4% |
| Share among top 1M ecommerce sites | 18.2% |
| Active stores (StoreLeads) | 4.53 million |
| Websites with WooCommerce elements | 6.5+ million |
| Cumulative plugin downloads | 211+ million |
| Average daily downloads | ~30,000 |
| Annual store count growth | ~6% |
| Estimated annual GMV | $30–35 billion |
| Available languages | 66 |
| WordPress themes compatible | 1,500+ |
| WooCommerce plugins (WordPress directory) | 6,000+ |
| WooCommerce extensions (official store) | 700+ free and paid |
| GitHub contributors | 1,100+ |
| Cost | Free (open source) |

### WooCommerce Regional Breakdown

WooCommerce has a genuinely global footprint:

* **United States**: ~245,000 sites
* **United Kingdom**: ~24,000 sites
* **India**: ~15,000 sites
* Strong adoption across Europe (25–30% regional share) and emerging markets where cost sensitivity makes the free, open-source model attractive.

## Shopify Market Share

Shopify leads the ecommerce platform space by most measures:

* **26.2%** of all ecommerce websites (BuiltWith, 2025)
* **28.8%** among the top 1 million ecommerce sites (BuiltWith, 2025)
* **10.32%** of the global ecommerce platform market more broadly (Statista, 2025)
* **~29–30%** of the US ecommerce software market — the clear domestic leader

That last point is important. Among high-traffic, high-revenue stores, Shopify punches well above its weight.

The platform dominates in the top 10K, top 100K, and top 1 million site categories, which suggests it's the platform of choice for established, growing brands.

### About Shopify

Unlike WooCommerce, Shopify is a standalone, hosted platform. You don't need WordPress or any other CMS - it's a self-contained system for building and running an online store.

Shopify also operates as a CMS, holding 6.2% of the total [CMS market](https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/cms-market-share) (second only to WordPress). But its core strength is ecommerce, and that's where it focuses nearly all of its development effort and resources.

### Key Shopify Statistics (2025–2026)

| Metric | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Ecommerce platform market share | 26.2% |
| Share among top 1M ecommerce sites | 28.8% |
| US ecommerce software market share | ~29% |
| Active stores worldwide | 4.8–6.5 million |
| US-based stores | ~3–3.5 million |
| UK stores | ~241,000 |
| Countries served | 175+ |
| 2024 annual GMV | $292 billion |
| 2024 annual revenue | $8.88 billion |
| Cumulative GMV (all time) | $1 trillion+ |
| 2024 Black Friday / Cyber Monday sales | $11.5 billion |
| Shoppers who bought from Shopify merchants (2024) | 875 million+ |
| Average store conversion rate | 1.4% |
| Top 10% store conversion rate | 4.7% |
| Apps on Shopify App Store | 13,000+ |
| Shopify Plus stores | ~76,600 |
| Shopify Plus new launches | 300+ per week |
| Mobile share of Shopify traffic | 68% |
| Mobile share of purchases | 79% |

### Shopify Growth Trajectory

Shopify's growth over the last five years has been dramatic:

| Year | Approximate Active Stores |
| --- | --- |
| 2020 | 1.7 million |
| 2021 | 2.1 million |
| 2022 | 2.9 million |
| 2023 | 4.4 million |
| 2024 | 4.6 million |
| 2025 | 4.8–6.5 million |

The COVID-19 pandemic was a major accelerant. Between March 2020 and January 2022, over 2.5 million new Shopify sites went live, a 201% increase.

Revenue growth has been equally strong. Shopify posted $8.88 billion in revenue for 2024 (up 26% year-over-year), with Q2 and Q3 2025 each showing 30%+ growth.

The company is projected to exceed $12 billion in revenue by 2026.

### Shopify's Enterprise Push

Shopify Plus (starting at $2,300/month) has become a meaningful part of the business, with roughly 76,600 stores and 300+ new merchants launching weekly.

Major brands like Gymshark, Red Bull, Nestlé, Pepsi, Tesla, and LVMH run on Shopify, which contributes to its outsized presence among high-traffic sites.

## WooCommerce vs Shopify: Head-to-Head Comparison

| Category | WooCommerce | Shopify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market share (BuiltWith) | 20.1% | 26.2% |
| Top 1M site share | 18.2% | 28.8% |
| Active stores | 4.53M (StoreLeads) | 4.8–6.5M |
| 2024 GMV | ~$30–35B (estimated) | $292B |
| Pricing model | Free (open source) | Paid subscription |
| Hosting | Self-hosted (BYO hosting) | Fully hosted |
| CMS dependency | Requires WordPress | Standalone |
| App / plugin ecosystem | 6,000+ plugins + 50,000+ WordPress plugins | 13,000+ apps |
| Enterprise tier | No official tier | Shopify Plus ($2,300/mo) |
| Primary strength | Flexibility, cost, WordPress ecosystem | Ease of use, scale, enterprise features |

### What the Numbers Tell Us

The market share data paints a nuanced picture. Here are my top takeaways:

**Shopify dominates among high-traffic, high-revenue stores.** Its lead in the top 1 million sites (28.8% vs 18.2%) and its massive GMV ($292 billion vs an estimated $30-35 billion) show that Shopify is where bigger, more established brands tend to land.

**WooCommerce has broader total adoption.** When you count all ecommerce sites (not just the biggest ones), WooCommerce's numbers are comparable or even higher than Shopify's. The free, open-source model makes it accessible to anyone with a WordPress site.

**They serve different audiences.** WooCommerce attracts merchants who want full control, already use WordPress, or are cost-sensitive. Shopify attracts merchants who want a managed, all-in-one platform and are willing to pay for convenience and reliability.

Neither platform is "winning" in an absolute sense - they've carved out different segments of a massive and still-growing market.

## How to Choose the Right Platform

The right platform depends on your business, not on market share rankings. Here's a practical framework:

**WooCommerce is typically a better fit if you:**

* Already have a WordPress website
* Want full control over your hosting, code, and data
* Are comfortable managing (or hiring someone to manage) updates, security, and performance
* Are working with a limited budget for platform fees
* Need deep customization that goes beyond what a hosted platform offers

**Shopify is typically a better fit if you:**

* Want a managed, all-in-one solution that handles hosting, security, and updates
* Prioritize ease of use and fast setup
* Are scaling quickly and need enterprise-grade infrastructure
* Want access to Shopify's native features (Shop Pay, Shopify Payments, POS)
* Don't want to manage the technical side of running an ecommerce site

### Both Platforms Work Well with Mobile Apps

Regardless of which platform you choose, mobile is a critical channel.

68% of Shopify traffic comes from mobile devices, and 79% of purchases happen on mobile - numbers that are broadly consistent across ecommerce.

Both [WooCommerce](https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/woocommerce-mobile-app-builders) and [Shopify](https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/shopify-mobile-app-builders) integrate well with mobile app solutions like [MobiLoud](https://www.mobiloud.com/), which lets you extend your existing store into a native iOS and Android app without rebuilding anything.

Whether you're running a WooCommerce store on WordPress or a Shopify storefront, your full website experience, including all your integrations, customizations, and checkout flow, carries over into the app.

> If you're curious whether a mobile app makes sense for your brand, [get a free app preview](https://www.mobiloud.com/preview) to see what your store would look like as a native app.

## Final Thoughts

The ecommerce platform market continues to grow, and both Shopify and WooCommerce are growing with it.

Shopify leads in market share, GMV, and presence among top-tier merchants. WooCommerce holds strong with its WordPress ecosystem, global accessibility, and open-source flexibility.

The numbers will shift as the market evolves, but the core dynamic is clear:

* Shopify is the go-to for merchants who want a managed, scalable platform.
* WooCommerce is the go-to for merchants who want control, flexibility, and the WordPress ecosystem.

Together, they power the majority of ecommerce on the internet. And that's unlikely to change anytime soon.

---

*Statistics sourced from BuiltWith, StoreLeads, W3Techs, Statista, Omnisend, Marketplace Pulse, Shopify earnings reports, and Red Stag Fulfillment research. All figures reflect the most recent available data as of early 2026.*

# 47 TikTok Shop statistics you need to know in 2026

47 TikTok Shop statistics for 2026: $112B GMV projected, 475K US shops, 53M US buyers. Real data on sales, categories, conversion rates and more.

![Ruben Boonzaaijer](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65dc77982d4c82c1f3ef59fb/6a366f729d169080ef92b02e_Profile%20Picture%202.0%20cropped.png)

Maurizio Isendoorn
