# Adobe Commerce vs Salesforce Commerce Cloud: A US Enterprise Buyer’s Guide to Cost, B2B, and Architecture (2026)

[Want to Discuss? Get in Touch!](#hero)

Adobe Commerce and Salesforce Commerce Cloud are both enterprise ecommerce platforms, but they price and architect commerce in opposite ways. Adobe Commerce charges a fixed license and lets you own the code and hosting. Salesforce Commerce Cloud charges a percentage of every dollar you sell and runs as a fully managed SaaS. That single difference drives most of the decision.

For a US enterprise choosing a platform in 2026, the real question is not which one is “better.” It is which cost structure, B2B feature set, and architecture match your revenue trajectory, your team, and the systems you already run. This guide compares the two on the terms that actually decide the outcome, with the numbers, the trade-offs, and the failure modes that most vendor comparisons skip.

## The core difference: fixed license vs revenue share

Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SFCC) prices commerce as a percentage of gross merchandise value (GMV). GMV is your total merchandise revenue minus tax and shipping. The B2C editions run roughly 1% to 3% of GMV depending on tier, and the B2B editions run about 1% (Growth) to 2% (Advanced) of GMV. Salesforce does not publish fixed pricing. Every quote is custom, negotiated on a sales call, and shaped by your GMV, contract length, and how many other Salesforce clouds you already license.

Adobe Commerce prices as a fixed annual license that scales in tiers with your GMV and average order value, but it does not take a percentage of each sale. Third-party estimates put the license in the range of roughly $40,000 to $125,000+ per year for mid-market and enterprise tiers, on top of which you pay for hosting (Adobe Commerce on cloud infrastructure, or your own), implementation, and ongoing development.

The practical consequence: SFCC’s cost rises in lockstep with your revenue, while Adobe Commerce’s license is flatter and more predictable. A brand growing fast can watch an SFCC bill climb into six or seven figures on GMV share alone, while the same growth on Adobe Commerce mostly adds hosting and support cost, not a revenue tax.

## Total cost of ownership: what each platform really runs

Sticker price is the least useful number in enterprise commerce. The honest comparison is total cost of ownership across three years, including the labor and systems around the platform.

| Cost component | Adobe Commerce | Salesforce Commerce Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core license | Fixed tier, roughly $40K–$125K+/yr | Revenue share, ~1–3% of GMV |
| Hosting / infrastructure | Separate (cloud or self-managed) | Included in SaaS |
| Implementation | $150K–$1M+ depending on scope | $200K–$2M+ depending on scope |
| Ongoing development | Agency retainer or in-house team | Certified SFCC developers (scarcer, pricier) |
| Upgrades | You schedule and run them | Handled by Salesforce (SaaS) |
| Extensions / apps | Large marketplace, mostly one-time | Cartridges, fewer, often bespoke |
| Cost trajectory as you grow | Flatter (license tiers) | Climbs with GMV |

The pattern most enterprises see: SFCC removes the burden of upgrades and infrastructure, but you pay for that convenience through GMV share and a scarcer, more expensive talent pool. Adobe Commerce shifts more operational responsibility onto you or your agency, but keeps the cost curve flatter as revenue scales and gives you full control of the code.

A useful rule of thumb from the field: below a certain GMV, SFCC’s revenue share can look cheaper than staffing an Adobe Commerce build. Above it, the percentage model becomes the more expensive path, sometimes dramatically so. Model your own three-year GMV forecast against both structures before you sign anything. If your growth plan is aggressive, the revenue share compounds against you.

## B2B feature depth

Neither platform was born for B2B. Both bolted enterprise B2B onto a B2C core. That said, the two have taken different paths, and for US manufacturers, distributors, and wholesalers the gap matters.

Adobe Commerce ships native B2B as part of the platform: company accounts with buyer hierarchies, shared catalogs with company-specific pricing, quote workflows, requisition lists, quick order, and purchase-order approval flows. Because the code is open, complex B2B logic (custom pricing rules, ERP-driven catalogs, negotiated terms) can be modeled directly rather than worked around. Adobe documents these capabilities in its [Adobe Commerce B2B feature guide](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/guide-overview), and they are deep enough that many distributors pick Adobe on B2B depth alone.

Salesforce Commerce Cloud offers B2B checkout features such as contract pricing and purchase-order approvals, and its strongest argument is unification: if your sales, service, and CRM already live in Salesforce, B2B Commerce plugs into that customer graph. The trade-off is that SFCC’s B2B is younger and its customization boundaries are tighter, because you are working inside a managed SaaS rather than an open codebase.

The honest read: choose Adobe Commerce when B2B complexity is the hard part of your build and you need to model unusual pricing, catalog, and approval logic. Choose SFCC B2B when the strategic priority is fusing commerce with an existing, heavily invested Salesforce CRM and service operation.

## Architecture and headless: how each goes composable

Both platforms support headless commerce, but they get there differently.

Salesforce Commerce Cloud has consolidated its APIs into the Salesforce Commerce API (SCAPI), a modern composable API layer, and offers the Composable Storefront built on PWA Kit (a React/JavaScript framework) deployed on Managed Runtime (MRT), Salesforce’s serverless hosting. It is a coherent, first-party path to a headless PWA, and it keeps you inside the Salesforce runtime.

Adobe Commerce exposes GraphQL and REST APIs and supports headless through decoupled frontends, PWA Studio, and API orchestration. But the more important 2026 architecture story for Adobe merchants is that you do not have to go fully headless to get headless-class performance. The Hyva frontend replaces Magento’s legacy Luma theme with a lightweight stack (Tailwind CSS plus Alpine.js) that strips the heavy RequireJS and Knockout layers, and it delivers large PageSpeed and Core Web Vitals gains without the cost and maintenance of a separate PWA codebase. [Hyva](https://www.hyva.io/) now runs on thousands of Magento and Adobe Commerce stores for exactly this reason.

That gives Adobe Commerce a middle option SFCC does not have a direct equivalent to: a fast, modern, server-rendered storefront that is far cheaper to build and maintain than full headless, while still leaving the door open to a decoupled architecture later. For teams weighing the jump, our practitioners have written separately about [when a Hyva frontend is enough and when full headless earns its cost](https://bemeir.com/articles/headless-adobe-commerce-multi-store-pwa-vs-hyva/).

## Talent, upgrades, and operational risk

Two operational factors decide more enterprise deployments than feature lists do.

Talent supply. Adobe Commerce and Magento have a deep global developer pool built over 16 years, which keeps agency and in-house hiring competitive. Certified Salesforce Commerce Cloud developers are scarcer, and that scarcity shows up in both rate and lead time when you need to staff a project or fix something under pressure.

Upgrade responsibility. As a SaaS, SFCC handles platform upgrades for you. Adobe Commerce upgrades are yours to schedule and run, which is real work but also real control. You decide when to move, you test against your own extensions, and you are never forced into a change that breaks a customization on Salesforce’s timeline. Adobe publishes its full [version release and support lifecycle](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-operations/release/versions) so you can plan upgrades against known support-end dates rather than guessing.

## Decision framework: which platform wins for you

Choose **Salesforce Commerce Cloud** when:

* You are already deeply invested in Salesforce (three or more clouds) and CRM-to-commerce unification is a strategic priority.
* You want a fully managed platform and will trade GMV share for not owning infrastructure or upgrades.
* Your B2B needs fit within SFCC’s feature set and you value the single-vendor customer graph over open customization.

Choose **Adobe Commerce** when:

* Your growth plan is aggressive and a percentage-of-GMV cost model would compound against you.
* B2B complexity (custom pricing, ERP-driven catalogs, negotiated terms, approval hierarchies) is the hard part of the build.
* You want to own the code, control your upgrade cadence, and hire from a deep talent pool.
* You want modern performance without full headless cost, using a Hyva frontend on an open platform.

Most US mid-market and enterprise merchants who are not already Salesforce shops find Adobe Commerce the more defensible choice on cost trajectory and B2B depth. The clearest case for SFCC is the enterprise whose commerce strategy is inseparable from an existing Salesforce investment.

## How Bemeir helps

Bemeir is a Brooklyn ecommerce agency and the USA’s first official Hyva Gold Partner. We build and support enterprise stores on [Adobe Commerce and Magento](https://bemeir.com/magento/), and we specialize in high-performance [Hyva frontend development](https://bemeir.com/partners-hyva/) that lifts Core Web Vitals and conversion without the cost of full headless. When a different platform is genuinely the better fit, we build there too, across [Shopify and Shopify Plus](https://bemeir.com/shopify/), [Shopware](https://bemeir.com/shopware/), and [BigCommerce](https://bemeir.com/bigcommerce/), so the platform recommendation you get from us is not the only tool we own.

Our differentiator is depth: a partner ecosystem of 60+ integrations across payments, personalization, shipping, fraud, and compliance, documented on our [technology partners page](https://bemeir.com/partners/), and a team that has shipped real B2B and enterprise builds rather than slide decks. You can read more about the team and our “we build it, you sell it” approach on the [about Bemeir page](https://bemeir.com/about-bemeir/), or start a platform conversation on the [Bemeir homepage](https://bemeir.com/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Salesforce Commerce Cloud more expensive than Adobe Commerce?

In most cases, yes, once you account for the full picture. SFCC’s revenue-share model (roughly 1–3% of GMV for B2C, 1–2% for B2B) means cost rises with sales, and total annual spend commonly lands 2–4x higher than a comparable Adobe Commerce deployment. Adobe Commerce carries a flatter fixed license but shifts hosting, upgrades, and development onto you or your agency. The crossover point depends on your GMV and growth rate, so model both against a three-year forecast.

### Which platform is better for B2B?

Adobe Commerce generally has deeper native B2B: company accounts, shared catalogs with company-specific pricing, quotes, requisition lists, and purchase-order approvals, all customizable because the code is open. Salesforce Commerce Cloud B2B is strongest when you are already invested in Salesforce CRM and want a unified customer graph. Pick Adobe for B2B complexity; pick SFCC for Salesforce ecosystem unification.

### Can Adobe Commerce match Salesforce Commerce Cloud on performance?

Yes. Salesforce pushes performance through its Composable Storefront (PWA Kit on Managed Runtime). Adobe Commerce reaches modern performance either through headless or, more affordably, through a Hyva frontend that replaces the legacy Luma theme and delivers large PageSpeed and Core Web Vitals gains at a fraction of full headless cost.

### Do I have to run my own upgrades on Adobe Commerce?

Yes, Adobe Commerce upgrades are your responsibility (or your agency’s), unlike SFCC’s managed upgrades. That is more work but also more control: you test against your own extensions and choose your timing against Adobe’s published support-end dates rather than being moved on the vendor’s schedule.

### Is Salesforce Commerce Cloud worth the premium?

It is worth the premium mainly when your enterprise already runs multiple Salesforce clouds and CRM-commerce unification is a core strategy. Without that ecosystem synergy, the 2–4x total-cost premium over Adobe Commerce is hard to justify on commerce features alone.

args.summary:
This webpage is a 2026 buyer's guide from Bemeir (a Brooklyn ecommerce agency and the USA's first official Hyva Gold Partner) comparing Adobe Commerce and Salesforce Commerce Cloud for US enterprise buyers. The core difference between the platforms is their pricing model: Adobe Commerce charges a fixed annual license (roughly $40,000–$125,000+ per year for mid-market and enterprise tiers, plus separate hosting and implementation costs), while Salesforce Commerce Cloud charges a percentage of GMV (roughly 1–3% for B2C editions and 1–2% for B2B editions). SFCC does not publish fixed pricing—every quote is custom and negotiated.

Key comparison points covered:
- **Total cost of ownership**: SFCC's cost rises in lockstep with revenue, while Adobe Commerce has a flatter, more predictable cost curve. Implementation costs run $150K–$1M+ for Adobe vs. $200K–$2M+ for SFCC. SFCC removes upgrade and infrastructure burden but has a scarcer, more expensive certified developer talent pool.
- **B2B depth**: Adobe Commerce ships native B2B (company accounts, buyer hierarchies, shared catalogs with company-specific pricing, quote workflows, requisition lists, quick order, PO approval flows) on an open codebase. SFCC's strongest B2B argument is unification with existing Salesforce CRM/service operations.
- **Architecture/headless**: SFCC uses the Salesforce Commerce API (SCAPI) with Composable Storefront on PWA Kit deployed on Managed Runtime. Adobe Commerce supports GraphQL/REST APIs and headless, but also offers the Hyva frontend (Tailwind CSS + Alpine.js) that replaces Magento's legacy Luma theme for large PageSpeed/Core Web Vitals gains without full headless cost—an option SFCC lacks a direct equivalent to.
- **Talent and upgrades**: Adobe/Magento has a deep 16-year global developer pool; certified SFCC developers are scarcer. SFCC handles upgrades as SaaS; Adobe Commerce upgrades are the merchant's responsibility but offer more control.

The decision framework recommends SFCC for enterprises deeply invested in Salesforce (3+ clouds) seeking CRM unification and a fully managed platform, and Adobe Commerce for aggressive growth plans (where revenue share would compound), complex B2B needs, teams wanting code ownership and upgrade control, and those wanting modern performance via Hyva without full headless cost. The guide concludes most US mid-market/enterprise merchants who aren't already Salesforce shops find Adobe Commerce more defensible, with SFCC's total annual spend commonly landing 2–4x higher than comparable Adobe deployments. The page includes an FAQ section and promotes Bemeir's services as a Magento/Adobe Commerce and Hyva specialist agency.

# Ecommerce Platform Comparison (2026): Cost & Speed

Ecommerce platform comparison of Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Adobe Commerce, and Salesforce Commerce Cloud, based on independent research into setup, fees, and total cost of ownership.

by [Gabrielle Shaver](/enterprise/blog/authors/gabrielle-shaver)

/ [Brinda Gulati](/enterprise/blog/authors/brinda-gulati)

![Ecommerce platform comparison and ecommerce platform price comparison](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0817/7988/4088/articles/5aVBXD8c6WiUze7dop8xuB_c615bfc4-5afe-4bc5-80e9-008d4f38b753.jpg?v=1781026294&originalWidth=1848&originalHeight=782)

An ecommerce platform comparison is a structured evaluation of commerce software solutions—such as Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Adobe Commerce, and Salesforce Commerce Cloud across total cost of ownership, performance, checkout conversion, and implementation burden, to help brands identify the right platform for their business model and scale.

Not every lost sale is avoidable. Some shoppers are just browsing. But when checkout friction, slow load times, and missing localization features get in the way, your ecommerce platform matters—especially when [fewer than 2%](https://www.statista.com/statistics/439576/online-shopper-conversion-rate-worldwide/) of global online shopping visits end in a purchase. Shopify alone accounts for more than 14% of US ecommerce, according to US Census Bureau Quarterly Retail E-Commerce Sales data for 2025.

This ecommerce platform comparison guide evaluates Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Adobe Commerce (formerly Magento), and Salesforce Commerce Cloud. Learn about hosting models, implementation burden, native B2B and international depth, pricing visibility, and real-world performance evidence.

## At-a-glance: Shopify vs. WooCommerce vs. BigCommerce vs. Adobe Commerce vs. Salesforce Commerce Cloud

| Shopify | WooCommerce | BigCommerce | Adobe Commerce | Salesforce Commerce Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Who it's for** | Enterprise and large t brands that want unified commerce , low total cost of ownership (TCO), and fast implementation | WordPress users adding ecommerce to an existing site | Mid-market brands that want native features without transaction fees | Large enterprise with in-house tech teams that need deep customization | Enterprises embedded in the Salesforce ecosystem |
| **Hosting model** | Fully managed software-as-a-service (SaaS) | Self-hosted (separate hosting required) | SaaS (hosted) | Self-hosted (third-party hosting required) | SaaS (cloud-hosted) |
| **Implementation burden** | 86% more likely to launch in less time than competitors; 56% lower cost vs. custom platforms | 89% higher implementation costs than Shopify; 5.8x less likely to stay on budget | 88% higher implementation costs than Shopify; TCO 45% higher over five years | 42% higher implementation costs; 40% slower to launch, developer required for most tasks | 22% slower implementation than Shopify; 35% higher costs; 2.6x worse on-time delivery |
| **Native B2B and international depth** | B2B, DTC, and point of sale (POS) in one admin; Managed Markets covers 150+ countries from a single store | Requires paid plugins for multilingual, multi-currency, and B2B features | Strong native B2B and international support; 140+ currencies; no transaction fees | Strong B2B features; international selling requires language code or extensions | B2B and B2C optional via APIs; POS requires a third-party app |
| **Performance evidence source** | CRO: 200,000 sites; 93% of stores 2.8x faster than competitors on average | CRUX: 34% of stores fast; Shopify renders 2.4x faster on average | CRUX: 80% of stores fast; Shopify renders 1.9x slower than Shopify | CRUX: 53% of stores fast; Shopify renders 2.8x slower than Shopify | CRUX: 65% of stores fast; Shopify renders 1.7x slower than Shopify |
| **Pricing, billed annually** | $29-$299+ per month; Plus from $2,300/mo on a 3-year term; hosting, PCI, and compliance included on all plans | Standard $39/month, Plus $39/month; Enterprise: custom, based on GMV | Plugin is free; hosting starts around $250/year, and $1/year, plus variable costs for extensions, SSL, security, and development | No published pricing; custom quotes | No published pricing |

## How to compare ecommerce platforms in 2026

Comparing ecommerce platforms in 2026 means looking past surface-level features to evaluate cost, performance, flexibility, support, and long-term fit.

### Total cost of ownership

The platform that looks cheapest at sign-up rarely stays that way. [Research from an independent study](/enterprise/blog/ecommerce-total-cost-of-ownership) across all five platforms in the North American market maps the real TCO of Shopify, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Adobe Commerce, WooCommerce, and BigCommerce: licensing fees, implementation costs, ongoing maintenance, and third-party integrations. All of those elements land on the bottom line eventually.

According to a study commissioned from a leading independent consulting firm, Shopify's TCO comes out 33% better than our competitors on average, and up to 36% better at the high end.

### Real-world performance and Core Web Vitals

[Google's Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals)—Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)—are the primary metrics that reflect how today's users experiences a page: how fast it loads, how quickly it responds to input, and how stable the layout is while it does.

The data behind these scores comes from the [Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX)](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux), Google's public dataset capturing real-world Chrome user experience across the web.

Two supporting diagnostics round out the picture: [Time to First Byte (TTFB)](/enterprise/blog/time-to-first-byte), which measures how quickly a server responds to a browser request, and [First Contentful Paint (FCP)](/enterprise/blog/first-contentful-paint), which tracks when the first content appears on screen.

Shopify sites [average a 0.51-second](/compare/sitespeed/download) server response time. Compare that to 1.4 seconds across other major platforms—nearly three times slower.

### Checkout conversion

More brands are finding that making their store's checkout process smoother can actually bump up their conversion rates. But how do you identify the [best converting ecommerce platform](/blog/best-ecommerce-platform-small-business)? It comes down to how innovative the platform really is.

A Big Three management consulting firm, commissioned by Shopify, given full data access and asked to study every major commerce platform, found that [Shopify's overall conversion rate](/enterprise/blog/shopify-checkout) outpaces competitors by up to 36%.

[Shop Pay](/shop-pay) sharpens that advantage further. When active, it lifts conversion by as much as 50% compared to guest checkout, and outperforms other accelerated checkouts by at least 10%.

Even its passive presence moves the needle: the mere availability of Shop Pay increases lower-funnel conversion by 5%. Over 150 million buyers are already pre-opted into one-click checkout, which means recognition, pre-filled fields, and a checkout that's four times faster than the guest experience.

[Shop Pay Installments](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shop-pay-installments) and [Shop Cash](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shop-cash) extend that logic into loyalty and flexible payment, all within the same wallet.

### Native features vs. app dependency

The hidden cost of platform choice often lives in the app stack: hosting, [PCI compliance](/enterprise/blog/shopify-checkout-compliance), SSL, fraud detection, abandoned cart recovery, international selling tools, and POS. These come built into every Shopify plan.

For functionality beyond the core, [Shopify's marketplace of more than 8,000 apps](https://apps.shopify.com) offers plug-and-play extensions without the developer overhead.

### B2B, international, and omnichannel fit

Running B2B and DTC on separate systems, managing international storefronts across fragmented back ends, stitching together omnichannel from disconnected tools: it all compounds into what Patrick Joyce, Shopify's senior VP of engineering, calls the "[fragmentation tax](/blog/retail-tech-total-cost-ownership)."

Shopify runs on a [unified commerce](/enterprise/blog/unified-commerce-examples) stack. A [study commissioned by Shopify](/pos/resources/pos-market-report), analyzing data from over 3,800 businesses, found that brands on unified commerce platforms see 22% better TCO and 20% faster implementation than those running fragmented stacks.

The omnichannel upside is equally measurable: brands on Shopify's unified stack report up to 150% omnichannel GMV growth quarterly. For international reach, [Shopify's Managed Markets](/enterprise/blog/managed-markets) enables selling across 150 countries from a single store.

Move, launch, and grow in record time

It's all possible with this comprehensive migration guide.

[Get the guide](/plus/guides/ecommerce-migration?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=bau_24q3_baubacbcaam&utm_term=en-US#download)

## What goes into calculating the cost of an ecommerce platform?

[TCO is a stack of costs](/enterprise/blog/total-cost-of-ownership) that compound over time, many of which don't appear on any pricing page. So calculating it accurately means accounting for four categories:

### 1. Implementation and setup costs

Getting a platform live is just the first bill—implementation covers front-end design, back-end build, system configuration, data migration, and third-party integrations.

Shopify's implementation costs are 23% better on average than competitors. For brands migrating from custom-built platforms specifically, [time-to-value research](/enterprise/blog/time-to-value) found Shopify implementations are 20% faster, three-times more predictable on budget, and 66% more likely to launch on time.

"It used to take us an entire day to launch a single product across our four regions," [says](/case-studies/skullcandy) Jenny Buchar, [Skullcandy](https://www.skullcandy.com/)'s director of global digital experience. "That's now condensed down to one hour, complete with quality assurance so that we can move on to the next region."

### 2. Platform fees and ecommerce stack costs

Subscription fees are the visible layer, but what sits underneath—like transaction fees, integration licensing, and the developer hours required to maintain it all—is where platforms diverge sharply.

Shopify's platform costs are [23% better](/enterprise/blog/ecommerce-total-cost-of-ownership) on average than competitors, driven by native functionality that reduces the need for third-party tooling and a transparent pricing model that doesn't obscure costs behind custom quotes.

### 3. Operational and support costs

These costs include hosting, security, maintenance, and support services.

Shopify's [operational costs](/enterprise/blog/reduce-it-costs) are 19% better on average, with managed hosting, automatic security updates, and PCI compliance handled at the platform level rather than passed down to internal teams.

"On Shopify, the marketing team can just do what they need to do," [says](/plus/customers/4ocean) Alex Schulze, cofounder and CEO at [4Ocean](https://www.4ocean.com/). "If they want to change a banner or run a new promotion, they can do that in a matter of a few clicks and get data back quickly, versus relying on multiple people and external vendors to drive the business."

### 4. Opportunity cost from conversion performance

A platform's [conversion rate](/enterprise/blog/ecommerce-conversion-rate-optimization) itself reflects costs, in terms of the potential revenue you could gain or lose based on the platform's conversion efficiency. And it has two dimensions that reinforce each other.

The first is conversion. Shopify's checkout [converts 18% higher](/enterprise/blog/faster-checkout-process) on average than the four competitors evaluated in the TCO study. Expressed against a 10% margin on goods sold, that translates to roughly a 1.8% TCO offset; revenue that competing platforms bleed on every transaction.

![Infographic showing Shopify's checkout conversion rates compared to Salesforce, WooCommerce, and other platforms.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0817/7988/4088/files/1infographic.png?v=1776305142) 

When you switch to Shopify, you could save anywhere from $0.5 million to $3.6 million in TCO-offset costs.

 

The second is [innovation capacity](/enterprise/blog/custom-established-platform-migration) to improve conversions. On a custom or [legacy stack](/enterprise/blog/legacy-to-digital-transformation), selling through ChatGPT, Google Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot means months of development per platform. On Shopify, [agentic storefronts](/agentic-plan) make products discoverable in AI conversations with direct checkout.

[Sidekick](/sidekick) handles the internal work that used to require custom development, and has powered nearly [100 million merchant conversations](/enterprise/blog/custom-wordpress-platform-migration) since January 2025.

## How to measure ecommerce platform performance

The right starting point is Google's Core Web Vitals—LCP, INP, and CLS—measured against CrUX, the public dataset of real-world Chrome user experience that also underpins Google's search rankings.

### Use Core Web Vitals and CrUX for real-user data

Core Web Vitals measure load speed, interaction responsiveness, and layout stability as real users encounter them, aggregated through CrUX. It's also what Google uses for search rankings, so the stakes extend well beyond user experience alone.

When CrUX data is applied across 200,000 sites at scale, [93% of Shopify stores pass the "fast" threshold](/enterprise/blog/shopify-site-speed)—more than any other major commerce platform.

### Use TTFB and FCP as supporting diagnostics

TTFB and FCP are useful for understanding why a platform performs the way it does.

On Shopify, average site speed is 1.2 seconds against a competitor average of 2.17 seconds, with server speeds running up to 3.9 times faster than competing platforms. TTFB and FCP help explain that gap at the diagnostic level.

Site speed impacts ecommerce sales

See how speed affects the entire customer journey in our ultimate guide. Learn how to increase site speed, performance, and sales.

[Get the guide](/resource/ultimate-guide-to-site-speed?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=bau_24q3_baubacbcaam&utm_term=en-US)

## Shopify vs. WooCommerce: TCO, conversion, and site speed comparison

WooCommerce's TCO runs [36% higher](/static/plus/documents/TCO_1Pager_WooCommerce.pdf) than Shopify's, and that number compounds across every category of cost.

### Platform fees and ecommerce stack costs

WooCommerce's plugin model provides only the basics out of the box, with third-party plugins required for most meaningful functionality. Those plugins carry their own costs, update cycles, and compatibility risks.

WooCommerce platform and stack costs run [32% higher](/compare/shopify-vs-woocommerce) than Shopify's, driven by Shopify's competitive platform fees and its significantly lower dependency on third-party tooling.

### Operational and support costs

WooCommerce is self-hosted, which means hosting, security patching, and compliance sit with the merchant's team rather than the platform.

Shopify handles all of that at the platform level, with [99.9% average uptime](/manual/intro-to-shopify/overview#shopify-uptime) and managed infrastructure that has handled some of the world's largest commerce events without intervention. WooCommerce's operational and support costs run 41% higher than Shopify's on average.

### Implementation and setup

Shopify is less costly to implement than WooCommerce due to the simplicity of

the platform and its developer-friendly back-end system. WooCommerce's limited native enterprise functionality means a significant share of implementation costs comes from customizing and integrating third-party plugins, including API gateways and payment infrastructure that Shopify provides natively.

WooCommerce [implementations cost 49% more](/static/plus/documents/TCO_1Pager_WooCommerce.pdf) on average compared to Shopify, and setting up a new storefront on Shopify is 41% faster.

### Conversion impact

Shopify's checkout converts 17% better than WooCommerce's on average. Expressed against a 10% margin on goods sold, that translates to a 1.7% TCO offset. That's the revenue WooCommerce stores are losing on every transaction before platform costs are even factored in.

### Storefront speed and server responsiveness

Some 93% of Shopify stores are fast versus only 15% of WooCommerce stores, with Shopify stores rendering 2.4 times faster on average.

On WooCommerce, speed is a hosting and configuration problem the business inherits, like plugins that conflict, and engineering resources are diverted to performance management rather than growth.

Shopify's fully managed hosting places server infrastructure closer to buyers globally, with storefronts executed at the network's edge. Server speed on Shopify is 3.9 times faster than WooCommerce on average. A half-second improvement in site speed, according to Shopify's own research, is enough to move conversion.

[CarBahn](https://carbahn.com/?srsltid=AfmBOoqQy63iAhlWeWWJmWAZJ0r9YwAca3ETqWW83UQogVX4NgQnCOre) migrated [from WooCommerce to Shopify](/case-studies/carbahn) in 10 weeks, and their load times dropped from 9 seconds to 1 second. Within 30 days, organic traffic had tripled, order count had tripled, and average order value (AOV) had increased by $200. Return and cancellation rates fell 43%—the lowest in the company's history.

"It almost was like WooCommerce was dictating our business versus us dictating our business back to them," says Zachary Burgeson, CarBahn's chief marketing officer. "We needed a platform like Shopify that could really understand how we work and let us do our jobs the best way we can."

## Shopify vs. BigCommerce: TCO, conversion, and site speed comparison

BigCommerce positions itself on openness, flexibility, and the absence of transaction fees. Those are real advantages, but they come with a trade-off that shows up in TCO.

BigCommerce's overall TCO [runs 45% higher](https://cdn.shopify.com/static/plus/documents/TCO_1Pager_BigCommerce.pdf) than Shopify's on average, because a platform that pushes development responsibility onto merchants compounds costs every time you need a new capability.

### Platform fees and ecommerce stack costs

Platform and stack costs on BigCommerce run 32% higher than Shopify on average.  
  
BigCommerce's limited native enterprise functionality—promotions, merchandising, analytics— means more third-party applications, plugins, and integrations to cover what competitors include out of the box.

Shopify's ecosystem of more than 8,000 apps also gives brands nearly six times the options for extending beyond native functionality. Shopify has also consistently been first to market on new channel integrations, including TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube Shopping, and Microsoft Advertising.

### Operational and support costs

Curbside pickup and omnichannel functionality require additional development investment on BigCommerce, while Shopify handles them natively. Operational and support costs on BigCommerce run 21% higher than those on Shopify.

### Implementation and setup

BigCommerce implementations cost 88% more on average than Shopify's, and launching a new storefront takes 36% longer, driven by the significant development investment BigCommerce's architecture can require.

[Lull](https://lull.com/)'s migration puts numbers to it. Their in-house team completed a [full migration to Shopify](/enterprise/blog/lull) in under six months, for under $10,000, with no prior Shopify experience. As a result, they saw a 25% reduction in infrastructure and software costs, a 25% decrease in payment processing fees, fulfillment time cut from seven to 10 days to four days, and product launches that now happen in minutes rather than months.

"Recognizing BigCommerce wasn't the solution, we made the bold decision to migrate to Shopify. Why? It was obvious! Ask your nanny, your friends' kids, your Uber driver … people know Shopify, and for good reason," says Mark Nagelmann, director of web operations at Lull.

### Conversion impact

Shopify's checkout converts 12% better than BigCommerce's on average: a 1.2% TCO offset when expressed against a 10% margin on goods sold.

### Storefront speed and server responsiveness

The speed comparison is closer here than with other platforms, but the advantage still sits clearly with Shopify. Some 93% of Shopify stores are fast versus 80% of BigCommerce stores, with Shopify rendering 1.4 times faster.

Shopify's server speed is 1.9 times faster on average than BigCommerce's, underpinned by a fully managed global hosting infrastructure that handles peak events without intervention.

![Comparison table of Shopify site speeds compared to BigCommerce, Salesforce, Adobe, and WooCommerce.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0817/7988/4088/files/2comparisontable.png?v=1776305142) 

Shopify stores are up to 2.4x faster than other ecommerce platforms.

 

## Shopify vs. Adobe Commerce: TCO, conversion, and site speed comparison

Adobe Commerce (formerly Magento) is built for enterprise teams with deep technical resources and a tolerance for complexity. That complexity has a clear cost: Adobe Commerce's overall TCO [runs 41% higher](/static/plus/documents/TCO_1Pager_Adobe.pdf) than Shopify's on average, across every category from implementation to platform fees to operations.

### Platform fees and ecommerce stack costs

Adobe's inflexible pricing model sits at the high end of the market, and the platform's reliance on third-party extensions for functions that Shopify provides natively compounds those costs further. Platform and stack costs on Adobe Commerce run 42% higher than Shopify on average.

Apparel retailer [Bombas](https://bombas.com/) saw this firsthand. After [migrating from Adobe Commerce to Shopify](/case-studies/bombas), they recorded $108,000 in annual platform cost savings.

### Operational and support costs

Adobe's legacy architecture requires more internal IT resources or agency partners for ongoing updates, security patches, and enhancements. Operational and support costs on Adobe Commerce run 24% higher than Shopify on average.

### Implementation and setup

Adobe requires more internal resources or partners to configure and customize for deployment, with complex back-end integrations all driving up implementation timelines and budgets.

Adobe Commerce's implementation costs run 42% higher than Shopify's on average, and launching a new storefront on Shopify is 40% faster.

### Conversion impact

Shopify's checkout converts 5% better than Adobe Commerce's on average; a 0.5% TCO offset when expressed against a 10% margin on goods sold. This sounds like a modest percentage, but it's meaningful at enterprise volume.

### Storefront speed and server responsiveness

[Gymshark](https://www.gymshark.com/) was founded by Ben Francis in a UK garage at 19, and the brand chose Adobe Commerce to handle their rapid early growth—but immediately regretted it. After a disastrous Black Friday, [Gymshark migrated to Shopify Plus](/case-studies/gymshark) and went on to post £41 million in sales in 2017, reaching 5.1 million social media followers across 131 countries—making them one of the fastest-growing global fitness and apparel brands in the world.

## Shopify vs. Salesforce Commerce Cloud: TCO, conversion, and site speed comparison

Salesforce Commerce Cloud's revenue-based pricing creates a structural problem: the more successful a brand becomes, the more it pays. Licensing runs an estimated [1% to 3%](https://www.code.digital/blog/salesforce-commerce-cloud-or-shopify-plus) of revenue before developer time, consultant hours, and third-party integrations are added.

Salesforce's overall TCO runs [54% higher](https://cdn.shopify.com/static/plus/documents/TCO_1Pager_Salesforce.pdf) than Shopify's on average.

### Platform fees and ecommerce stack costs

Salesforce's inflexible pricing keeps platform costs at the high end of the market, regardless of a brand's actual usage or growth trajectory. Platform and stack costs on Salesforce run 14% higher than Shopify on average.

"If you go under, they charge overages. If you buy too much, shame on you, you eat it," says David Cost, VP of digital and ecommerce at [Rainbow Shops](https://www.rainbowshops.com/).

Rainbow Shops [replatformed to Shopify](/case-studies/rainbow-shops) and reduced their platform fees by 80%.

"With Shopify, not only is the fee 80% less expensive, we pay monthly for exactly what we use," David says. "No more, no less. Shopify has to earn our business every month."

### Operational and support costs

Operational costs on Salesforce run 6% higher than Shopify on average, with Shopify's fully managed infrastructure absorbing the ongoing maintenance that Salesforce passes to its merchants.  
  
Maintaining Salesforce's legacy architecture requires more internal IT resources or agency partners for ongoing updates and enhancements.

### Implementation and setup

Every change on Salesforce Commerce Cloud requires a developer, slowing launches and tying up resources. Salesforce implementation fees run 16% higher than Shopify's on average, and launching a new storefront on Shopify is 28% faster.

[CQL](/partners/directory/partner/cql1), a leading enterprise commerce agency, now runs more than [80% of their total business on Shopify](/partners/blog/cql) after working with both platforms for years. They've seen a 50% to 75% reduction in implementation timelines on Shopify compared to Salesforce Commerce Cloud.

"Gone are the days of 24-month [Salesforce] Commerce Cloud implementations. We can do things on Shopify in half or a quarter of the time that we used to on other platforms," says Ryan Donahue, Shopify practice lead at CQL.

### Conversion impact

Shopify's checkout converts 36% better than Salesforce Commerce Cloud's on average: a 3.6% TCO offset expressed against a 10% margin on goods sold. No other platform comparison in this guide comes close.

Within six months of [migrating from Salesforce to Shopify](/case-studies/bauer), Bauer Hockey posted a 60% revenue increase, a 30% increase in orders, an 18% conversion rate increase, and 20% cost savings.

"The move to Shopify has been so beneficial to our business. We get so much out of the box, plus a huge pipeline of new features dropping regularly. And the Shopify ecosystem of apps and developers helps us move fast," says Chris Cocca, chief digital officer.

### Storefront speed and server responsiveness

Some 93% of Shopify stores are fast versus only 32% of Salesforce Commerce Cloud stores, with Shopify rendering 1.5 times faster on average.

Shopify's fully managed global cloud infrastructure, with storefronts executed at the network edge, runs [server speeds 2.2 times faster](https://cdn.shopify.com/static/compare/documents/Sitespeed_1Pager_SFCC_R4_0605.pdf) than Salesforce on average.

## How to choose the right ecommerce platform?

Before signing anything, these are the questions worth pressure-testing:

* **What is the honest total cost of ownership over five years?** Licensing, implementation, third-party apps, hosting, developer overhead, and maintenance all compound. Use the [Shopify TCO Calculator](/compare/tco) to model your specific situation against alternatives.
* **How predictable is implementation?** A platform that takes twice as long to launch as scoped costs more than a platform that charges higher up-front fees but delivers on time. Ask vendors for time-to-launch data from real implementations.
* **Does the platform handle peak traffic without intervention?** Validate 99.9% uptime claims against independent data, and look at how the platform performed for other brands during their biggest days.
* **What does checkout conversion look like?** Request conversion benchmarks specific to your category and order value.
* **How much native functionality replaces third-party spend?** Every integration is a maintenance dependency and a potential failure point. Map your current stack against what each platform provides natively.

Shopify ships over 150 product updates twice a year through[Editions](/editions), and has already launched agentic storefronts, making products discoverable in AI conversations with direct checkout.

The data across this ecommerce platform comparison guide points in one direction: Shopify's TCO is 33% better than competitors on average, and up to 36% better. Shopify's checkout converts up to 36% better than the competition, and 15% better on average.

Shopify has also been named a [Leader in the 2024 IDC B2C Commerce MarketScape](/resources/idc-marketscape-report). The [$1.5 billion invested in R&D in 2025](/enterprise?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=custom-builds-switcher_q126fucsbo&utm_content=other-blog-v1) is what funds the platform that keeps producing those results.

### What are the top 5 ecommerce platforms?

# Amazon Seller Statistics *2025 – 2026*

200+ verified statistics across 12 categories covering marketplace scale, FBA, advertising, listings, revenue, and global data, with real agency analysis of what each number means for active sellers. Every figure is dated, sourced, and put in context.

Last Updated

June 11, 2026

Contents – 12 Sections

[01Amazon Marketplace Overview](#marketplace) [02Seller Count & Demographics](#sellers) [03Seller Revenue & Earnings](#revenue) [04FBA Fulfillment Statistics](#fba) [05Fees & Profitability Data](#fees) [06Amazon PPC & Advertising](#advertising) [07Listings & Conversion Rates](#listings) [08Buy Box Statistics](#buybox) [09Category & Product Data](#categories) [10Prime & Shopper Behaviour](#prime) [11Brand Registry & IP Protection](#brand) [12Global Marketplace Data](#global)

Marketplace Overview

## The scale of the Amazon *marketplace in 2025*

Amazon controls roughly 40% of all US ecommerce. The platform processed approximately $1.96 billion in sales every single day in 2025. Below are the verified headline figures that define the environment every seller operates inside. If you are new to selling, start with [what Seller Central is and how it works](https://ecombrainly.com/what-is-amazon-seller-central/) before diving into the stats.

$716.9*B*

Amazon net sales revenue in 2025, up 12% from $638B in 2024

Roughly $1.96 billion per day. Advertising alone contributed $68.6B of this, making Amazon the third-largest ad platform globally behind Google and Meta. Q4 2025 alone delivered a record $213.4B in net sales.

Amazon Q4 2025 Earnings Release

40.5*%*

Amazon’s share of total US retail ecommerce in 2025

Nearest competitor Walmart sits at around 9.2%, with Apple a distant third at 3.2%. Amazon earns roughly 40 cents of every retail ecommerce dollar spent in the United States.

eMarketer / Statista 2025

310*M+*

Active customer accounts worldwide in 2025

Amazon.com attracts roughly 2.4-2.7 billion web visits per month, the most of any ecommerce site globally. Third-party sellers list over 350 million products on the platform in total.

Amazon / Similarweb 2025

8,600*+*

Products sold per minute by US sellers on Amazon’s third-party marketplace

That works out to over 143 products per second, or about 12 million items per day, all sold through independent US-based sellers on the 3P marketplace.

Amazon Small Business Empowerment Report

**Third-party sellers now represent 61-62% of all Amazon unit sales**, an all-time high first recorded in Q4 2024 and held throughout 2025 (61% in Q4 2025, a normal seasonal dip). Third-party sellers now account for roughly 69% of total marketplace GMV, up from 60% in 2019. Amazon’s revenue from third-party seller services, which includes commissions and FBA fees, reached $172.2 billion in 2025, up 11% year over year.

Amazon is deliberately transitioning from retailer to platform operator. The company profits on both sides: referral and fulfillment fees from 3P transactions, and advertising sold to those same sellers. If you are deciding how to structure your catalogue, our breakdown of [the 1P vs 3P model](https://ecombrainly.com/1p-vs-3p-amazon/) is a good place to start.

62*%*

3P share of all Amazon unit sales

Amazon Quarterly Earnings 2025

**Amazon’s advertising business generated $68.6 billion in 2025, up 22% from $56.2 billion in 2024**, with Q4 2025 ad revenue alone hitting $21.3 billion, up 22% year over year. In 2018, fewer than 40% of sellers ran any paid advertising at all. By 2025 that figure is around 70%.

Understanding [all Amazon ad formats](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-ad-types/) and how they interact with organic ranking has shifted from a nice-to-have to a baseline requirement for any seller who wants page-one visibility.

$68.6*B*

Amazon advertising revenue, 2025

Amazon Q4 2025 Earnings Release

The 62% third-party share is often treated as a headline stat and nothing more. What it actually tells you is that **Amazon has structurally committed to growing seller revenue because its own revenue grows with it.** Platform fees, storage fees, and advertising all scale with 3P seller performance. Sellers who understand this stop seeing every policy update as adversarial and start reading it as Amazon protecting its own interests, which usually align with sellers who perform well.

* Build Amazon advertising into your cost of goods from day one, not as a discretionary line you cut when things get tight. It is not optional in competitive categories.
* The search intent data inside [Brand Analytics](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-brand-analytics/) is the most valuable keyword research tool on the planet for Amazon sellers. Use it first, not as a secondary check.
* Before you source any product, model your unit economics with total Amazon costs at 30-40% of selling price. Products that look profitable on a spreadsheet often are not once fees stack up.

Seller Count & Demographics

## Who is actually *selling on Amazon* right now?

The seller base changed dramatically in 2024-2025. Fewer new sellers are joining, those who remain are generating more revenue per seller than at any point in the platform’s history, and the top tier is pulling further ahead. The data tells a clear story of consolidation.

9.7*M*

Total registered seller accounts worldwide in 2025

Of these, only around 1.65 million are actively selling, down from 2.4 million in 2021. The rest are dormant, suspended, or abandoned accounts that never gained traction.

Marketplace Pulse / AMZScout 2025

165*K*

New sellers who launched on Amazon.com in 2025, the lowest in a decade

Down 44% from 2024 and the lowest annual total since Marketplace Pulse began tracking in 2015. During the pandemic peak of 2021, over 700,000 new sellers joined in a single year. The bar to meaningful entry has risen considerably since then.

Marketplace Pulse, January 2026

235

Sellers now generating $100M or more annually

Up from just 50 four years ago. Over 100,000 sellers now generate $1M or more per year, up from roughly 60,000 in 2021. The top of the marketplace keeps growing even as total seller count falls.

Marketplace Pulse 2025 Year in Review

**The “Great Compression” of 2024-2025:** Active sellers dropped from 2.4 million in 2021 to 1.65 million by end of 2025. At the same time, traffic per active seller increased 31% since 2021. More than 60% of the top 10,000 sellers launched before 2019, which shows longevity remains the strongest predictor of success. The result is fewer sellers competing for a larger per-seller revenue opportunity. This is not a declining marketplace. It is a consolidating one, and that creates real opportunity for sellers who stay in and perform.

50*%+*

Share of Amazon’s global active seller base now made up of China-based sellers

Chinese sellers crossed 50% of the global active seller base in 2025 and represent roughly 60% of new registrations. US sellers still generate higher total GMV on Amazon.com, at an estimated $157B vs China’s $132B. [Selling internationally](https://ecombrainly.com/selling-globally-on-amazon/) requires understanding how different seller origins compete in each marketplace.

Marketplace Pulse 2025-2026

1.36*M*

US-registered seller accounts, the largest single country

UK has around 330,000 active sellers. Germany has around 244,000. US-based sellers still generate more revenue per seller than any other nationality, but that edge is being compressed by Chinese-origin sellers with lower cost structures.

Capital One Shopping Research 2025

| Seller Attribute | Statistic | Source Year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sellers who are male | 50%+ | 2024 |
| Largest seller age group | 25-34 years old (33% of sellers) | 2024 |
| Pre-2019 registrations still actively selling | Less than 8% | 2025 |
| 2023 registrations still actively selling | Less than 30% | 2025 |
| Sellers with at least one local employee | 65%+ | 2025 |
| Sellers renting office or warehouse space | 49% | 2025 |
| Sellers with physical retail locations | 31% | 2025 |
| Amazon sellers also selling on eBay | 40% | 2024 |
| US jobs supported by independent Amazon sellers | 2 million+ | Amazon Empowerment Report 2025 |

Fewer new sellers joining is not a sign that Amazon is dying. It is a sign that casual and undercapitalised sellers have mostly tried and moved on. **The sellers who are gaining ground right now are running real businesses with proper inventory funding, professional listing assets, and a real advertising budget.** We see this consistently across the accounts we manage.

* Chinese-origin sellers have genuine supply chain cost advantages that you cannot beat on price alone. Your route to profitability is [building brand equity](https://ecombrainly.com/how-to-build-brand-equity/), stacking reviews faster, and creating listing content that converts at a higher rate.
* If you are entering a category where Chinese sellers already dominate the low-price end, focus your energy on better imagery, Premium A+ Content, and customer experience that generates reviews organically rather than trying to undercut on price.
* Only 30% of 2023 registrations are still active. Roughly two-thirds of the sellers who started when you did have already left. Patience and staying power are themselves competitive advantages on Amazon.

03

Seller Revenue & Earnings

## What Amazon sellers *actually earn*, the full picture

The average US seller generated more than $375,000 in annual sales in 2025, up from $290,000 in 2024. That number is accurate, but it hides an enormous skew. Here is the complete earnings picture across all revenue tiers, including the data most aggregator pages leave out entirely.

$375*K+*

Average annual sales per US-based seller in 2025, up from $290K in 2024

This is a mean pulled upward by a small number of very high-revenue operators. The median seller earns considerably less. More than 75,000 independent sellers surpassed $1M in sales in 2025, a 36% jump from 55,000+ in 2024. Use this figure for context, not for setting your own expectations.

Amazon Small Business Empowerment Report 2025

28.5*%*

Median per-product net profit margin in Q1 2025

A healthy Amazon margin sits at 15-20%. Above 25% is strong. Below 5% is hard to sustain without significant volume. The 28.5% median reflects well-chosen private label products after all fees have been accounted for.

Capital One Shopping Research 2025

42*%*

Of sellers earning under $500 per month, or currently making no sales at all

A further 10% earn $500-$1,000 per month, meaning roughly half of all active sellers make $1,000 or less monthly despite the $375K average. A small number of high-volume operators pull the mean far above where most sellers actually land.

Capital One / Jungle Scout 2024

**What the distribution actually means:** Only 2% of sellers earn $250,000+ per month. 10% earn $25,000-$250,000 per month. 28% earn $1,000-$25,000 per month. Roughly 52% earn $1,000 or less per month, including the 20% who are registered but currently making no sales (8% did not disclose). The gap between tiers tracks directly with advertising investment, catalogue depth, review velocity, and operational infrastructure. Knowing where you sit and what separates you from the next tier up is far more useful than staring at the $375K average.

$30*K*

Average first-year sales for new Amazon sellers

58% of new sellers become profitable within their first year. 22% never reach profitability at all. Sellers who focus on [Buy Box eligibility](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-buy-box/), fast delivery, and early review accumulation tend to reach positive ROI in 3-4 months on average.

Capital One Shopping Research 2024

6.3*x*

More first-year sales generated by FBA sellers vs non-FBA sellers

FBA delivers Prime eligibility and Buy Box advantage from the first day you go live. For new sellers without an established review base or brand recognition, those two advantages often make the difference between gaining traction and stalling out completely.

Amazon / RevenueGeeks 2024

| Product Category | Typical Net Margin | Primary Driver |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beauty & Personal Care | 25-35% | Small and light items, low FBA fees, strong repeat purchase rate |
| Health & Household | 22-30% | Consumable, high repeat rate, strong keyword intent |
| Pet Supplies | 20-28% | Brand loyalty, subscription behaviour, consumables |
| Home & Kitchen | 18-25% | Wide range; accessories significantly outperform large items |
| Sports & Outdoors | 17-25% | Accessories strong; large equipment runs thin margins |
| Toys & Games | 15-22% | Heavy Q4 seasonality; margins spike significantly October through December |
| Electronics | 5-15% | High competition, sustained price pressure, elevated return rates |

The single most common root cause of underperformance we find when auditing new seller accounts is launching products with margins modelled before fees, not after. **The $375K average is meaningless if your unit economics cannot survive 30-40% total Amazon fee load on top of 10-15% in advertising spend.** We see this pattern at every revenue level.

* Before launching any product, run the full cost stack: cost of goods, referral fee, FBA fulfillment fee, storage, PPC budget, and selling plan. “We’ll make it work at scale” almost never arrives before you run out of capital.
* The categories with the best margin profiles in 2025 are consumables in Beauty, Health, and Pet Supplies. Not because they are quiet, but because their repeat purchase economics mean each customer is worth more over time. Learn how to [improve customer lifetime value](https://ecombrainly.com/improving-customer-lifetime-value/) in these categories.
* The 6.3x FBA advantage for new sellers is real. In account launches we manage, FBA listings consistently outperform FBM on conversion rate and review accumulation speed in the first 90 days.

$15*B*

04

FBA: Fulfillment Statistics

## FBA adoption rates, real performance data, *and what the numbers reveal*

Fulfillment by Amazon is now the primary fulfillment method for 82% of serious Amazon sellers. These are the verified adoption, cost, and performance statistics stripped of the promotional framing you find in Amazon’s own materials. For a full side-by-side comparison, see our [FBA vs FBM breakdown](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-fba-vs-fbm/).

82*%*

Amazon sellers using FBA as their primary fulfillment method in 2025

Up from around 50% in 2019. Adoption has risen every year as Amazon ties Prime delivery benefits exclusively to FBA-fulfilled products, making the Prime badge increasingly difficult to access through other methods.

AMZScout / Amazon 2025

$98.5*B*

Amazon’s total fulfillment spend in 2024, up 8.7% year over year

Amazon deployed its one millionth warehouse robot in July 2025 across 300+ facilities, and around 75% of customer orders are now robot-assisted. This is the infrastructure that makes 1-2 day Prime delivery possible for FBA sellers at scale.

Amazon Annual Report 2024 / Amazon Robotics 2025

70*%*

Lower per-unit shipping cost via FBA vs comparable premium carrier options

FBA saves roughly 30% vs standard carrier shipping and 70% vs premium options for most standard-size products. This advantage compounds at volume and matters most for sub-$30 products where shipping is a meaningful cost component.

Amazon Seller Facts 2024

60*%+*

FBA sellers running private label brands

Private label is the dominant FBA business model. Over half of all FBA users have built their own branded product rather than reselling existing branded goods. Read our guide to [launching a private label product on Amazon](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-private-label/) for the full process.

AMZScout 2025

300*K+*

Third-party sellers using Amazon’s Multi-Channel Fulfillment services

Amazon’s fulfillment network now processes orders from Shopify stores, direct websites, and wholesale channels too. This lets you use one inventory pool across multiple sales channels, which changes the economics considerably for multichannel brands.

Capital One Shopping Research 2025

![Amazon FBA Adoption Rate Growth 2019 to 2025](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHdpZHRoPSIxMzc2IiBoZWlnaHQ9Ijc2OCIgdmlld0JveD0iMCAwIDEzNzYgNzY4Ij48cmVjdCB3aWR0aD0iMTAwJSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxMDAlIiBzdHlsZT0iZmlsbDojY2ZkNGRiO2ZpbGwtb3BhY2l0eTogMC4xOyIvPjwvc3ZnPg==)

FBA adoption rate growth from 2019 to 2025. Source: AMZScout / Amazon 2025

The 82% FBA adoption rate makes sense when you put it alongside the conversion rate data. **FBA listings in the accounts we manage consistently convert 20-30% higher than equivalent FBM listings in the same category, all else being equal.** The Prime badge does most of that work. It signals two-day delivery and easy returns without the customer needing to think about it.

* For any product priced above $25 and weighing under 3 lbs, FBA almost always wins on unit economics. For heavier items, model FBM carefully because at $8+ per unit in FBA fulfillment fees, self-fulfillment can genuinely come out ahead.
* 48% of FBA sellers launch their first product within 3 months of starting. That speed matters because Amazon’s algorithm weighs early sales velocity when setting initial ranking positions. A [well-structured launch plan](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-product-launch/) captures that window. A slow one wastes it.
* Multi-Channel Fulfillment is consistently underused by mid-stage sellers. If you run both FBA and a Shopify store, MCF removes the need for a separate 3PL and simplifies inventory management considerably.

05

Fees & Profitability Data

## The real cost of selling on Amazon, *fee by fee*

Total Amazon FBA fees typically consume 25-40% of selling price. Sellers who stay consistently profitable know which fees are unavoidable, which ones can be reduced, and which ones quietly destroy margin over time if left unmanaged. Full breakdown in our [Amazon seller fees guide](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-fees-for-seller/), and you can also use our [profit margin calculator](https://ecombrainly.com/how-to-calculate-profit-margins/) to run your own numbers.

15*%*

Average Amazon referral fee across most categories

Range is 6% for personal computers up to 45% for Amazon device accessories. Apparel under $15 dropped to 5% effective January 2024. This fee applies to every sale regardless of how you fulfill it.

Amazon Fee Schedule 2025

$3.18*+*

FBA fulfillment fee per unit for small standard items (4 oz or less) in 2026

Up from $3.06 in 2025. Low-price items under $10 start around $2.37. The most common large standard tier (2-2.5 lbs) runs $6.63 per unit. FBA fulfillment fees rose by an average of $0.08 per unit effective January 15, 2026.

Amazon FBA Fee Schedule 2026

$39.99

Monthly Professional Seller plan fee

The Individual plan charges $0.99 per item sold with no monthly fee, but excludes advertising and bulk listing tools. The Professional plan pays for itself at 40 or more monthly sales and is required to run any paid advertising.

Amazon 2025

25-40*%*

Of selling price consumed by total FBA fees on an average product

This includes the referral fee, FBA fulfillment fee, storage, and selling plan. PPC advertising costs are on top of this. Most unprofitable sellers underestimated total fee load before launching.

Titan Network FBA Analysis 2025

**The fee that catches most sellers off guard:** Long-term storage fees apply to inventory stored for over 365 days at $6.90 per cubic foot or $0.15 per unit, whichever is higher. For slow-moving products, this can eat through the entire per-unit profit within a few months. Good [inventory management](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-inventory-management/) is not just an operational preference, it is a direct profitability lever.

| Fee Category | Rate / Range | Key Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Referral fee (most categories) | 8-15% | Non-negotiable; applies to every sale regardless of fulfillment method |
| FBA fulfillment, small standard size | $2.37-$3.87/unit (2026) | Based on size tier, weight, and price band; updated annually |
| Monthly inventory storage, off-peak | $0.87/cubic ft | Rises to $2.25/cubic ft during Q4 2026 (down from $2.40 in 2025) |
| Long-term storage (365+ days) | $6.90/cubic ft | Or $0.15/unit, whichever is greater; systematically destroys margins on slow-moving SKUs |
| Inbound placement fee (introduced 2024) | $0.25-$1.58/unit | Largely avoidable with optimised inbound shipment routing |
| Low inventory fee (below 35-day supply in 2026) | Varies by size tier | Threshold loosened from 28 to 35 days of supply for 2026 |
| Peak holiday fulfillment surcharge | Oct 15 to Jan 14 | Annual; consistent rate maintained through 2025-2026 |
| Professional selling plan | $39.99/month | Required for advertising access and bulk listing tools |

**Sellers who proactively adjusted packaging and pricing in 2024-2025 saw 4-6% higher net ROI** compared to sellers who reacted after fee changes had already landed. Moving from the large standard to medium standard FBA size tier saves $0.50-$2.00 per unit. At 2,000 units per month, that packaging change alone is worth $1,000-$4,000 per year with no change to the product itself.

Some products are genuinely better off fulfilled by merchant, especially heavy or oversized items where FBA fees exceed what you would pay to ship them yourself. Evaluating [FBA vs FBM at the ASIN level](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-fba-vs-fbm/) rather than across your whole account is how you find those opportunities.

4-6*%*

ROI uplift from proactive fee management

Seller Labs Analysis 2025

When we dig into client profitability problems, the referral fee is rarely the issue. Sellers know that one. The problem is almost always slow-moving inventory stacking up storage charges on top of the inbound placement fee that was introduced in 2024. **In accounts we managed through 2025 and 2026, these two fees together reduced net margins by 4-8 percentage points on products with weak sell-through rates.** That is a meaningful hit on otherwise healthy products.

* Set a 90-day sell-through threshold on every SKU as your maximum comfort level. If a product is not moving in 90 days at current velocity, start a price reduction or submit a removal order before the 180-day storage fee tier kicks in.
* Build the inbound placement fee into your unit economics from the start when you are sourcing. Sellers who route shipments to Amazon’s preferred distribution points (typically through Amazon Warehousing and Distribution) substantially reduce this cost.
* Review your size tier classification on every SKU at least once a year. [Packaging and labelling changes](https://ecombrainly.com/amazon-label-requirements/) are often the highest-ROI optimisation available to mid-stage sellers and they are consistently overlooked.

06

These benchmarks show what is normal, what is achievable, and what separates growing accounts from ones that are stalling out. Average cost-per-click for Sponsored Products in the US, 2025

Up 15.5% from $0.97 in 2024. Category range runs from $0.89 in fashion to $2.50-$7.00 or more in supplements and competitive health categories. CPC is projected at $1.18-$1.25 in 2026.

Average Amazon PPC conversion rate in 2025

This is 7-8x higher than the typical ecommerce site conversion rate of 1.33%. It is the core reason Amazon advertising delivers stronger per-click ROI than most other digital channels.

Average ACoS across all Amazon sellers
