### [Blog](/blog)

# 7 Best commercetools Alternatives for 2026

Discover the best commercetools alternatives for 2026, comparing cost, features, headless flexibility, B2B tools, subscriptions, and implementation speed. Find the right platform for your budget and tech stack.

Swell Team | January 05, 2026

While commercetools leads enterprise composable commerce with its MACH architecture, many businesses find themselves priced out or overwhelmed by its complexity. The platform's [$50,000-$200,000+ first-year costs](https://litextension.com/blog/commercetools-pricing/) and 3-12 month implementation timelines push growing brands toward alternatives that deliver headless flexibility without enterprise-grade budgets or massive development teams. From API-first platforms like [Swell](https://www.swell.is/headless-commerce) to hybrid SaaS solutions like BigCommerce, these seven alternatives serve different business models, technical requirements, and growth stages across the ecommerce landscape.

The [headless commerce market](https://www.webyking.com/blog/headless-commerce-statistics/) is projected to reach $11.8 billion by 2028, growing at 17.5% CAGR as brands prioritize flexibility over monolithic platform constraints. With headless adoption accelerating across major retailers, choosing the right commercetools alternative has become a strategic imperative for mid-market and enterprise businesses alike.

## **Key Takeaways**

* **Total cost of ownership varies dramatically**: commercetools requires $65,000-$200,000+ in year one while alternatives like Swell deliver comparable headless capabilities starting at [$29/month](https://www.swell.is/pricing)—evaluate based on revenue stage and technical resources
* **Native subscription capabilities eliminate app dependency**: Swell includes [full subscription billing](https://www.swell.is/for/subscription-ecommerce) on all plans, saving $3,600-$6,000/year compared to Shopify Plus merchants who must purchase third-party apps like ReCharge
* **Implementation timelines impact time-to-revenue**: [Swell enables B2B marketplace](https://www.swell.is/blog/swell-vs-shopify) launches in 3 months versus 9-12 months on Shopify Plus and 3-12+ months for commercetools—factor deployment speed into platform selection
* **Product modeling flexibility determines catalog scalability**: Swell offers unlimited variants and 4+ product option types while Shopify Plus caps products at 100 variants and 3 options—audit your catalog complexity before committing
* **Integration ecosystem size doesn't equal business fit**: commercetools offers 125+ extensions and Shopify Plus has 1,000+ apps, but Swell's 40+ native integrations cover essential needs while custom API connections fill gaps without bloating your tech stack

## **1. Swell — Native Subscriptions and Unlimited Product Flexibility**

Swell stands as the strongest commercetools alternative for businesses that need headless architecture without enterprise complexity or pricing. The platform delivers API-first commerce with built-in [subscription management](https://www.swell.is/for/subscription-ecommerce) that competitors require expensive apps or custom development to replicate.

**Core Platform Strengths:**

* Native subscription billing across all pricing tiers—no third-party apps required
* Unlimited product variants and 4+ option input types for complex catalogs
* Mixed cart capabilities combining physical, digital, and subscription products in single checkout
* Multi-warehouse management built into the platform
* Full checkout customization via API without tier restrictions
* 0% transaction fees on external payment gateways

**Pricing Structure:**

* Starter: [$29/month](https://www.swell.is/pricing) (up to $50K annual sales)
* Basic: $79/month (up to $250K annual sales)
* Standard: $299/month (up to $1M annual sales)
* Unlimited: $2,250/month (up to $5M annual sales)
* Custom/Enterprise: Negotiated for $10M+ merchants

Swell's greatest advantage lies in its native subscription engine. While commercetools requires custom development for recurring billing logic and Shopify Plus merchants spend [$300-$500/month](https://www.swell.is/alternative/shopify) on apps like ReCharge, Swell includes pause/resume functionality, dunning management, and separate billing/fulfillment schedules on every plan.

The platform's product modeling capabilities address limitations that frustrate merchants on other platforms. Where [Shopify caps variants](https://www.swell.is/alternative/shopify) at 100 with only 3 option types, Swell supports unlimited variants with multiple option input types for technical products, made-to-order items, and complex catalogs.

Implementation speed proves equally compelling. Swell customers report B2B marketplace launches in 3 months compared to 9-12 months on Shopify Plus—a difference that translates directly to faster revenue generation. One subscription brand documented [45% cost reduction](https://www.swell.is/blog/swell-vs-shopify) after switching from Shopify Plus to Swell.

For [developers building custom storefronts](https://www.swell.is/for-developers), Swell provides GraphQL and REST APIs with modern framework support including Next.js, Nuxt, and Remix. The platform balances headless flexibility with managed backend infrastructure, eliminating the extensive custom development that commercetools demands.

## **2. Shopify Plus — Extensive App Ecosystem with Merchant-Friendly Interface**

Shopify Plus maintains its position as the dominant enterprise ecommerce platform, offering the largest integration ecosystem and lowest learning curve for non-technical teams.

**Platform Capabilities:**

* 1,000+ pre-built app integrations covering every ecommerce function
* Hydrogen framework for headless storefront development
* Shopify Payments with competitive processing rates
* Extensive agency and developer partner network
* Proven enterprise scalability with Fortune 500 clients

**Pricing Model:**

* Starting at $2,500/month
* 2.9% + $0.30 transaction fees when not using Shopify Payments
* Additional costs for subscription apps ($300-$500/month)

Shopify Plus serves businesses prioritizing speed-to-market with minimal technical overhead. The platform powers major brands including Pepsi, Staples, and Nestle, demonstrating proven scalability for high-volume operations.

However, significant limitations push merchants toward alternatives. The [100-variant product limit](https://www.swell.is/alternative/shopify) with only 3 options creates workarounds for complex catalogs. Checkout customization remains restricted even at Plus tier, and subscription functionality requires third-party apps that add both cost and integration complexity.

## **3. BigCommerce — Native B2B Features with Hybrid Flexibility**

BigCommerce occupies the middle ground between fully headless platforms and traditional SaaS solutions, offering 600+ pre-built integrations with strong out-of-box B2B capabilities.

**B2B-Focused Features:**

* Customer organizations and account hierarchies
* Multiple product catalogs per customer segment
* Customer-specific pricing and payment terms
* Quote management and approval workflows
* 55+ global payment gateways

**Pricing Tiers:**

* Standard: $39/month
* Plus: $105/month
* Pro: $399/month
* Enterprise: Custom pricing

BigCommerce excels for B2B merchants who need organizational account structures without custom development. The platform charges no transaction fees regardless of payment gateway choice, unlike Shopify's mandatory fees for non-Shopify Payments transactions.

The hybrid SaaS + API architecture provides headless capabilities while maintaining merchant-friendly interfaces for non-technical users. However, subscription commerce still requires third-party apps, and sales volume thresholds trigger automatic tier upgrades that increase costs as businesses scale.

## **4. Saleor — Open-Source GraphQL-Native Architecture**

Saleor represents the leading open-source commercetools alternative, built from the ground up with GraphQL-native architecture for developers who want complete control over their commerce stack.

**Technical Foundation:**

* Python/Django backend with React storefront
* GraphQL API covering all commerce operations
* Self-hosted or cloud deployment options
* No licensing fees for self-hosted implementations
* Active open-source community with regular contributions

**Deployment Options:**

* Self-hosted: Free (infrastructure and development costs only)
* Saleor Cloud: Usage-based pricing

Saleor appeals to development teams with Python expertise who prioritize architectural freedom over managed services. The platform's open-source model eliminates licensing costs while providing full access to source code for customization.

The tradeoff involves significant development investment. Unlike Swell's managed backend approach, Saleor requires technical teams to handle hosting, scaling, security, and ongoing maintenance—costs that can exceed commercial platform fees for businesses without dedicated engineering resources.

## **5. Elastic Path — Enterprise B2B with Product Experience Management**

Elastic Path targets large enterprises requiring sophisticated product information management alongside composable commerce architecture, with pricing reflecting its enterprise positioning at $50,000/year minimum.

**Enterprise Capabilities:**

* Advanced Product Experience Management (PXM)
* Composable architecture supporting mix-and-match commerce components
* Complex B2B pricing and catalog management
* Multi-brand and multi-region deployment support
* Extensive enterprise integration capabilities

**Target Market:**

* Large enterprises with $50M+ annual revenue
* Complex product information requirements
* Multi-brand portfolio management needs
* Sophisticated B2B commerce operations

Elastic Path serves organizations where product data complexity justifies significant platform investment. The platform competes directly with commercetools for enterprise deals requiring advanced PIM capabilities integrated with commerce functionality.

For mid-market businesses, Elastic Path's pricing and complexity create barriers that platforms like Swell address at a fraction of the cost while delivering comparable headless flexibility.

## **6. Adobe Commerce (Magento) — Legacy Enterprise with Headless Capabilities**

Adobe Commerce evolved from Magento's open-source roots into an enterprise platform, offering both traditional and headless deployment options.

**Platform Options:**

* Magento Open Source: Free (self-hosted)
* Adobe Commerce: Customized pricing
* Adobe Commerce Cloud: Managed hosting with licensing

**Strengths:**

* Extensive customization through module ecosystem
* Large developer community and agency network
* Proven scalability for high-volume merchants
* PWA Studio for headless frontend development

Adobe Commerce suits enterprises with existing Magento investments or specific Adobe ecosystem requirements. The platform's flexibility comes with complexity—implementation timelines often extend 6-12 months, and total cost of ownership frequently exceeds initial licensing estimates due to hosting, security, and maintenance requirements.

## **7. Medusa — Modern Open-Source for Developer-Led Teams**

Medusa offers a JavaScript-based open-source alternative designed specifically for developer-led commerce projects requiring modern tooling and full customization control.

**Developer-Focused Features:**

* Node.js/TypeScript backend architecture
* Plugin system for extending core functionality
* REST and GraphQL API support
* Self-hosted with cloud deployment options
* Active community and documentation

**Implementation Model:**

* Open-source: Free (development and hosting costs)
* Enterprise support: Custom pricing

Medusa appeals to JavaScript development teams building custom commerce experiences without platform constraints. The modern tech stack integrates naturally with frontend frameworks like Next.js and Remix, creating cohesive development workflows.

Like Saleor, Medusa requires significant technical investment that may exceed commercial platform costs for businesses lacking dedicated engineering teams. The platform trades managed services for complete architectural control.

## **The commercetools Challenge: Why Users Seek Alternatives**

Analysis of market feedback reveals consistent pain points driving organizations away from commercetools despite its market leadership position.

**High Total Cost of Ownership**: The platform's [annual license starting at $50,000](https://litextension.com/blog/commercetools-pricing/) represents only the starting point. Custom development for features other platforms include natively—subscription billing, B2B pricing rules, merchant-friendly admin interfaces—adds [$10,000-$100,000+](https://elogic.co/blog/commercetools-pricing/) in implementation costs.

**Developer Dependency**: commercetools' API-only architecture requires extensive custom development for most features. Business users cannot make routine changes without engineering support, creating bottlenecks that slow operations and increase ongoing costs.

**Extended Implementation Timelines**: While Swell customers launch in weeks and build B2B marketplaces in 3 months, commercetools implementations typically span 3-12+ months before generating revenue—a delay that impacts cash flow and competitive positioning.

**Limited Merchant Center**: commercetools' Merchant Center lacks depth for day-to-day operations, requiring custom development for business user needs that competing platforms address out-of-box.

## **Choosing Your Alternative Based on Business Model**

Platform selection should align with your specific commerce requirements, technical resources, and growth trajectory.

**By Business Type:**

* **Subscription-first businesses**: Swell delivers native recurring billing without app dependencies
* **Complex product catalogs**: Swell's unlimited variants handle technical and configurable products
* **B2B wholesale operations**: BigCommerce offers customer organizations and tiered pricing natively
* **Developer-led projects**: Saleor or Medusa provide open-source flexibility with full code access
* **Enterprise multi-brand**: Elastic Path or Adobe Commerce support complex organizational structures

**By Budget and Resources:**

* **$30-300/month**: Swell (full headless with subscriptions included)
* **$2,000-5,000/month**: Shopify Plus or BigCommerce Enterprise
* **$50,000+/year**: commercetools, Elastic Path, or Adobe Commerce

**Three-Year TCO Comparison (Growing $500K to $2M Revenue):**

* Swell: $55,000-$70,000
* BigCommerce: $66,000-$94,000
* Shopify Plus: $222,000-$250,000
* commercetools: $275,000-$525,000

For businesses seeking headless architecture with native subscription support, unlimited product flexibility, and rapid implementation at accessible pricing, [Swell's platform](https://www.swell.is/pricing) delivers the strongest value proposition among commercetools alternatives.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**

### **What makes Swell a strong alternative to commercetools?**

Swell delivers comparable headless commerce capabilities at 75-85% lower total cost of ownership. The platform includes native subscription billing on all plans—functionality that commercetools requires custom development to achieve. Swell's unlimited product variants and mixed cart capabilities (physical + digital + subscription in single checkout) address use cases that demand significant engineering investment on commercetools. Implementation timelines of weeks versus months accelerate time-to-revenue for growing brands.

### **How does Swell handle international sales with multiple currencies and languages?**

Swell supports multi-currency functionality with explicit pricing rules per currency for products, shipping, and discounts, plus automatic exchange rate conversions. Multi-language support localizes all customer-facing content including products, categories, checkout, and email notifications through the admin dashboard or API. Tax calculation integrates with Avalara and TaxJar for region-specific compliance, with support for creating custom tax rule groups by location and product type.

### **Are there transaction fees on external payment gateways with Swell?**

Swell charges 0% transaction fees on external payment gateways. The platform integrates with Stripe, PayPal, Authorize.Net, Amazon Pay, Braintree, and Buy Now Pay Later services including Affirm and Resolve. This contrasts with Shopify's 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction when merchants don't use Shopify Payments, representing significant savings at scale.

### **What technical flexibility does Swell offer for developers?**

Swell provides RESTful Backend API with full CRUD access to all data models, Frontend API for browser-based usage, and Checkout API for custom payment flows. Developers can build storefronts in any JavaScript framework including React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js, and Nuxt. The platform supports custom fields on all standard models, custom model creation for business-specific data, and webhooks for real-time event notifications—all while maintaining managed backend infrastructure that eliminates hosting and scaling complexity.

### **How long does migration from commercetools to an alternative platform typically take?**

Migration timelines vary by platform and data complexity. Swell implementations typically complete in 2-12 weeks including data migration, while Shopify Plus and BigCommerce migrations require 2-6 months. The primary factors affecting timeline include catalog complexity, custom data model requirements, and integration scope. Swell provides CSV import/export for products, customers, and orders, with API access enabling custom migration scripts for complex data structures.

This article from the Swell blog (dated January 05, 2026) presents seven alternatives to commercetools for 2026 ecommerce needs, targeting businesses that find commercetools too expensive or complex. The headless commerce market is projected to reach $11.8 billion by 2028 with a 17.5% CAGR.

Key alternatives covered:
1. **Swell** - API-first commerce with native subscription billing (no third-party apps needed), unlimited product variants, mixed carts (physical+digital+subscription), multi-warehouse management, 0% transaction fees on external gateways. Pricing: Starter $29/month to Custom/Enterprise negotiated for $10M+ merchants. B2B marketplace launches in 3 months (vs. 9-12 months on Shopify Plus), with one brand reporting 45% cost reduction after switching from Shopify Plus.
2. **Shopify Plus** - 1,000+ apps, Hydrogen headless framework, starts at $2,500/month with 2.9% + $0.30 transaction fees without Shopify Payments. Limited to 100 variants/3 options, restricted checkout customization, subscriptions require third-party apps ($300-500/month).
3. **BigCommerce** - Native B2B features (customer organizations, catalog hierarchies, quote management), 55+ payment gateways, no transaction fees. Pricing: Standard $39/month to Enterprise custom. Sales volume thresholds trigger auto tier upgrades.
4. **Saleor** - Open-source GraphQL-native (Python/Django), free self-hosted or usage-based cloud pricing. Requires significant dev investment for hosting, scaling, security.
5. **Elastic Path** - Enterprise B2B with Product Experience Management, $50,000/year minimum, targets $50M+ revenue companies.
6. **Adobe Commerce (Magento)** - Free open source or customized enterprise pricing, flexible module ecosystem, but 6-12 month implementations with hidden TCO.
7. **Medusa** - JavaScript/Node.js open-source, free with cloud options, developer-led use cases.

**Why users leave commercetools**: $50,000+ annual license with $10,000-$100,000+ in custom implementation costs, API-only architecture requiring developer dependency, 3-12+ month implementation timelines, and limited Merchant Center functionality.

**Cost comparisons (3-year TCO for a business growing $500K to $2M revenue)**: Swell $55,000-70,000; BigCommerce $66,000-94,000; Shopify Plus $222,000-250,000; commercetools $275,000-525,000.

**Selection guidance**: Swell for subscription-first businesses and complex catalogs; BigCommerce for B2B wholesale; Saleor or Medusa for developer-led projects; Elastic Path or Adobe Commerce for enterprise multi-brand operations. Swell migration completes in 2-12 weeks vs. 2-6 months for Shopify Plus/BigCommerce.

# 8 best practices for your enterprise-grade B2B commerce implementation

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6a38f6b817cf6c8da550757a/6a622c68b3f793b967b8dc3e_CTA_Button.svg)

Publish date: March 27, 2026

Get weekly updates on markets, new features, and exclusive investment insights delivered straight to your inbox.

**Key takeaways:**

* Modern B2B commerce requires flexibility, faster innovation and better buyer experiences.
* Launching a B2B eCommerce MVP or pilot project helps test assumptions, reduce risk and validate strategies before full-scale implementation.
* Integrating ERP systems seamlessly and adopting cloud-native commerce security ensures operational efficiency, data protection and regulatory compliance.
* Continuous monitoring, testing and optimization are essential to maximize revenue, improve performance and adapt to evolving customer expectations.

## The case for modern commerce in B2B

According to [Gartner](https://commercetools.com/resources/analyst-report/gartner-magic-quadrant), 75% of B2B organizations will complete their highest revenue deals via digital channels. Even more striking:

* [85% of B2B organizations](https://dynamicweb.com/resources/downloads/white-papers/key-b2b-ecommerce-trends-for-2025) now operate an eCommerce storefront or self-service portal, and over 50% are tapping into online marketplaces to reach customers.
* [56% of B2B organizations](https://www.valtech.com/whitepapers/the-voice-of-digital-leaders-in-manufacturing-2025/) drove new-product revenue growth through eCommerce in 2025.

Given this landscape, B2B organizations relying on legacy platforms risk missing these opportunities. Taking advantage of modern commerce — especially as [agentic AI](https://commercetools.com/products/agentic-commerce) rises — has become critical for manufacturers, wholesalers and distributors. Leveraging modern digital infrastructure helps them elevate buyer experiences, automate workflow and drive revenue growth.

To make the switch from monolithic to modern commerce faster, safer and more strategic, here are **eight best practices** to guide your journey.

## Best practice #1 — Identify your business and customer needs

The crucial mistake many B2B leaders make is assuming they know [what buyers want](https://commercetools.com/blog/what-makes-b2b-buyers-tick-in-digital-commerce) and creating implementation plans without involving the people they need to impress. While it may seem obvious, uncovering customer expectations and the issues they face is critical.

Here’s a great example: [Mars](https://commercetools.com/blog/sweet-success-lessons-from-mars-on-its-build-and-buy-approach) (the company behind M&M’S, Skittles and Snickers) also offers products to businesses. Despite their sweet success, the B2B ordering process for the ice cream unit was far from palatable. After receiving frequent customer complaints, the Mars team decided to act.

The first step? Talking to customers to create a prototype that they could test and give feedback on. In 90 days, the Mars team developed a prototype delivering what customers asked for. After implementing additional feedback, Mars created a frictionless order experience that wowed customers.

In addition to customer feedback, identify internal business needs:

* [Reduce total costs of ownership (TCO)](https://commercetools.com/tco-and-roi).
* Eliminate technical debt.
* Enable hybrid sales teams.
* Support omnichannel and personalization.

Answering these questions ensures your platform selection aligns with both business and customer requirements.

## Best practice #2 — Build a modular and flexible architecture

Now that you know the business and customer needs, it’s time to think about your tech stack. If you’re on a legacy commerce platform and plan to migrate to a modular, [composable architecture](https://commercetools.com/commerce-platform), you can do so in a phased approach (instead of the traditional “big bang” switchover).

Migrating off a monolithic architecture to a modular one is ideal with a phased approach (AKA, the [strangler pattern](https://commercetools.com/blog/how-to-migrate-to-composable-with-a-faster-roi-with-the-strangler-pattern)), which enables you to move one component at a time to the new infrastructure. This way, you can reduce the risk associated with the big-bang approach while reaping short-term benefits by shortening your migration’s time-to-value.

## Best practice #3 — Evaluate and select best-of-breed solutions

Which components do you need to elevate the buyer experience? The beauty of a modular platform is that it lets you break down your commerce infrastructure into components, so you can best evaluate what you need, what you can develop yourself and what to buy from [best-of-breed vendors](https://commercetools.com/blog/best-of-breed-how-to-pick-a-composable-commerce-tech-partner). This may include (but is not limited to) payment service providers (PSPs), inventory management, search and CMS systems.

Next, assess the B2B eCommerce features that matter to you, such as personalized pricing, reordering and order scheduling, quote management. This ensures your commerce stack supports business objectives while avoiding unnecessary [technical debt](https://commercetools.com/blog/overcoming-technical-debt-with-composable-commerce).

It’s worth noting that many B2B enterprises have invested time and money in [homegrown commerce platforms](https://commercetools.com/blog/homegrown-vs-composable-commerce-why-build-and-buy-is-the-right-approach-for-businesses-to-grow) in the hope of capturing their business-specific uniqueness in their tech stack. However, this approach usually falls short, as maintaining an internal DIY platform requires significant resources and, over time, tends to accumulate technical debt.

A modular commerce platform provides the best combination of the build-and-buy approach: You can build what makes your business unique and buy the components that you don’t have the internal capability to create from scratch.

## Best practice #4 — Integrate seamlessly (including ERP)

Start integrating the components you need. With a modular, API-first approach, you can integrate seamlessly, regardless of whether they’re built in-house, sourced from best-of-breed vendors or a mix of both.

Most B2B enterprises should consider [integrating ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems](https://commercetools.com/blog/making-your-b2b-ecommerce-smarter-with-a-seamless-erp-integration) with their commerce platform to maximize operational efficiency, automate processes, minimize expensive order errors and eliminate data discrepancies.

While some B2B organizations buy their ERP and commerce solutions from a single vendor for simplicity’s sake, this approach doesn’t necessarily yield the best results. This is because such solutions are tightly integrated (and therefore, monolithic in nature), which prevents the company from adapting customer experiences faster, customizing features and innovating at a fast pace.

Decoupling commerce and ERP systems is not as complicated as you think. This is possible because, by definition, modular, API-first platforms enable seamless integrations without affecting the rest of your infrastructure.

## Best practice #5 — Create an MVP or pilot project

Whether you call it a proof of concept (POC), a minimum viable product (MVP), a minimum testable product (MTP), a pilot project or a prototype, this is the stage in which you can test assumptions, collect data, refine your approach, mitigate risk by starting with a small-scale trial — and prove that a larger investment will pay off.

This approach also helps validate assumptions before investing significant resources in a full-scale implementation, as well as identify potential problems or limitations early on, saving time and money in the long run.

The pilot approach should test key hypotheses related to your business needs, such as:

* Will implementing a new checkout process reduce cart abandonment by 15%?
* Is it feasible to address tier 2 and tier 3 customers through digital channels?
* Can eCommerce generate revenue for low-complexity transactions, e.g., reordering?

While you can select more than one hypothesis to test, don’t fall into the trap of overloading your pilot with multiple variables or objectives because it makes it harder to measure success. Instead, focus on a singular problem that directly impacts your business outcomes, such as improving revenue, reducing costs or enhancing operational efficiency.

Finally, ensure your pilot adheres to the principles of incremental change and reversibility, so you can roll back the results if needed. By testing in a controlled environment, such as a subset of your customer base or a specific product line, you can assess the viability of your approach before making broader changes. This minimizes risk and allows you to adjust your strategy without causing disruptions.

Finally, prioritize pilot programs that test new capabilities — like self-service portals, pricing automation or product availability tools — aligned with core business KPIs. Structure your roadmap to be 80% fixed, based on strategic priorities, and 20% agile, allowing flexibility to respond to urgent issues or new opportunities.

💡Check our [practical guide](https://commercetools.com/resources/whitepaper/making-the-business-case-for-change "”practical") to navigate and succeed in B2B digital transformation.

## Best practice #6 — Prioritize security and compliance

With the continuous growth and evolution of eCommerce, it’s paramount to ensure the security of online transactions and safeguard user data. That’s why B2B enterprises should prioritize [security and compliance](https://commercetools.com/technology/trust-center) and watch out for:

* A governance framework.
* Risk management.
* Real-time monitoring.
* Data analysis.
* Complete isolation and segregation of persistent data.
* Regular penetration tests.
* Compliance based on industry standards, which may include (but are not limited to) ISO/IEC 27001, TISAX, GDPR, etc.

Using [cloud-native commerce security](https://commercetools.com/blog/what-s-cloud-native-saas-and-why-is-it-a-core-trait-of-composable-commerce) further enhances protection. In contrast to on-premises IT, where you need to build and maintain all servers yourself, a cloud-native approach from Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides the highest level of data separation. It also includes:

* Automated security measures like backups and real-time threat detection.
* Multi-layered security, including network firewalls, virtual private networks (VPNs) and encryption, to help ensure data protection at every level.
* Data recovery in the event of a disaster or system failure.

## Best practice #7 — Test rigorously and constantly

Test every component and integration in your composable stack to:

* Identify compatibility issues across different tech stack components to avoid system crashes or data loss.
* Ensure data integrity by verifying that data is accurately transferred between components of the tech stack, preventing data errors or corruption.
* Optimize performance by identifying any bottlenecks to improve overall system performance and reduce downtime.

For testing to become an integral part of your process, you can follow these four steps:

1. Develop a testing plan outlining what components will be tested, how testing will be performed and what metrics will be used to measure success.
2. Use testing tools, such as load-testing software and performance-monitoring tools.
3. Test constantly to ensure everything works without issues — or anticipate problems before they become a blocker.
4. Record and analyze each test's results, identifying any areas of concern or opportunities for improvement.

## Best practice #8 — Monitor, optimize and adapt

Here are a few ways B2B enterprises can monitor their digital commerce solution:

* **Performance monitoring:** Keep track of performance metrics such as page load time, server response time and transaction processing time to identify areas that could be optimized. Also, with real-time monitoring tools, you can identify issues as they occur, such as system crashes or slow page load times.
* **User monitoring:** How does the B2B buyer behave? What areas of your platform is the user interacting with? By tracking the customer journey through the platform, analyzing user search queries and monitoring shopping cart behavior, you can spot expectations and issues that can be improved.
* **Analytics:** Analyze data like customer behavior, product performance and sales data to identify trends and patterns that could be used to optimize performance.

More than monitoring and analytics, open and continuous communication with customers will help you stay on top of expectations and demands, so your innovations can cater to the people that matter the most — and your business is ready to capitalize on that.

## FAQs

### What business metrics should you define before a migration to modern commerce?

Define KPIs for revenue growth, operational efficiency, cost reduction, conversion rates, and customer satisfaction before the migration. These metrics help measure the success of your B2B composable commerce implementation.

### How does the strangler pattern reduce risk during a monolithic to composable migration?

The strangler pattern eCommerce migration allows moving components incrementally from a monolithic system to microservices. This reduces risk by avoiding a full-scale disruption and delivers short-term benefits with each phase.

### How should B2B companies evaluate the “build vs. buy” approach for their commerce stack?

Assess your internal capabilities versus vendor offerings. Build components that create differentiation, and buy proven solutions for standard features to save time and reduce technical debt.

### What are the best methods to integrate an ERP system with composable commerce?

Use API-first, modular connections to decouple ERP from commerce systems. This allows seamless integration while maintaining flexibility and agility in your platform.

### Why is launching a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) crucial for B2B commerce projects?

A B2B eCommerce MVP prototype tests hypotheses with minimal risk, validates assumptions, and identifies issues early, ensuring resource-efficient scaling of full deployments.

### What security and compliance standards are critical for a B2B digital commerce architecture?

Standards like ISO/IEC 27001, TISAX, GDPR and industry-specific compliance regulations ensure your system protects customer data and business operations.

### How does cloud-native infrastructure improve data security compared to on-premise IT?

Cloud-native commerce security offers multi-layered protection, automated threat detection, encrypted data storage and disaster recovery, reducing the operational burden and improving resilience versus on-premises solutions.

7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.

### Dive Brief:

### Dive Insight:

The collaboration with Shopify is part of YouTube’s ongoing investment in social commerce. In 2022, David Katz, vice president of shopping product at YouTube, [announced the company’s partnership with Shopify](https://www.retaildive.com/news/youtube-partners-shopify-shopping-features/627783/) to let creators link to their Shopify store on their channels. At that time, the company said it would continue to expand its Live, short-form and long-form video shoppable content capabilities.

“In 2023, people watched over 30 billion hours of shopping-related videos on YouTube, helping make connections between shopping creators and their fans deeper, easier, and more fulfilling,” Suyog Karnawat, product manager at YouTube Shopping, wrote in a statement, citing the tech company’s internal data. “Over the past few months, we’ve introduced updates so viewers can shop for new favorites, have made tagging easier for creators, and more.”

YouTube is enhancing its content shopping features as other platforms roll out similar features and bring their platforms into the social commerce playing field. 

In 2022, Wish [introduced its Wish Clips feature](https://www.retaildive.com/news/wish-debuts-shoppable-video-tool-for-merchants/618943/), which lets users view product information and buy products in the app’s short-form videos. The following year, TikTok [launched the TikTok Shop](https://www.retaildive.com/news/tiktok-shop-launches-us/693404/) in the U.S., enabling businesses to showcase their products on the social media app. Earlier this year, Amazon Live [debuted its shoppable, free ad-supported channel on Prime Video](https://www.retaildive.com/news/amazon-shoppable-ad-supported-fast-channel-prime-video-freevee/713693/), allowing viewers browse, shop and engage with content they’re watching on TV or their mobile devices.

When handling different types of content:

# Top 10 Most Popular Social Media Platforms in 2026

Learn what the most popular social media platforms are in 2026 and why they stand out.

![](https://www.gravatar.com/avatar/d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e?s=200&d=404)
![](https://cdn.shopify.com/b/shopify-brochure2-assets/0403b8057ba0c10adc7f114e663d3ffe.jpg?originalWidth=1848&originalHeight=782)

On this page

Start your online business today.

For free.

The world’s most popular social media platforms’ rankings are constantly changing. For example, from February to October 2025, WhatsApp overtook YouTube and tied with Instagram to become the second most popular platform in the world.

Posting on popular social media platforms is a strong tactic to increase [brand awareness](/blog/brand-awareness) and [drive visitors to your website](/blog/how-to-increase-website-traffic), if it’s where your audience spends their time. [Knowing your audience](/blog/know-your-audience) well enough to know which platforms they use most helps focus your [social media marketing strategy](/blog/social-media-marketing-strategy) and build meaningful connections.

Statistically, people in different demographics prefer different social platforms and sometimes, for different purposes. To make the most impact and return on investment ([ROI](/blog/what-is-return-on-investment)), especially if you’re a [solopreneur](/blog/solopreneur) or have a lean team, choose the social [channel marketing](/blog/channel-marketing) strategy best aligned with your [target audience](/blog/target-audience).

Read on to learn about the most popular social media platforms and the unique strengths they offer brands like yours.

## Most popular social media platforms

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rank** | **Social media platform** | **No. of monthly active users (as of October 2025)** |
| 1 | Facebook | 3.070 million |
| 2 | WhatsApp | 3,000 million |
| 3 | Instagram | 3,000 million |
| 4 | YouTube | 2,580 million |
| 5 | TikTok | 1,990 million |
| 6 | WeChat | 1,410 million |
| 7 | Telegram | 1,000 million |
| 8 | Messenger | 942 million |
| 9 | Snapchat | 932 million |
| 10 | Reddit | 765 million |

Your brand doesn’t need a social media presence on all the [social media apps](/blog/social-media-apps). It’s more efficient to match your brand with the platform used by your ideal customer. Otherwise, you risk spreading yourself too thin or investing in a platform with low returns. By learning more about each, it’s easier to determine which channels best suit your business:

## 1. Facebook (3.07 billion users)

With more than three billion users worldwide, [Facebook](/blog/facebook-marketing) is the top social media platform. Nearly three out of every five of the estimated [5.66 billion](https://datareportal.com/social-media-users) social media users around the world are active on Facebook.

In the United States, the biggest share of Facebook users is 25- to 34-year-olds, at [24.2%](https://www.statista.com/statistics/187549/facebook-distribution-of-users-age-group-usa/), followed by 35- to 44-year-olds, at 19%. Since the rise of Instagram and TikTok, Facebook’s image has skewed older than that, but it’s not the reality.

Reels are the [most engaging format](https://www.statista.com/statistics/934749/average-facebook-page-user-engagement-rates-selected-posts-worldwide/) on the platform, giving [ecommerce](/blog/what-is-ecommerce) businesses an opportunity to show off their personalities. For example, luxury bedding brand [Brooklinen](https://www.brooklinen.com/) shares a humorous post about a dog that doesn’t want to get out of its comfortable bed.

#### Why it stands out:

Start selling your products on Facebook

Shopify comes with powerful tools that help you list, promote and sell products on Facebook. Create product collections, showcase your brand and products, and make sales on Facebook from one place.

## 2. WhatsApp (3 billion users)

Known for personal messaging, voice, and video calls, WhatsApp is also a rising business communications platform. Featuring end-to-end encryption, it’s ideal for connectivity via Wi-Fi or local data without traditional, costly SMS services.

For global businesses or those serving global customers, WhatsApp’s free, internet-based messaging and voice/video calls eliminate expensive roaming charges.

According to WhatsApp’s 2026 report, The State of Business Messaging, [73.3%](https://business.whatsapp.com/resources/resource-library/state-of-business-messaging) of adults prefer to communicate with businesses through messages, making WhatsApp’s conversational aspect useful for [customer service](/blog/what-is-customer-service). Glove brand [T1tan](https://t1tan.com/), for example, encourages customers to reach out via various channels, including WhatsApp, with questions.

![Glove brand T1tan’s contact us options for consumers.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/T1tan.png?v=1776348253)

#### Why it stands out:

## 3. Instagram (3 billion users)

Instagram initially [found its niche](/blog/6187532-dont-follow-your-passion-a-smarter-way-to-find-a-product-to-sell) as a home for visuals—both users’ photos and brands with a strong visual component, like fashion, beauty, or travel—versus status updates or an online bulletin board. Since then, it’s become known as the go-to platform for brands and [influencers](/enterprise/blog/influencer-marketing-strategy) connecting with the 25-to-34 crowd—its [largest US demographic](https://www.statista.com/statistics/398166/us-instagram-user-age-distribution/).

To stay fresh, Instagram introduces new updates regularly. For example, in 2026, it let creators reorganize their carousel images and added new effects for videos. It offers [Meta AI](https://www.meta.ai/) to users to [create content](/blog/what-is-content-creation) for their Instagram accounts.

![Creators can use Meta AI to ask questions or create content.](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0070/7032/files/meta_AI.png?v=1776349565)

Clothing brand [Alex Mill](https://www.alexmill.com/) saw success with [influencer marketing](/blog/influencer-marketing) on Instagram. When founder Alex Drexler started the company, there weren’t enough resources to dedicate to different platforms.

“We had to sort of pick and choose,” Alex says on *[Shopify Masters](/blog/alex-mill-following)*. “One of the most successful places has been Instagram. The brand has developed a cult following. We reach out to people who are genuinely interested in mixing Alex Mill with their personal style. Whether or not they have a small number of Instagram followers or a larger number, we want to work with everyone.”

#### Why it stands out:

Start selling your products on Instagram

Shopify comes with powerful tools that help you list, promote and sell products on Instagram. Create product collections, showcase your brand and products, and make sales on Instagram from one place.

## 4. YouTube (2.58 billion users)

Launched in 2005, [YouTube](/blog/youtube-marketing) combines social media with video streaming. According to [Nielsen](https://www.nielsen.com/data-center/the-gauge/), the platform is the top streaming service in the US, accounting for 12.5% of TV viewing. It’s also the second largest search engine, trailing only its parent company Google.

YouTube’s long-form videos are an opportunity for brands to educate audiences about their [products or services](/blog/products-and-services). Take [Luxy Hair](/blog/10908445-how-luxyhair-com-built-a-seven-figure-ecommerce-business-with-youtube-marketing): The brand grew its YouTube audience through [educational content](/blog/customer-education), such as tutorials showing viewers how to wear its [hair extensions](/za/sell/hair-extensions) and keep hair healthy.

Mimi Ikonn, the cofounder of Luxy Hair who now runs journal brand [Intelligent Change](https://www.intelligentchange.com/), grew a community on YouTube by showing different hairstyles. She believes that to be successful on the platform, you need to show that you genuinely care about the topic.

“When people tell me they want to go on YouTube, I say, ‘It’s never too late as long as it’s a topic that you’re really interested in,’” she says on *[Shopify Masters](/blog/mimi-ikonn-grow-a-youtube-channel)*. “If you can simplify it, people will watch and they will engage with that content.”

YouTube also offers YouTube Shorts, generally 15 seconds to three minutes long and vertical, making them ideal for phone screens. They’re an opportunity to get in front of new audiences and potentially, [go viral on YouTube](/blog/go-viral-on-youtube).

#### Why it stands out:

Start selling your products on YouTube from Shopify

Shopify comes with powerful tools that help you promote and sell products on YouTube. Sync your product catalog, tag or pin products in livestreams, and manage all your sales from Shopify.

## 5. TikTok (1.99 billion users)

[TikTok](/blog/what-is-tiktok) has captured the attention of [18- to 34-year-olds](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1299771/tiktok-global-user-age-distribution/) (its largest demographic) with its swipeable videos and a [For You page](/blog/tiktok-algorithm) that continually surfaces new, relevant content.

When [SadieB](https://sadieb.co/) founders and sisters Sadie and Abby Bowler [started the hair-care business](/blog/how-to-start-a-beauty-business), they knew that TikTok would be the best way to [market to Gen Z](/blog/how-to-market-to-gen-z). They used [micro-influencers](/blog/micro-influencer) to [build their community](/blog/building-community) on TikTok.

“We reached out to micro-influencers with about 2,000 to 5,000 followers on TikTok that just represent the SadieB core values and sent them all products,” Sadie says on *[Shopify Masters](/blog/sadieb-mentorship-in-the-beauty-industry)*. “We sent about 65 packages and have just seen this community grow because it came from such a genuine place. We’re getting tagged in these videos where these girls are just raving about SadieB—as they unbox the product—and how much they feel SadieB cares about them.”

Since launching [TikTok Shop](/blog/tiktok-shopping) in 2023, the app has opened up new direct selling opportunities for entrepreneurs.

#### Why it stands out:

## 6. WeChat (1.41 billion users)

In China, [WeChat](/blog/sell-on-wechat) combines social networking, instant messaging, payments and ecommerce. Global brands targeting Chinese customers can set up a store on the superapp.

Ecommerce is central to WeChat—[61%](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1483254/china-wechat-channels-users-purchase-intention/) of WeChat Channel users have made a purchase, and 87% say they’ll shop there again.

MìLà used WeChat to help launch their business. The [direct-to-consumer](/blog/what-is-direct-to-consumer) dumpling and noodle brand started as a restaurant. When it had to shut down for a few weeks, cofounders Jen Liao and Caleb Wang tried to come up with ways to pivot and landed on selling frozen soup dumplings.

Jen’s mom created a WeChat group and invited her friends and their friends. Because many of them accepted, Jen and Caleb felt the group was big enough to give significant [feedback](/blog/customer-feedback). They sent the group a Google Form, where they could learn more about the product.

#### Why it stands out:

## 7. Telegram (1 billion users)

Russian-founded, Dubai-based Telegram is a social media and communication platform. It’s popular for personal and group communications, and for broadcasting messages to up to 200,0000 members.

Telegram is more than a messaging app; ecommerce stores can send push messages to customers, set up customer service chat functions, and sell physical and digital products directly via mini-apps and bots.

In 2025, [India](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1336855/telegram-downloads-by-country/?srsltid=AfmBOoq5iaBiBzdaZSSnGK6vq7T9CWkO-Vb3K3IfP5pgiY4cxkepvm1k) led in the most app downloads of Telegram, followed by Russia and the United States.

#### Why it stands out:

## 8. Messenger (942 million users)

Messenger, formerly known as Facebook Messenger, is a messaging platform used for personal conversations. Because Meta owns it, brands can tap into one of the most popular social media ecosystems. In the US, Messenger leads among [25- to 34-year-olds](https://www.statista.com/statistics/951142/facebook-messenger-user-share-in-usa-age/).

Brands can use Messenger to talk to customers through [chatbots](/blog/why-conversational-commerce-isn-t-all-about-bots) or live [customer service](/blog/customer-service), or to sell products and accept payments.

#### Why it stands out:

## 9. Snapchat (932 million users)

[Snapchat](/blog/75307013-snapchat-marketing-the-key-to-discovering-and-engaging-your-most-loyal-fans) launched in 2011 as a way for users to send each other photos and messages that disappear shortly after viewing. The app gained popularity among school-age kids who were drawn in part to the ability to use Snapchat on non-smartphone devices (like the iPod Touch).

Snapchat remains popular with younger users, with ads on its platform reaching [75% of 13- to 34-year-olds](https://forbusiness.snapchat.com/) in more than 25 countries.

#### Why it stands out:

## 10. Reddit (765 million users)

Reddit is a social media network built on niche community forums called subreddits. Each subreddit is dedicated to specific industries, topics, and interests.

Unlike other platforms that surface content based on an algorithm, Reddit users (known as Redditors) upvote topics to help spread their reach. (Users can also downvote content they think is irrelevant.)

Some Redditors use the platform to learn more about products. In a February 2026 survey, [84% of shoppers](https://redditinc.com/news/introducing-more-ways-to-tap-into-shopping-on-reddit) said they felt more secure in their purchases after researching products on Reddit.

Reddit has multiple advertising formats, and the platform is currently testing “Redditors Top Pick” overlays that can indicate a product is already popular with their audience.

Some brands form organic connections with Redditors. For example, [Sock Candy](/blog/sock-candy-reddit-and-creative-marketing-tips) founder Mary Gui posted daily outfits as herself instead of her brand on Reddit. When people ask where her socks are from, she lets them know about Sock Candy.

#### Why it stands out:

This Shopify article ranks the world's most popular social media platforms by monthly active users as of October 2025 and explains why each stands out for brands. The rankings are: 1) Facebook (3.07 billion), 2) WhatsApp (3 billion), 3) Instagram (3 billion), 4) YouTube (2.58 billion), 5) TikTok (1.99 billion), 6) WeChat (1.41 billion), 7) Telegram (1 billion), 8) Messenger (942 million), 9) Snapchat (932 million), and 10) Reddit (765 million).

Key highlights per platform: Facebook is the top platform with its largest US demographic being 25-34 year olds (24.2%), and Reels is its most engaging format. WhatsApp grew rapidly from February to October 2025, overtaking YouTube, and features end-to-end encryption; 73.3% of adults prefer messaging businesses. Instagram is the go-to for brands and influencers connecting with the 25-34 crowd, and now offers Meta AI for content creation. YouTube is the top US streaming service (12.5% of TV viewing) and second largest search engine, with long-form educational content and Shorts opportunities. TikTok captures 18-34 year olds and offers TikTok Shop for direct selling since 2023. WeChat combines social networking, payments and ecommerce in China, where 61% of channel users have made purchases. Telegram supports ecommerce via mini-apps and bots, and had its most downloads from India in 2025. Messenger (Meta-owned) supports chatbots and payments. Snapchat reaches 75% of 13-34 year olds in 25+ countries. Reddit uses upvoting instead of algorithmic content and had 84% of shoppers feeling more secure after researching products there. The article includes several real-world brand examples (Brooklinen, T1tan, Alex Mill, Luxy Hair, SadieB, MìLà, Sock Candy) and an FAQ section noting the top 5 platforms, that Facebook is No. 1, and that Gen Z favors TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat.

# 7 User Retention Metrics for Shopify Stores in 2025

Unlock growth by tracking the right user retention metrics. Our 2025 guide for Shopify merchants covers CLV, churn, NPS, and more to boost loyalty.

In the competitive world of e-commerce, acquiring a new customer is just the beginning. The real, sustainable growth for your Shopify store lies in turning those first-time buyers into loyal, repeat customers. But how do you measure loyalty? How do you know if your strategies are truly working? The answer is in the data. Before diving into specific metrics for e-commerce, it's beneficial to gain a deeper understanding of [the broader concept of retention](https://motimatic.com/retention/) and its significance. This foundation helps frame why tracking these numbers is so critical for long-term success.

By focusing on the right **user retention metrics**, you can move from guesswork to a data-driven strategy that builds a resilient brand. Vague feelings about customer happiness won't cut it; you need concrete numbers to pinpoint what's working and what needs immediate attention. This guide eliminates the noise and breaks down the seven most critical metrics every Shopify merchant needs to track. We'll provide clear definitions, simple formulas, industry benchmarks, and actionable steps you can take, especially using tools like Toki, to not just measure but actively improve customer loyalty. Let's transform your analytics from a confusing spreadsheet into a powerful roadmap for growth.

## 1. Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)

Customer Lifetime Value (CLV or LTV) is the keystone of user retention metrics, representing the total net profit a business can reasonably expect from a single customer throughout their entire relationship with the brand. It shifts the focus from short-term gains, like a single transaction, to the long-term health and profitability of your customer base. By understanding what a customer is worth over time, you can make smarter decisions about marketing spend, product development, and customer service investments.

This metric is foundational because it directly connects retention efforts to revenue. A high CLV signifies a loyal, engaged customer base that repeatedly chooses your Shopify store over competitors, highlighting the success of your retention strategies.

### How to Calculate CLV

While several formulas exist, a straightforward method for Shopify merchants is:

**CLV = Average Purchase Value x Average Purchase Frequency Rate x Average Customer Lifespan**

For example, if your average customer spends $75 per order, makes 3 purchases a year, and stays with your brand for 2 years, their historical CLV is $450 ($75 x 3 x 2). Toki can help you easily surface the data points needed for this calculation, like purchase frequency and order value, directly from your Shopify data.

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing CLV

Improving CLV is a direct result of enhancing the customer experience and encouraging repeat business. Here’s how to put this metric into action:

* **Segment Your Customers:** Don't treat all customers the same. Use Toki to segment your audience by CLV. Identify your "VIPs" (high CLV) and create exclusive loyalty tiers or personalized offers to nurture them. For low-CLV segments, deploy re-engagement campaigns or targeted discounts to encourage their next purchase.
* **Set Your Acquisition Budget:** Your CLV provides a clear ceiling for your Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC). A common rule of thumb is to keep your CAC to CLV ratio at 1:3 or better, meaning a customer should be worth at least three times what you paid to acquire them.
* **Inform Product Strategy:** Analyze the purchasing habits of your highest CLV customers. What products do they buy together? What categories do they frequent? Use these insights to create product bundles, inform new product development, and refine your upselling and cross-selling strategies at checkout.

## 2. Churn Rate

Churn Rate is the direct antagonist to retention, measuring the percentage of customers who stop doing business with you over a specific period. It is one of the most critical user retention metrics because it acts as a health monitor for your customer relationships. A high churn rate is a red flag, indicating potential problems with your product, pricing, customer service, or overall user experience that are driving customers away.

This metric is vital for any business, but especially for subscription models common on Shopify. It quantifies customer attrition, forcing you to look inward and address the root causes of why customers leave. Effectively managing churn is essential for sustainable growth, as it's far more cost-effective to keep an existing customer than to acquire a new one.

### How to Calculate Churn Rate

The formula is a straightforward percentage calculation:

**Churn Rate = (Customers Lost During Period / Total Customers at Start of Period) x 100**

For instance, if you started the month with 1,000 customers and lost 50 by the end of the month, your monthly churn rate would be 5% ([50 / 1,000] x 100). For non-subscription stores, "churn" can be defined as a customer not making a repeat purchase within an expected timeframe (e.g., 90 days).

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing Churn Rate

Reducing churn involves proactively improving the customer journey and identifying at-risk customers before they leave. Here’s how to put this metric into action:

* **Segment Your Churn:** Not all churn is equal. Use a tool like Toki to differentiate between **voluntary churn** (customers actively choosing to leave) and **involuntary churn** (e.g., failed payments). Analyze churn by acquisition channel, first product purchased, or customer segment to pinpoint specific problem areas.
* **Implement Early Warning Systems:** Monitor customer behavior for signs of disengagement, such as a drop in purchase frequency or a long period since their last visit. Create automated re-engagement campaigns in Toki that trigger based on these behaviors, offering a personalized incentive to return.
* **Gather Feedback at the Source:** When a customer does churn, use an exit survey to understand why. Was it the price, product quality, or a poor support experience? Use this direct feedback to make meaningful improvements that will prevent future customers from leaving for the same reasons. For a deeper dive into this process, explore our complete guide on [customer churn analysis](https://www.buildwithtoki.com/blog-post/customer-churn-analysis).

## 3. Net Promoter Score (NPS)

Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a powerful metric that gauges customer loyalty and satisfaction by asking one simple, ultimate question: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend our brand/product to a friend or colleague?" This metric provides a clear, quantitative score that reflects your customers' overall sentiment and their potential to act as brand advocates, making it a critical component of any user retention metrics toolkit.

Based on their responses, customers are segmented into three categories: **Promoters** (score 9-10), who are loyal enthusiasts; **Passives** (score 7-8), who are satisfied but unenthusiastic; and **Detractors** (score 0-6), who are unhappy customers that can damage your brand. A high NPS indicates a healthy, loyal customer base primed for long-term retention.

### How to Calculate NPS

The calculation is straightforward and results in a score ranging from -100 to +100.

**NPS = % of Promoters - % of Detractors**

For example, if you survey 100 customers and find that 50 are Promoters (50%), 30 are Passives, and 20 are Detractors (20%), your NPS would be 30 (50% - 20%). Using Toki, you can trigger NPS surveys at key moments in the customer journey, like post-purchase or after a customer support interaction, to gather this crucial feedback.

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing NPS

Improving your NPS is about actively listening to feedback and closing the loop to enhance the customer experience. Here’s how to put this metric into action:

* **Follow Up with Open-Ended Questions:** The score is just the beginning. Always follow the rating question with a qualitative question like, "What is the primary reason for your score?" This gives you actionable insights into what you're doing right (from Promoters) and what needs fixing (from Detractors).
* **Close the Loop with Detractors:** Act fast. Reach out to Detractors personally to understand their issues and offer a resolution. This immediate action can sometimes turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one and provides invaluable feedback to prevent future issues.
* **Leverage Your Promoters:** Mobilize your biggest fans. Use Toki to segment your Promoters and invite them to your referral or loyalty programs. Encourage them to leave reviews or share user-generated content, turning their positive sentiment into powerful social proof that drives new customer acquisition.
* **Track Trends, Not Just Scores:** A single NPS score is a snapshot. The real value comes from tracking your score over time. Analyzing trends helps you understand the impact of your product updates, marketing campaigns, and customer service initiatives on overall satisfaction. To dive deeper into this and other related methods, you can [learn more about customer satisfaction measurement on buildwithtoki.com](https://www.buildwithtoki.com/blog-post/customer-satisfaction-measurement-methods).

## 4. Cohort Retention Rate

Cohort Retention Rate is a powerful diagnostic tool that groups users into "cohorts" based on a shared characteristic, most commonly their sign-up or first purchase date. It then tracks what percentage of each cohort returns over time. Instead of looking at overall retention, which can be misleading, cohort analysis isolates the behavior of specific user groups, providing a much clearer picture of your product's long-term stickiness and the impact of your marketing or product changes.

This metric is essential for understanding how user behavior evolves. For example, you can see if customers acquired during a big holiday sale behave differently than those acquired organically a month later. It's one of the most revealing user retention metrics because it moves beyond a single, blended number to tell a story about your customer lifecycle.

### How to Calculate Cohort Retention Rate

The calculation involves tracking a group of users over a set period.

**Cohort Retention Rate = (Number of users from cohort still active in Period N / Total users in cohort) x 100**

For instance, if you acquired 1,000 new customers in January (your cohort) and 150 of them made another purchase in March (Period N = 3 months later), your Month 3 retention for the January cohort is 15%. Toki can help you segment customers by their acquisition date, making it simple to pull the data needed for this analysis directly from your Shopify store.

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing Cohort Retention

Using cohort analysis effectively means turning observations into strategic actions. Here’s how to leverage this metric for growth:

* **Pinpoint Onboarding Issues:** Compare the early retention rates (Day 1, Day 7, Day 30) of different weekly or monthly cohorts. A sudden drop-off in a new cohort might signal a problem with a recent app update, a confusing new feature, or a flawed onboarding email sequence that needs immediate attention.
* **Validate Product Improvements:** Did you launch a new loyalty program or improve your site's checkout flow in March? By comparing the retention curve of the March cohort against the February and January cohorts, you can get clear, data-backed validation on whether your changes positively impacted long-term customer engagement.
* **Optimize Acquisition Channels:** Analyze and compare cohorts based on their acquisition source (e.g., Facebook Ads, Google Search, TikTok). You may find that customers from one channel have a significantly higher long-term retention rate, indicating you should double down on that channel and adjust your spending on underperforming ones.

## 5. Product Stickiness (DAU/MAU Ratio)

Product Stickiness is a powerful user retention metric that reveals how frequently your customers return and engage with your brand. Calculated as the ratio of Daily Active Users (DAU) to Monthly Active Users (MAU), it measures how many of your monthly customers interact with your store or app on a daily basis. It’s a direct indicator of habit formation and shows how integral your brand is becoming to a user's routine.

Unlike metrics that just count monthly visits, stickiness provides a deeper understanding of engagement quality. A high stickiness ratio signifies that you've created a compelling experience that draws customers back consistently, not just when they need to make a purchase. This is crucial for building a loyal community around your Shopify store.

### How to Calculate Product Stickiness

The formula is straightforward and focuses on active engagement:

**Product Stickiness = (Daily Active Users / Monthly Active Users) x 100%**

For example, if you had 5,000 unique customers visit your store in a month (MAU) and an average of 1,250 of those customers visited each day (DAU), your stickiness ratio would be 25% (1,250 / 5,000). A ratio above 20% is considered good, while platforms like Facebook often exceed 50%, indicating exceptional daily value.

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing Product Stickiness

Improving stickiness means giving customers a reason to visit your store even when they aren't planning an immediate purchase. Here’s how to put this metric into action:

* **Create Engaging, Non-Transactional Content:** Don't limit your store to just product pages. Add a blog with valuable industry insights, publish "how-to" guides related to your products, or run weekly polls and quizzes. This content gives users a reason to check in daily, boosting your DAU and building a community.
* **Leverage Push Notifications and Email for Daily Value:** Use tools like Toki to send timely, relevant notifications about more than just sales. Announce new blog posts, share user-generated content, or offer a "deal of the day" to create a daily engagement habit. The goal is to provide value, not just a sales pitch.
* **Identify Your Stickiest Features:** Analyze user behavior to see what brings people back. Is it your loyalty program dashboard, a specific product category they browse, or your customer reviews section? Double down on what works by making these features more prominent and easier to access, encouraging the daily check-in behavior that drives a high stickiness score.

## 6. Revenue Retention Rate

Revenue Retention Rate goes beyond counting customers and focuses directly on the money. It measures the percentage of recurring revenue you keep from existing customers over a specific period, factoring in revenue changes from upgrades, downgrades, and cancellations. This makes it one of the most powerful user retention metrics for subscription-based Shopify stores.

Unlike metrics that only track customer counts, revenue retention shows the financial impact of your customer relationships. A rate over 100%, known as Net Revenue Retention (NRR), indicates that revenue growth from existing customers (upsells and cross-sells) is outpacing revenue lost from churn and downgrades. This is a clear sign of a healthy, scalable business model.

### How to Calculate Revenue Retention Rate

There are two primary ways to calculate this, each telling a different story:

**Net Revenue Retention (NRR) = ((Starting MRR + Expansion MRR - Churn MRR - Contraction MRR) / Starting MRR) x 100**

**Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) = ((Starting MRR - Churn MRR - Contraction MRR) / Starting MRR) x 100**

For example, if you start a month with $10,000 in Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR), gain $1,500 from upgrades (Expansion), lose $500 from downgrades (Contraction), and lose $1,000 from cancellations (Churn), your NRR is 100% (($10,000 + $1,500 - $500 - $1,000) / $10,000). Your GRR, which ignores the expansion, would be 85%.

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing Revenue Retention

Improving this metric means focusing on both keeping customers and increasing their value over time.

* **Track Both Gross and Net Rates:** Use Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) to measure your baseline ability to retain customers and their initial revenue. Use Net Revenue Retention (NRR) to evaluate the success of your upselling and cross-selling initiatives. A high NRR with a low GRR might hide a serious churn problem.
* **Focus on Expansion Revenue:** Identify opportunities to upgrade customers. Use Toki to segment customers on lower-tier subscription plans and create targeted campaigns showcasing the benefits of higher tiers. Offer add-on products or services that complement their existing subscriptions to boost their spending.
* **Guide Customer Success Investments:** Analyze revenue retention by customer cohort or plan type. If enterprise-level subscribers have a very high retention rate, it justifies investing more in dedicated account managers or premium support for that segment to protect and grow that stable revenue stream.

## 7. Customer Health Score

Customer Health Score is a predictive, composite metric that moves beyond single data points to give you a holistic view of a customer's relationship with your brand. It combines multiple indicators, such as purchase frequency, support interactions, and engagement with your marketing, into a single, actionable score. This score helps you proactively identify customers who are highly engaged and loyal, as well as those who are at risk of churning, long before they actually leave.

Unlike reactive metrics that measure past events (like churn), a health score is a forward-looking tool. For a Shopify merchant, this could mean flagging a previously loyal customer whose purchase cadence has suddenly dropped, allowing you to intervene with a personalized outreach before they are lost for good.

### How to Calculate Customer Health Score

A Customer Health Score is unique to each business, as it's built from the specific actions that correlate with retention for your brand. There isn't a universal formula, but a common approach is to assign weighted points to key customer behaviors.

**Example Health Score Model for an E-commerce Store:**

* **Purchase Recency:** (e.g., +20 points for a purchase in the last 30 days, -10 for no purchase in 90 days)
* **Purchase Frequency:** (e.g., +15 points for >3 lifetime purchases)
* **Email Engagement:** (e.g., +5 points for high open/click rates)
* **Customer Support Tickets:** (e.g., -5 points for a recent negative interaction)

Using a platform like Toki, you can track these underlying data points to build your own custom scoring model. The goal is to create a score (e.g., out of 100) that segments customers into categories like "Healthy," "At-Risk," and "Poor."

### Actionable Tips for Optimizing with Customer Health Score

A health score is only valuable if you act on it. It’s a powerful tool for prioritizing your customer success and marketing efforts.

* **Automate Proactive Outreach:** Set up automated workflows based on health score changes. If a "Healthy" customer drops into the "At-Risk" category, trigger an automated email from your support team asking for feedback or offering a special incentive. This shows you're paying attention.
* **Refine Your Segmentation:** Use health scores as a primary segmentation tool. Target your best marketing campaigns, new product announcements, and loyalty program perks to your "Healthy" segment. For "At-Risk" customers, deploy targeted win-back campaigns focused on addressing potential issues.
* **Validate and Iterate Your Model:** Your first health score model won't be perfect. Regularly check if your scores are accurately predicting churn. Did the customers who churned last quarter have low scores? Use this feedback to adjust the weights and actions included in your calculation. To get started, you can learn more about the specific inputs needed by diving into [customer behavior analytics](https://www.buildwithtoki.com/blog-post/customer-behavior-analytics).

## User Retention Metrics Comparison Table

| Metric | Implementation Complexity 🔄 | Resource Requirements ⚡ | Expected Outcomes 📊 | Ideal Use Cases 💡 | Key Advantages ⭐ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) | Medium to High - requires data integration and predictive modeling | Moderate - historical purchase and behavior data | Long-term revenue prediction and customer segmentation | Businesses focusing on retention & acquisition budgeting | Justifies acquisition costs; guides pricing and development |
| Churn Rate | Low - simple formula, easy tracking | Low - basic customer count data | Immediate insights into customer loss trends | Subscription/non-subscription businesses monitoring retention health | Easy to calculate and benchmark; highlights satisfaction issues |
| Net Promoter Score (NPS) | Low - single question survey implementation | Low - survey distribution and analysis | Customer loyalty score with segmentation potential | Measuring customer satisfaction and loyalty | Simple, standardized, predictive of growth; qualitative feedback |
| Cohort Retention Rate | High - requires advanced tracking and cohort analysis | High - historical data with segmentation | Reveals retention patterns and product impact over time | Product analytics and onboarding effectiveness evaluation | Shows true retention trends; actionable for product improvements |
| Product Stickiness (DAU/MAU) Ratio | Low to Medium - requires engagement data tracking | Moderate - standard user activity metrics | Measures habitual usage and engagement consistency | Assessing product-market fit and daily engagement | Simple metric; predicts long-term retention; compares features |
| Revenue Retention Rate | High - complex revenue tracking, multiple pricing tiers | High - detailed revenue and customer account data | Direct measurement of revenue growth and retention | Subscription businesses focusing on financial retention impact | Links retention to revenue growth; captures upsell and expansion |
| Customer Health Score | High - composite metric with multiple data inputs | High - data infrastructure and modeling needed | Predictive identification of at-risk customers | Proactive customer success and risk mitigation | Holistic view; automates alerting and prioritization; predictive |

## From Metrics to Momentum: Building a Retention-Powered Brand

Navigating the landscape of e-commerce growth requires more than just attracting new customers; it demands a deep, strategic focus on keeping the ones you have. Throughout this guide, we've dissected seven critical **user retention metrics** that serve as your brand's vital signs. From the financial forecasting power of Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) to the raw sentiment captured by Net Promoter Score (NPS), each metric provides a unique piece of the puzzle.

You've learned how to calculate Churn Rate to plug leaks in your customer base and how Cohort Retention reveals the long-term impact of your onboarding and product changes. We explored how Product Stickiness (DAU/MAU) measures daily engagement, Revenue Retention Rate highlights your financial health among existing customers, and a holistic Customer Health Score predicts future behavior before it happens. These aren't just abstract numbers; they are direct reflections of your customer experience.

### Turning Insights into Actionable Strategy

The true power of these metrics is unlocked when they are used not in isolation, but as an interconnected system. Think of them as a diagnostic dashboard for your business.

* A **low NPS** from a **high-CLV segment** is a critical red flag, signaling that your most valuable customers are unhappy. This is a direct mandate to engage that segment immediately with personalized outreach or exclusive perks.
* A **declining Cohort Retention Rate** points to a potential issue in your post-purchase experience. Is your shipping communication clear? Is the unboxing experience memorable? Is your day-30 follow-up email effective?
* A **high Churn Rate** paired with **low Product Stickiness** suggests your product or store experience isn't compelling enough for daily or weekly engagement. This is where gamification, loyalty points, or community features can transform passive buyers into active participants.

By weaving these data points together, you move from reactive problem-solving to proactive brand-building. You stop guessing what customers want and start responding to what their actions and feedback are telling you. This data-driven approach allows you to invest your resources with precision, focusing on the initiatives that will have the greatest impact on loyalty and repeat purchases.

Ultimately, mastering **user retention metrics** is about more than just improving your KPIs. It's about building a resilient, profitable brand that fosters genuine relationships. It's about creating a community of advocates who don't just buy from you but believe in you. Use these metrics as your guide, and you will transform your store from a simple transactional platform into a destination your customers are proud to return to again and again.
